docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A complete first course in financial accounting for readers with no background in the subject. It explains the purpose and users of accounting, the concepts, conventions and standards behind it (with how IFRS and Ind AS fit in), the accounting equation and double entry, the journal, ledger and trial balance, subsidiary books and the cash book, bank reconciliation, bills of exchange, rectification of errors, depreciation, provisions and reserves, and then builds up to the final accounts of a sole proprietor, a non-profit organisation, a partnership and a company. The last chapters cover the cash flow statement, ratio analysis, accounting software and ethics. Every chapter has fully worked examples in rupees laid out as journals, ledgers and statements, exercises with answers and a quiz.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Accounting, Its Users and Its Framework
docs.text:
What accounting is for, who relies on it, and the rules that make it trustworthy

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define accounting and distinguish it from bookkeeping.
  2. Name the main users of accounting information and the question each one asks.
  3. Explain the basic terms of accounting: asset, liability, capital, revenue, expense, drawings and the rest.
  4. Distinguish the cash basis from the accrual basis and compute profit on each.
  5. State and apply the main accounting concepts and conventions.
  6. Describe the qualitative characteristics of useful financial information.
  7. Explain, in general terms, what accounting standards are and how IFRS and Ind AS fit together.

docs.title: 1.1 What accounting is
docs.text:
Every business makes hundreds of small exchanges: it buys goods, sells them, pays wages, borrows money, collects from customers. Each exchange on its own is easy to understand. Taken together, they are impossible to grasp unless someone records them, sorts them and adds them up. That is the work of accounting.

A widely used definition describes accounting as the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating economic information about an organisation, so that the people who use the information can make informed judgements and decisions. Each word in that definition matters:

  • Identifying. Deciding which events are economic transactions of the business. A sale is; a friendly chat with a customer is not.
  • Measuring. Expressing the transaction in money. Accounting records only what can be measured in money.
  • Recording. Writing the transaction down, in date order, in the books of the business.
  • Classifying. Grouping similar transactions together (all sales in one place, all rent payments in another).
  • Summarising. Condensing the classified records into a small number of reports: the financial statements.
  • Analysing and interpreting. Drawing meaning from the reports: is the business profitable, is it safe, is it improving?
  • Communicating. Presenting the results to the people who need them, in a form they can understand.

docs.title: Bookkeeping and accounting
docs.text:
Bookkeeping is the recording part of the process: writing up the journal, posting the ledger, keeping the cash book. It is routine and follows fixed rules. Accounting includes bookkeeping and goes further: it decides how transactions should be measured and classified, prepares the financial statements, and interprets them. A bookkeeper records that a machine was bought; an accountant decides how much of its cost should be charged as depreciation this year.

Key idea

Bookkeeping records; accounting records, summarises, interprets and communicates. Bookkeeping is the foundation on which accounting is built, so an error in the books is carried into every report built on them.

docs.text:
The work of a year follows a regular cycle, which the chapters of this book follow too.

Step What is done Where it is learned 1 A transaction occurs and a source document (invoice, receipt, cheque) is prepared Chapter 3 2 The transaction is recorded in a book of original entry (journal, cash book, sales book) Chapters 3 and 4 3 The entries are posted to accounts in the ledger Chapter 3 4 The accounts are balanced and a trial balance is prepared Chapter 3 5 Errors are corrected and year-end adjustments are made Chapters 6 and 7 6 Financial statements are prepared Chapters 8 to 12 7 The statements are analysed and interpreted Chapter 13

docs.title: 1.2 The purpose of accounting and its limits
docs.text:
Accounting exists because people need to make decisions about organisations they cannot see into directly. Its main purposes are:

  1. To keep a systematic record of every transaction, so that nothing is forgotten and the business does not rely on memory.
  2. To find the profit or loss of a period, by comparing the revenue earned with the expenses incurred to earn it.
  3. To show the financial position at a date: what the business owns (its assets) and what it owes (its liabilities), and the owner's interest in it.
  4. To provide information to users inside and outside the business, so that they can make decisions.
  5. To protect the property of the business, by recording what it owns and owes, so that losses and fraud are noticed.
  6. To meet legal requirements. Companies, and many other businesses, are required by law to keep books and to publish or file financial statements; tax returns are based on accounting records.

Accounting also has limits, which a careful reader should keep in mind:

  • It records only what can be measured in money. The skill of the workforce, the loyalty of customers and the reputation of the business are important but do not appear in the accounts (unless bought, as goodwill).
  • It is largely historical. Most assets are shown at what they cost, not at what they are worth today. In times of rising prices, cost may be far below current value.
  • It involves estimates and judgement. The useful life of a machine, the part of debtors that will never pay, the value of unsold goods: all are estimates.
  • It can be manipulated. Within the rules there is room for choice, and a dishonest preparer can present a misleading picture. Accounting standards, audit and ethics (Chapter 14) exist to limit this.

docs.title: 1.3 The users of accounting information
docs.text:
Many different people rely on the same financial statements, each looking for an answer to a different question. They are usually divided into internal users, who run the business, and external users, who deal with it from outside.

Figure 1.1 Users of accounting information. Internal users (owners, managers, employees, partners and directors) and external users (investors, lenders, suppliers, customers, government and the public) all draw on the same financial statements. User Main question What they look at Owner of a small business Is the business earning enough to be worth my time and money? Profit, capital, drawings Managers Which products, branches or costs need attention? Detailed revenue and cost figures, budgets Employees and their unions Is the business stable, and can it afford better pay? Profitability, growth, job security Investors and shareholders Should I buy, hold or sell my investment? Profit, return on investment, dividends, growth Lenders and banks Will the loan and its interest be repaid on time? Cash flow, liquidity, security, debt level Suppliers Will I be paid for goods supplied on credit? Liquidity, payment record Customers Will the business survive to honour its guarantees and keep supplying? Stability, continuity Government and tax authorities How much tax is due? Are the laws being followed? Taxable income, statutory returns Researchers and the public How does the business affect the economy and society? Overall results, disclosures

Table 1.2. Users of accounting information and their questions.

Because so many users depend on the same statements, those statements are prepared according to common rules, so that a lender in one city and an investor in another read them in the same way. Those common rules are the subject of the rest of this chapter.

docs.title: 1.4 Branches of accounting
docs.text:
Accounting has grown into several branches, each serving a different need.

  • Financial accounting records the transactions of the business and prepares the general-purpose financial statements for external users. It is the subject of this book.
  • Cost accounting finds the cost of each product, job or process, so that prices can be set and costs controlled.
  • Management accounting provides information to managers for planning, control and decision-making: budgets, forecasts and the analysis of alternatives.
  • Tax accounting prepares the computations and returns required by tax law, which has its own rules that often differ from the rules of financial accounting.
  • Auditing is the independent examination of financial statements, so that users can trust them.
  • Social and environmental reporting describes the effect of the business on employees, society and the environment.

Financial accounting looks mainly backwards and reports to outsiders in a standard form; management accounting looks mainly forwards and reports to insiders in whatever form is useful.

docs.title: 1.5 The basic terms
docs.text:
A small set of terms is used throughout the book. They are summarised here and developed in later chapters.

Term Meaning Example Transaction An exchange or event, measurable in money, that changes the financial position of the business Buying goods, paying rent Capital The amount invested in the business by the owner; the owner's claim on the business Cash of ₹2,00,000 brought in by the owner Drawings Money or goods taken out of the business by the owner for personal use The owner takes ₹5,000 for household expenses Assets Resources owned or controlled by the business, from which it expects future benefits Cash, bank balance, inventory, debtors, furniture, machinery Liabilities Amounts the business owes to outsiders Creditors, bank loans, outstanding expenses Revenue Amounts earned by the business from its ordinary activities Sales, commission received, interest earned Expenses Costs incurred in earning revenue Rent, wages, salaries, electricity Income Revenue and gains taken together; also used loosely for profit Sales plus a gain on the sale of an old asset Profit or loss The excess of revenue over expenses (profit) or of expenses over revenue (loss) for a period Revenue ₹5,00,000, expenses ₹4,20,000: profit ₹80,000 Goods The things a business buys in order to sell them Shirts in a clothing shop Purchases Goods bought for resale, for cash or on credit Shirts bought from a manufacturer Sales Goods sold, for cash or on credit Shirts sold to customers Inventory (stock) Goods held for sale at a date Unsold shirts at 31 March Debtors (trade receivables) Persons who owe money to the business, usually for goods sold on credit A customer who has not yet paid Creditors (trade payables) Persons to whom the business owes money, usually for goods bought on credit A supplier not yet paid

Table 1.3. The basic terms of accounting.

Caution

Purchases means goods bought for resale only. When a clothing shop buys a computer for its office, that is the purchase of an asset, not "purchases". The same computer bought by a computer dealer to sell is purchases. What counts as goods depends on the business.

docs.title: Capital and revenue items
docs.text: Spending that brings benefit for more than one year (buying a machine, a building, a vehicle) is capital expenditure: it creates an asset. Spending whose benefit is used up within the year (wages, rent, repairs) is revenue expenditure: it is an expense of the year. The same distinction applies to receipts: the sale proceeds of an old machine are a capital receipt, while the proceeds of selling goods are a revenue receipt. Getting this distinction wrong changes the profit, as Chapter 6 shows.

docs.title: 1.6 The cash basis and the accrual basis
docs.text:
When should a sale or an expense be recorded: when the cash moves, or when the sale is made and the expense is incurred? There are two answers, and they give different profits.

  • Under the cash basis, revenue is recorded when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid.
  • Under the accrual basis, revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash has moved.

The accrual basis gives a truer picture of the performance of a period, because it matches what was earned in the period with what was spent to earn it. Financial statements prepared under accounting standards use the accrual basis. The cash basis survives in some very small organisations and in some professional practices.

Example 1.1 Profit on the cash basis and on the accrual basis

During March, a small trading business:

  • sold goods for ₹80,000, of which ₹60,000 was received in cash and ₹20,000 was still owed by customers at the end of the month;
  • received ₹5,000 from a customer for goods sold in February;
  • incurred expenses of ₹50,000, of which ₹44,000 was paid and ₹6,000 was unpaid at the end of the month;
  • paid ₹4,000 in advance as rent for April.

Cash basis. Count only the cash that moved in March.

Item ₹ Cash received from March sales 60,000 Cash received for February sales 5,000 Total receipts 65,000 Cash paid for March expenses 44,000 Rent paid in advance for April 4,000 Total payments 48,000 Profit on the cash basis (65,000 − 48,000) 17,000

Accrual basis. Count what was earned and incurred in March.

Item ₹ Sales made in March (cash and credit) 80,000 Less: Expenses incurred in March (paid and unpaid) 50,000 Profit on the accrual basis 30,000

The February receipt belongs to February's revenue and the April rent to April's expenses, so neither enters March's profit on the accrual basis.

Reconciling the two profits. The accrual profit exceeds the cash profit by 30,000 − 17,000 = ₹13,000.

Reason for the difference Effect on (accrual − cash) ₹ Credit sales not yet received: in accrual revenue only +20,000 February sale collected in March: in cash receipts only −5,000 Expenses not yet paid: in accrual expenses only −6,000 April rent paid in March: in cash payments only +4,000 Net difference +13,000

Reconciliations like the one at the end of Example 1.1 are a good habit: whenever two methods give two answers, explain the gap item by item until it is fully accounted for.

docs.title: 1.7 The accounting concepts
docs.text: Accountants around the world rely on a set of basic ideas, usually called accounting concepts, assumptions or principles. They are not laws of nature; they are agreements that make accounts consistent and comparable. The most important are described below.

docs.title: Business entity concept
docs.text:
The business is treated as separate from its owner. Its transactions are recorded from the point of view of the business, and the owner's personal transactions are kept out. When the owner brings in cash, the business owes that amount to the owner as capital. When the owner takes cash out for personal use, it is drawings, not an expense of the business.

Example 1.2 Applying the entity concept

Sunita runs a bakery. In one month the bakery's cash pays: rent of the bakery ₹12,000; electricity of the bakery ₹3,000; Sunita's household electricity bill ₹1,800; her daughter's school fees ₹6,000.

Payment ₹ Treatment in the bakery's books Rent of the bakery 12,000 Expense of the business Electricity of the bakery 3,000 Expense of the business Household electricity 1,800 Drawings School fees 6,000 Drawings

Expenses of the business are ₹15,000; drawings are ₹7,800. Treating the personal items as expenses would understate the bakery's profit by ₹7,800.

docs.title: Money measurement concept
docs.text: Only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded. The number of employees, the morale of staff or the quality of management may matter a great deal but are not recorded. A related consequence is that the value of money is assumed to be stable, so ₹1 spent ten years ago and ₹1 spent today are added together as if they were the same, which is not strictly true when prices rise.

docs.title: Going concern concept
docs.text: The business is assumed to continue in operation for the foreseeable future, with no intention or need to close down. This is why a machine is shown at cost less depreciation rather than at what it would fetch if sold tomorrow: the business means to use it, not sell it. If a business is about to close, the going concern assumption no longer holds and its assets are valued at what they would realise.

docs.title: Accounting period concept
docs.text: The life of a business is divided into equal periods, usually a year, so that results can be measured and compared regularly. Owners, lenders and the government cannot wait until a business closes to learn whether it made a profit. The accounting period is the reason year-end adjustments (Chapter 8) are needed: some revenue and expenses straddle two periods and must be divided between them.

docs.title: Historical cost concept
docs.text: Assets are recorded at the price paid to acquire them, including the costs needed to bring them into use (transport, installation). This cost is the basis for later accounting. Cost is objective and can be verified from invoices; current value is often a matter of opinion. Accounting standards do allow some assets to be measured at fair value in particular cases, but cost remains the starting point.

docs.title: Dual aspect concept
docs.text: Every transaction has two aspects, and both are recorded. When a business buys furniture for cash, it gains furniture and loses cash. When it borrows from a bank, it gains cash and gains a liability to the bank. This concept gives rise to the accounting equation (Chapter 2) and to double entry (Chapter 3).

docs.title: Revenue recognition (realisation) concept
docs.text: Revenue is recognised when it is earned, which for a sale of goods is normally when control of the goods passes to the customer, not when an order is received or when cash is collected. An order for goods to be delivered next month is not this month's revenue; goods delivered on credit this month are.

docs.title: Matching concept
docs.text: Expenses are matched with the revenue they help to earn, in the same period. If goods sold this year were bought last year, their cost is an expense of this year. If a salary for March is paid in April, it is still an expense of March. The matching concept and the accrual basis together produce the adjustments for outstanding and prepaid items studied in Chapter 8.

docs.title: Objectivity (verifiability) concept
docs.text: Accounting records should be based on objective evidence, such as invoices, receipts, cheques and contracts, so that two independent people looking at the same evidence reach the same figures.

docs.title: 1.8 The accounting conventions
docs.text: Alongside the concepts, practice has settled on a few conventions: customs that guide how the concepts are applied.

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text: Once a business has chosen an accounting method (for example a method of depreciation or of valuing inventory), it should use the same method from year to year. Otherwise a change in profit might be caused by a change of method rather than by a change in performance. A method may be changed when there is good reason, but the change and its effect must be disclosed.

docs.title: Prudence (conservatism)
docs.text:
When there is uncertainty, accountants take care not to overstate assets or income, nor to understate liabilities or expenses. The traditional statement of the convention is "anticipate no profit, but provide for all possible losses". Modern standards temper this: prudence means caution in judgement, not the deliberate creation of hidden reserves. A familiar application is the valuation of inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value (the estimated selling price less the costs needed to sell).

Example 1.3 Inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value

At 31 March a shop holds three lines of goods.

Item Cost (₹) Net realisable value (₹) Lower of the two (₹) A 12,000 15,000 12,000 B 8,000 6,500 6,500 C 5,000 5,000 5,000 Total 25,000 26,500 23,500

Inventory is shown at ₹23,500. The expected profit on item A (₹3,000) is not anticipated, but the expected loss on item B (₹1,500) is recognised now. The comparison is made item by item, not on the totals: comparing the totals (₹25,000 against ₹26,500) would hide the loss on B.

docs.title: Materiality
docs.text: An item is material if leaving it out, or misstating it, could influence the decisions of users. Material items must be shown accurately and separately; immaterial items may be treated in the simplest way. A box of pens costing ₹200 that will last two years is, strictly, an asset, but it is simply charged as an expense, because the effort of depreciating it would serve no one. Materiality depends on size and nature together: a small payment to a director may be material because of who received it.

docs.title: Full disclosure
docs.text:
The financial statements, with their notes, should disclose all information that is significant to users: the accounting policies used, contingent liabilities (such as a pending legal claim), events after the year end that change the picture, and so on. This is why published accounts carry many pages of notes.

Key idea

Concepts say what is recorded and how it is measured: the entity, in money, as a going concern, period by period, at cost, with two aspects, revenue when earned, expenses matched to it. Conventions guide judgement in applying them: be consistent, be prudent, focus on what is material, and disclose what matters.

docs.title: 1.9 The conceptual framework and qualitative characteristics
docs.text:
Standard-setters have gathered the ideas above into a conceptual framework: a statement of the objective of financial reporting and of the qualities that make information useful. The International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) publishes such a framework, and national frameworks are built on similar lines.

The framework states that the objective of general-purpose financial reporting is to provide information that is useful to present and potential investors, lenders and other creditors in making decisions about providing resources to the entity. It then describes the qualitative characteristics of useful information.

Fundamental characteristics (information must have both):

  • Relevance. The information can make a difference to decisions, because it helps users predict the future or confirm or correct their past expectations. Materiality is an aspect of relevance.
  • Faithful representation. The information represents what it claims to represent: it is complete, neutral (not slanted) and free from error.

Enhancing characteristics (they make relevant and faithful information more useful):

  • Comparability. Users can compare the information with that of other entities and of other periods.
  • Verifiability. Independent, knowledgeable observers could agree that the information is a faithful representation.
  • Timeliness. The information is available while it can still influence decisions.
  • Understandability. The information is classified and presented clearly and concisely, for users who have a reasonable knowledge of business and study it with diligence.

The framework also recognises a cost constraint: producing information has a cost, and that cost should be justified by the benefits of the information to users.

Concept or convention The quality it mainly serves Objectivity, historical cost Verifiability, faithful representation Consistency Comparability Accounting period Timeliness, comparability Materiality Relevance Full disclosure Relevance, understandability Prudence (as caution) Faithful representation (neutral, not biased upward)

Table 1.4. How the traditional concepts relate to the qualitative characteristics.

docs.title: 1.10 Accounting standards: IFRS and Ind AS
Why standards are needed
docs.text: Left alone, different businesses would account for similar transactions in different ways. One might charge the full cost of an advertising campaign as an expense; another might spread it over three years. One might value inventory at cost; another at selling price. Their profits would not be comparable, and a careless or dishonest preparer could present almost any result. Accounting standards are authoritative written statements that say how particular transactions and events are to be recognised, measured, presented and disclosed. They reduce the range of choice, make statements comparable and give auditors a benchmark against which to judge them.

docs.title: International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS)
docs.text: The IASB, an independent body overseen by the IFRS Foundation, issues International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Older standards issued by its predecessor, the International Accounting Standards Committee, are called International Accounting Standards (IAS) and many remain in force. IFRS are required or permitted for listed companies in a large number of countries, which allows investors to compare companies across borders.

docs.title: Standards in India
docs.text:
India has chosen to converge with IFRS rather than adopt them word for word. The result is the Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), which are based on and largely aligned with IFRS, with some differences (called carve-outs) suited to Indian conditions. Ind AS are notified by the central government for companies under company law, on the recommendation of the national advisory body on accounting standards, after being formulated by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI).

Ind AS apply to specified classes of companies, broadly listed companies and larger unlisted companies, defined by criteria such as listing and net worth; certain regulated sectors such as banking and insurance follow their own timetables. Other companies continue to follow the earlier set of Accounting Standards (AS), also formulated by the ICAI and notified for companies. Non-corporate entities such as sole traders, partnerships and many non-profit organisations follow the AS issued by the ICAI, with relaxations for smaller entities. The criteria and the applicable standards are revised from time to time, so the current notifications should be checked for any particular case.

Body or set of standards What it is IASB Independent international board that issues IFRS IFRS / IAS International standards used in many countries ICAI The professional body of chartered accountants in India; formulates AS and Ind AS Ind AS Indian standards converged with IFRS, for specified classes of companies AS Earlier Indian standards, for other companies and non-corporate entities

Table 1.5. The main standard-setting bodies and sets of standards mentioned in this book.

Note

The principles taught in this book (double entry, accruals, depreciation, the structure of the financial statements) are common to all these sets of standards. Where Ind AS and AS differ, the differences lie mostly in advanced topics such as fair value measurement and financial instruments, which are beyond a first course. Specific standards are mentioned in later chapters only where they help to explain a practice.

docs.title: Standards and the law
docs.text: For companies, accounting is governed by company law as well as by standards. Company law requires books of account to be kept, prescribes the general format of the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss (Chapter 11), and requires the statements to give a true and fair view and to comply with the notified standards. Tax law has its own rules for computing taxable income, which is why taxable profit often differs from accounting profit.

docs.title: 1.11 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Accounting identifies, measures, records, classifies, summarises, interprets and communicates financial information. Bookkeeping is its recording part.
  • Its purposes are to keep systematic records, find profit or loss, show the financial position, inform users, protect property and meet legal requirements. It records only money-measurable items, mostly at historical cost, and involves estimates.
  • Internal users (owners, managers, employees) and external users (investors, lenders, suppliers, customers, government, the public) rely on the same statements for different decisions.
  • The accrual basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred; the cash basis records them when cash moves. Standards require the accrual basis.
  • The main concepts are business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period, historical cost, dual aspect, revenue recognition, matching and objectivity. The main conventions are consistency, prudence, materiality and full disclosure.
  • Useful information is relevant and faithfully represented, and is made more useful by comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability.
  • Accounting standards narrow the choices open to preparers. IFRS are issued by the IASB; India's Ind AS are converged with IFRS and apply to specified companies, while others follow the earlier AS.

docs.title: 1.12 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each of the following as an asset, a liability, capital, revenue, an expense or drawings, from the point of view of the business: (a) money owed to a supplier; (b) delivery van; (c) wages paid; (d) commission earned; (e) cash introduced by the owner; (f) goods taken by the owner for family use; (g) amount owed by a customer; (h) bank loan.

Answer

(a) liability (creditor); (b) asset; (c) expense; (d) revenue; (e) capital; (f) drawings; (g) asset (debtor); (h) liability.

Exercise 2

In June a consultant billed clients ₹1,20,000 for work done in June, of which ₹90,000 was received in June. She also received ₹15,000 for work done in May. Her expenses for June were ₹40,000, of which ₹32,000 were paid in June; she also paid ₹8,000 of May's expenses in June. Compute her June profit on (a) the cash basis and (b) the accrual basis.

Answer

(a) Cash basis: receipts 90,000 + 15,000 = ₹1,05,000; payments 32,000 + 8,000 = ₹40,000; profit ₹65,000.

(b) Accrual basis: revenue earned in June ₹1,20,000; expenses incurred in June ₹40,000; profit ₹80,000.

Exercise 3

Name the concept or convention applied in each case: (a) a building bought for ₹50,00,000 is still shown at cost less depreciation although its market value is ₹80,00,000; (b) a firm does not record that its manager is highly skilled; (c) a stapler costing ₹150 is charged as an expense; (d) a firm continues to use the straight line method of depreciation every year; (e) the owner's personal car insurance paid from the business bank account is recorded as drawings.

Answer

(a) Historical cost (supported by going concern); (b) money measurement; (c) materiality; (d) consistency; (e) business entity.

Exercise 4

A trader's closing inventory consists of four items: P (cost ₹20,000, net realisable value ₹24,000), Q (cost ₹15,000, NRV ₹11,000), R (cost ₹9,000, NRV ₹9,500), S (cost ₹6,000, NRV ₹4,000). At what amount should inventory be shown? What would the amount be if the totals were compared instead?

Answer

Item by item: P 20,000 + Q 11,000 + R 9,000 + S 4,000 = ₹44,000.

Totals: cost ₹50,000, NRV ₹48,500, lower ₹48,500. Comparing totals would let the expected gains on P and R hide part of the losses on Q and S, overstating inventory by ₹4,500. The item-by-item figure of ₹44,000 is correct.

Exercise 5

Explain the difference between relevance and faithful representation, and give an example of information that is relevant but not faithfully represented.

Answer

Relevance means the information can make a difference to a decision; faithful representation means it shows what it claims to show, completely, neutrally and without error. A forecast of next year's sales prepared by a manager whose bonus depends on it is relevant to an investor, but if it is deliberately optimistic it is not neutral and so not a faithful representation.

Exercise 6

State whether each is capital or revenue expenditure: (a) purchase of a delivery van; (b) petrol for the van; (c) cost of installing a new machine; (d) repainting the shop; (e) legal fees paid to buy a piece of land.

Answer

(a) capital; (b) revenue; (c) capital (part of the machine's cost); (d) revenue (maintenance); (e) capital (part of the land's cost).

Exercise 1

Which of the following is an external user of accounting information?

  1. The manager of a branch
  2. A bank considering a loan
  3. The owner of a sole proprietorship
  4. The production supervisor
Answer

Exercise 2

The owner pays his personal income tax from the business bank account. This is treated as

  1. an expense of the business
  2. drawings
  3. a liability of the business
  4. capital
Answer

drawings

Under the business entity concept, personal payments by the owner are drawings.

Exercise 3

Which concept explains why assets are shown at cost less depreciation rather than at their forced-sale value?

  1. Money measurement
  2. Going concern
  3. Materiality
  4. Dual aspect
Answer

Going concern

A business expected to continue will use its assets, not sell them now.

Exercise 4

Sales ₹50,000 (₹10,000 still owed by customers); expenses incurred ₹30,000 (all paid). What is the profit on the accrual basis, in rupees?

Answer

20000 / 20,000 / ₹20,000 / Rs 20000

Accrual profit is 50,000 − 30,000 = 20,000, whether or not the customers have paid.

Exercise 5

Valuing inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value is an application of

  1. consistency
  2. prudence
  3. full disclosure
  4. the accounting period concept
Answer

prudence

Exercise 6

Which pair are the fundamental qualitative characteristics in the conceptual framework?

  1. Comparability and timeliness
  2. Relevance and faithful representation
  3. Verifiability and understandability
  4. Consistency and prudence
Answer

Relevance and faithful representation

Exercise 7

Match each body or set of standards with its description.

ABIASBIndian standards converged with IFRSInd ASformulates Indian standardsICAIissues IFRS Answer

IASB — issues IFRS; Ind AS — Indian standards converged with IFRS; ICAI — formulates Indian standards

docs.title: Chapter 14: Accounting Software and Ethics
docs.text:
Computerised accounting, its controls, and the professional duties of those who prepare accounts

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain what changes, and what does not, when accounts are kept by computer.
  2. Design a simple coded chart of accounts and describe masters, vouchers and reports.
  3. Build a trial balance from journal data with spreadsheet formulas or a short program.
  4. Describe the main controls in a computerised accounting system, including the audit trail.
  5. State the fundamental principles of professional ethics and the main threats to them.
  6. Recognise window dressing and earnings management, and measure their effect on reported figures.

docs.title: 14.1 From books to software
docs.text:
Almost every business today keeps its accounts by computer, from a spreadsheet in a small shop to a large enterprise system that links sales, purchasing, inventory, payroll and accounting. Accounting software performs, in a fraction of a second, the steps that earlier chapters did by hand: it posts every voucher to the ledger, balances the accounts, prepares the trial balance and produces the financial statements.

What changes is the mechanics. Posting, casting, balancing and transferring are done by the program, so the errors of Chapter 6 that arise from them (wrong totals, postings to one side only, wrong balances carried forward) largely disappear. Reports can be produced for any date or period at any time, rather than once a year.

What does not change is the accounting. The software does not know whether a payment is for a machine or for repairs, whether a sale belongs to this year or next, or how much of the debtors will never pay. Every decision about which account to debit and credit, every year-end adjustment, every estimate, is still made by a person. A wrong entry is processed just as fast as a right one. The principles of the earlier chapters are therefore as necessary as ever: the computer only removes the drudgery.

Key idea

Software automates recording, posting and reporting. It does not automate judgement. Errors of principle and of original entry, and deliberate misstatements, pass through software untouched.

docs.title: 14.2 The chart of accounts
docs.text:
Before any transaction is entered, the business sets up its chart of accounts: the list of every ledger account, arranged in groups that correspond to the headings of the financial statements. Each account is often given a numeric code so that it can be sorted and reported consistently.

Code range Group Examples of accounts (code) 1000-1999 Assets Cash (1010), Bank (1020), Trade receivables (1100), Inventory (1200), Prepaid expenses (1300), Office equipment (1510), Accumulated depreciation: office equipment (1515) 2000-2999 Liabilities Trade payables (2010), Outstanding expenses (2100), Bank loan (2500) 3000-3999 Capital (equity) Capital (3010), Drawings (3020) 4000-4999 Revenue Sales (4010), Sales returns (4020), Commission received (4500) 5000-5999 Cost of sales Purchases (5010), Purchases returns (5020), Carriage inwards (5100) 6000-6999 Operating expenses Salaries (6010), Rent (6020), Electricity (6030), Depreciation (6100)

Table 14.1. A simple coded chart of accounts.

Good coding makes reports reliable: if every expense account sits within its group, the profit and loss account and the balance sheet are produced simply by adding the groups. The groups also reflect the rules of debit and credit: accounts in the asset and expense groups normally carry debit balances, those in the liability, capital and revenue groups credit balances.

docs.title: 14.3 Masters, vouchers and reports
docs.text:
Most accounting packages organise work in three layers.

Figure 14.1 How accounting software is organised. Masters (company, financial year, groups and ledgers, inventory items and tax rates) are set up once; vouchers (receipt, payment, contra, sales, purchase, journal, debit note, credit note) are entered every day and must balance; both feed a database that posts automatically and keeps an audit trail, from which reports such as the day book, ledgers, trial balance, financial statements, cash flow, ageing, bank reconciliation and tax returns are produced on demand.

Masters are the standing data, entered once and changed rarely: the company's name and financial year, the groups and ledger accounts (with opening balances), customers and suppliers with their credit terms, inventory items, and tax rates.

Vouchers are the transactions, entered daily. Each voucher type corresponds to a book of original entry of Chapter 4:

Voucher type Used for Manual equivalent Receipt Money received in cash or bank Debit side of the cash book Payment Money paid in cash or by bank Credit side of the cash book Contra Transfers between cash and bank Contra entries Sales Credit (and cash) sales of goods Sales book Purchase Credit (and cash) purchases of goods Purchases book Credit note Goods returned by customers, allowances Sales returns book Debit note Goods returned to suppliers Purchases returns book Journal Adjustments, depreciation, rectification, other non-cash items Journal proper

Table 14.2. Voucher types and their manual equivalents.

Reports are produced from the posted data whenever needed: the day book, the cash and bank book, any ledger account, the trial balance, the profit and loss account and balance sheet, the cash flow statement, the ageing of receivables (how long each customer's balance has been outstanding), stock summaries, and the statements needed for tax returns.

docs.title: Features that support the earlier chapters
docs.text:
• Bank reconciliation. The bank statement is imported or entered, and cleared items are matched with the cash book; the unmatched items are exactly the timing differences of Chapter 5.
  • Fixed asset register. Assets are recorded with cost, date and rate, and depreciation is computed and posted (Chapter 7).
  • Credit control. Ageing reports and reminders support the estimate of doubtful debts.
  • Tax. Sales and purchase vouchers carry tax rates, and the tax accounts and returns are prepared from them (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 14.4 Spreadsheets
docs.text:
Many small businesses, and many accountants for analysis, use spreadsheets. A spreadsheet is not an accounting system (it does not stop unbalanced entries or keep an audit trail unless designed to), but it is an excellent tool for understanding one.

Example 14.1 A trial balance with spreadsheet formulas

Suppose the journal of Sharma Electricals (Example 3.1) is typed into a sheet named Journal, one entry per row: column A the date, column B the account debited, column C the account credited, column D the amount (rows 2 to 15). A second sheet, TB, lists the account names in column A from row 2. The formulas are:

B2  (net balance)  =SUMIF(Journal!$B$2:$B$15,A2,Journal!$D$2:$D$15)-SUMIF(Journal!$C$2:$C$15,A2,Journal!$D$2:$D$15)
C2  (debit)        =IF(B2>0,B2,0)
D2  (credit)       =IF(B2<0,-B2,0)
C15 (total debit)  =SUM(C2:C14)
D15 (total credit) =SUM(D2:D14)
E15 (check)        =IF(C15=D15,"Agrees","Does not agree")

The first formula adds every amount debited to the account and subtracts every amount credited to it, which is exactly what posting and balancing do. Copied down for the thirteen accounts, the sheet reproduces the trial balance of Example 3.4: total debits ₹3,03,000 and total credits ₹3,03,000.

docs.title: 14.5 A small program
docs.text:
The heart of any accounting program is short. The Python program below holds the vouchers of Sharma Electricals, refuses any voucher whose debits and credits differ, posts them to a ledger and prints the trial balance.

Example 14.2 Posting vouchers and printing a trial balance in Python

from collections import defaultdict

# Each voucher: (date, [(account, debit, credit), ...])
vouchers = [
    ("2025-04-01", [("Cash", 200000, 0), ("Capital", 0, 200000)]),
    ("2025-04-02", [("Bank", 120000, 0), ("Cash", 0, 120000)]),
    ("2025-04-03", [("Purchases", 80000, 0), ("Mehta & Co", 0, 80000)]),
    ("2025-04-05", [("Office Equipment", 30000, 0), ("Bank", 0, 30000)]),
    ("2025-04-08", [("Gupta Stores", 45000, 0), ("Sales", 0, 45000)]),
    ("2025-04-10", [("Cash", 25000, 0), ("Sales", 0, 25000)]),
    ("2025-04-12", [("Mehta & Co", 50000, 0), ("Bank", 0, 50000)]),
    ("2025-04-15", [("Cash", 30000, 0), ("Gupta Stores", 0, 30000)]),
    ("2025-04-18", [("Purchases", 12000, 0), ("Cash", 0, 12000)]),
    ("2025-04-20", [("Rent", 8000, 0), ("Cash", 0, 8000)]),
    ("2025-04-25", [("Drawings", 4000, 0), ("Cash", 0, 4000)]),
    ("2025-04-28", [("Cash", 3000, 0), ("Commission Received", 0, 3000)]),
    ("2025-04-30", [("Salaries", 10000, 0), ("Bank", 0, 10000)]),
    ("2025-04-30", [("Electricity", 2000, 0), ("Cash", 0, 2000)]),
]

def post(vouchers):
    """Post balanced vouchers to a ledger; a positive balance is a debit."""
    ledger = defaultdict(int)
    for date, lines in vouchers:
        dr = sum(d for _, d, _ in lines)
        cr = sum(c for _, _, c in lines)
        if dr != cr:                       # the software refuses an unbalanced voucher
            raise ValueError(f"Voucher of {date} does not balance: {dr} vs {cr}")
        for account, d, c in lines:
            ledger[account] += d - c
    return ledger

ledger = post(vouchers)
total_dr = total_cr = 0
print(f"{'Account':<22}{'Debit':>10}{'Credit':>10}")
for account, bal in ledger.items():
    dr, cr = (bal, 0) if bal > 0 else (0, -bal)
    total_dr += dr
    total_cr += cr
    print(f"{account:<22}{dr or '':>10}{cr or '':>10}")
print(f"{'Total':<22}{total_dr:>10}{total_cr:>10}")

Its output is the trial balance of Example 3.4:

Account                    Debit    Credit
Cash                      112000          
Capital                             200000
Bank                       30000          
Purchases                  92000          
Mehta & Co                           30000
Office Equipment           30000          
Gupta Stores               15000          
Sales                                70000
Rent                        8000          
Drawings                    4000          
Commission Received                   3000
Salaries                   10000          
Electricity                 2000          
Total                     303000    303000

A voucher such as ("2025-05-01", [("Cash", 5000, 0), ("Sales", 0, 4500)]) is rejected with the message "Voucher of 2025-05-01 does not balance: 5000 vs 4500". Because every voucher must balance before it is posted, the trial balance of a computerised system always agrees; that is why, in software, the trial balance stops being a useful check on arithmetic, and the review of what was posted becomes all the more important.

docs.title: 14.6 Controls in a computerised system
docs.text:
Computerisation removes some risks and creates others: one careless or dishonest user can now change many records at once, and a single failure can destroy all the data. Good systems include:

  • Access controls. Each user has a password and a role, and can see and do only what the role requires. A sales clerk can enter sales vouchers but not alter the bank ledger.
  • Segregation of duties. No one person should be able to authorise a payment, record it and reconcile the bank account; dividing these tasks makes fraud harder.
  • Authorisation and approval. Vouchers above a limit, or of certain kinds (write-offs, credit notes), need approval by a second person.
  • Audit trail (edit log). The system records who entered or changed each transaction, when, and what the old and new values were, and the log cannot be switched off or altered. Company law in some countries, including India, now requires the accounting software used by companies to maintain such an audit trail.
  • Period locking. Once a period has been closed and reported, it is locked so that entries cannot be back-dated into it without authorisation.
  • Validation checks. The software rejects unbalanced vouchers, invalid dates and unknown account codes, and warns about unusual entries (a credit balance in cash, a duplicate invoice number).
  • Backups and recovery. Data is copied regularly to a secure separate location, and the restore process is tested.
  • Regular reconciliation and review. Bank reconciliations, confirmations from customers and suppliers, physical counts of inventory and review of unusual journal entries catch what validation cannot.

Caution

A balanced trial balance from software proves nothing about the correctness of the accounts. The errors that matter in a computerised system are those of principle, omission, wrong classification and wrong cut-off, plus deliberate manipulation. These are found only by review, reconciliation and audit.

docs.title: 14.7 Why ethics matters in accounting
docs.text:
Financial statements are used by people who cannot check them for themselves: investors, lenders, employees, the government. They rely on the people who prepare and audit them to act honestly and competently. When that trust fails, the damage spreads far beyond one business: investors lose savings, employees lose jobs, lenders lose money, and confidence in all financial reporting falls. Many of the rules of company law, the accounting standards and the audit profession were tightened after such failures.

Accounting also offers many opportunities for choice: estimates of useful lives and doubtful debts, the timing of revenue, the classification of an item as capital or revenue. Most of these choices are legitimate; the duty of the accountant is to make them honestly, so that the statements are a faithful representation (Chapter 1), not a picture that suits the preparer.

docs.title: The fundamental principles
docs.text:
The international code of ethics for professional accountants, issued by the International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants (IESBA) and adopted, with modifications, by many national professional bodies including those in India, sets out five fundamental principles:

Principle What it requires Integrity Be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships; do not be associated with information you believe to be false or misleading Objectivity Do not allow bias, conflict of interest or undue influence of others to override professional judgement Professional competence and due care Keep knowledge and skill at the level required, and act diligently in accordance with applicable standards Confidentiality Respect the confidentiality of information acquired through professional work; do not disclose it without proper authority unless there is a legal or professional right or duty to do so, and do not use it for personal advantage Professional behaviour Comply with laws and regulations and avoid any conduct that discredits the profession

Table 14.3. The fundamental principles of professional ethics.

docs.title: Threats and safeguards
docs.text:
The same code groups the circumstances that can undermine these principles into categories of threats:

  • Self-interest: a financial or other interest will inappropriately influence judgement (an accountant whose bonus depends on reported profit).
  • Self-review: an accountant will not appropriately evaluate work that he or she did earlier (auditing a system one designed).
  • Advocacy: an accountant promotes a client's or employer's position to the point that objectivity is compromised.
  • Familiarity: a long or close relationship makes an accountant too sympathetic to the interests of others or too accepting of their work.
  • Intimidation: an accountant is deterred from acting objectively by actual or perceived pressure, including threats of dismissal.

Safeguards reduce threats to an acceptable level: independent review by another person, rotation of staff, separating duties, clear policies, board audit committees, and, ultimately, refusing or withdrawing from the work.

docs.title: 14.8 Window dressing and earnings management
docs.text:
Window dressing means arranging transactions around the year end so that the financial statements look better than the underlying position. Earnings management means using the choices available in accounting, or the timing of transactions, to report a desired profit. Some timing choices are ordinary business decisions; the line is crossed when the purpose or effect is to mislead users. Recording sales that have not happened, or that belong to the next period, is plainly wrong.

Example 14.3 The effect of window dressing on reported figures

(a) Dressing the current ratio. On 30 March a company's current assets are ₹4,00,000 (including bank ₹1,80,000) and its current liabilities ₹2,50,000. On 31 March it pays ₹1,50,000 of trade payables from the bank, intending to buy on credit again in April.

Before payment After payment Current assets (₹) 4,00,000 2,50,000 Current liabilities (₹) 2,50,000 1,00,000 Current ratio 1.6:1 2.5:1

Paying a genuine debt is not wrong in itself, but a ratio of 2.5 at the year end suggests far more liquidity than the business usually has. A reader who knows the trick looks at the cash flow statement and at the ratio during the year, not only at the year end.

(b) Bringing forward revenue. A business with a profit of ₹2,00,000 for 2025-26 records in March goods invoiced for ₹60,000 (cost ₹40,000) that are not dispatched until April.

Correct With early recording Profit for 2025-26 (₹) 2,00,000 2,20,000 Effect on 2026-27 profit (₹) — 20,000 lower Trade receivables at 31 March (₹) unaffected 60,000 higher Inventory at 31 March (₹) unaffected 40,000 lower

Profit is overstated by ₹20,000 (10%) this year and understated by the same amount next year. Revenue recognition rules (Chapter 1) forbid this: the sale is not complete until control of the goods passes to the customer.

Example 14.4 Ethical dilemmas

Case 1. An accounts assistant is told by the sales manager to record next month's sales in this month "to meet the target", and is reminded that her contract is up for renewal. Threats: self-interest and intimidation. Principles at stake: integrity and objectivity. A proper response: decline, explain that the entry would breach revenue recognition, and if the pressure continues, raise it with a more senior person, the finance head or the audit committee, keeping a written record.

Case 2. An accountant preparing a client's accounts notices that a large debtor has gone into insolvency, but the client refuses to make any provision because "the bank must not see a loss". Principle at stake: integrity (being associated with misleading information) and professional competence (applying the standards). A proper response: explain that a provision is required by prudence and the standards; if the client refuses, decline to be associated with the statements.

Case 3. A friend asks an accountant whether a listed company she audits is about to report a large loss. Principle at stake: confidentiality. A proper response: refuse; using or passing on such information would also breach the law on insider trading.

docs.title: 14.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Software automates posting, balancing and reporting; it does not make accounting judgements. Errors of principle, omission and cut-off, and deliberate misstatements, pass through it.
  • A coded chart of accounts, organised in groups that match the financial statements, is the foundation of a computerised system. Masters are standing data; vouchers are transactions; reports are produced on demand.
  • A trial balance can be built with spreadsheet formulas (SUMIF of debits minus credits) or with a short program that rejects unbalanced vouchers.
  • Controls include access controls, segregation of duties, authorisation, an unalterable audit trail, period locking, validation, backups and regular reconciliation.
  • The fundamental ethical principles are integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour; the main threats are self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity and intimidation.
  • Window dressing and earnings management can flatter ratios and profit; they are detected by looking beyond year-end figures and are wrong when they mislead.

docs.title: 14.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Assign each account to a group of the chart of accounts in Table 14.1 and suggest a code: (a) discount received; (b) delivery van; (c) outstanding salaries; (d) carriage inwards; (e) advertisement; (f) drawings.

Answer

(a) Revenue, for example 4600; (b) Assets, for example 1520 (with accumulated depreciation 1525); (c) Liabilities, for example 2110; (d) Cost of sales, 5100 in the table; (e) Operating expenses, for example 6200; (f) Capital, 3020 in the table.

Exercise 2

Name the voucher type used for: (a) cash withdrawn from the bank for office use; (b) depreciation for the year; (c) goods returned by a customer; (d) rent paid by cheque; (e) a credit sale.

Answer

(a) contra; (b) journal; (c) credit note; (d) payment; (e) sales.

Exercise 3

In the spreadsheet of Example 14.1, what would the formula in B2 return for Gupta Stores, and why?

Answer

15,000. Gupta Stores was debited ₹45,000 (the credit sale) and credited ₹30,000 (cash received), so the formula gives 45,000 − 30,000 = 15,000, a positive figure, which appears in the debit column.

Exercise 4

The accountant of a small firm authorises supplier payments, makes the payments through internet banking and prepares the monthly bank reconciliation. What control weakness does this show, and how could it be reduced?

Answer

There is no segregation of duties: one person could create a false supplier, pay it and hide the payment in the reconciliation. The owner (or a second person) should approve payments and review or prepare the bank reconciliation, and supplier master data should be changed only by someone other than the person who pays.

Exercise 5

A firm has current assets of ₹3,00,000 and current liabilities of ₹2,00,000. On the last day of the year it takes a 15-day bank loan of ₹1,00,000, keeping the money in its bank account. What happens to the current ratio? Is the loan a current or non-current liability?

Answer

The loan is repayable within a year, so it is a current liability. Current assets become ₹4,00,000 and current liabilities ₹3,00,000: the ratio falls from 1.5 to 1.33. (Borrowing short-term and holding the cash lowers a ratio that is above 1; window dressing usually does the opposite, paying off current liabilities.)

Exercise 6

Identify the ethical principle and threat: an auditor has audited the same company for twelve years and is a close friend of its finance director.

Answer

The threat is familiarity: the long and close relationship may make the auditor too accepting of the finance director's work. The principle at risk is objectivity. Safeguards include rotating the audit partner and having the work reviewed by another partner.

docs.title: 14.11 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 14

  1. An error in casting a total
  2. A posting to one side only
  3. An error of principle

Answer

Exercise 2

  1. journal voucher
  2. contra voucher
  3. sales voucher

Answer

contra voucher

Exercise 3

  1. a chart of accounts
  2. an audit trail
  3. a trial balance
  4. a master
Answer

an audit trail

Exercise 4

  1. Profitability
  2. Confidentiality
  3. Conservatism
  4. Materiality
Answer

Exercise 5

Match each situation with the threat it creates.

ABBonus depends on reported profitintimidationAuditing a system you designedfamiliarityThreat of dismissalself-interestTwelve years with the same clientself-review Answer

Bonus depends on reported profit — self-interest; Auditing a system you designed — self-review; Threat of dismissal — intimidation; Twelve years with the same client — familiarity

Exercise 6

Current assets ₹5,00,000 and current liabilities ₹3,00,000. A creditor of ₹1,00,000 is paid from the bank on the last day. What is the new current ratio? (write as a number, e.g. 1.5)

Answer

2 / 2.0 / 2:1

(5,00,000 − 1,00,000) ÷ (3,00,000 − 1,00,000) = 4,00,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Accounts of Non-Profit Organisations
docs.text:
Clubs, societies and charities: receipts and payments, income and expenditure, and the capital fund

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Describe a non-profit organisation and the special features of its accounts.
  2. Prepare a receipts and payments account and explain its limitations.
  3. Distinguish the receipts and payments account from the income and expenditure account.
  4. Treat the special items of non-profit organisations: subscriptions, entrance fees, donations, legacies and specific funds.
  5. Find the opening capital fund and prepare an income and expenditure account and a balance sheet from a receipts and payments account with additional information.

docs.title: 9.1 Organisations that do not seek profit
docs.text:
Not every organisation exists to make a profit for its owners. Sports clubs, residents' welfare associations, libraries, professional associations, schools and hospitals run by trusts, religious bodies and charities exist to serve their members or the public. They are called non-profit organisations (or not-for-profit organisations). Their income comes mainly from members' subscriptions, donations, grants, entrance fees, and the income from their investments and activities.

Such an organisation still needs accounts. Its members want to know how their money has been used, donors want assurance that their gifts went where they were meant to, and the law (registration of societies and trusts, and tax exemptions) usually requires accounts to be kept and audited. The principles are the same as for a business, with differences of name and emphasis:

In a business In a non-profit organisation Capital Capital fund (general fund, accumulated fund) Profit Surplus (excess of income over expenditure) Loss Deficit (excess of expenditure over income) Trading and profit and loss account Income and expenditure account Cash book (summarised) Receipts and payments account Owner Members; no one is entitled to the surplus

Table 9.1. Business terms and their non-profit equivalents.

The surplus is not distributed to anyone. It is added to the capital fund and used for the organisation's purposes.

The final accounts of a non-profit organisation usually consist of:

  1. a receipts and payments account, a summary of the cash book;
  2. an income and expenditure account, the equivalent of the profit and loss account;
  3. a balance sheet.
Figure 9.1 How a non-profit organisation's statements are linked. The receipts and payments account summarises all cash movements. Its revenue items, adjusted for accruals, go to the income and expenditure account; donations for a stated purpose go to specific funds; capital items and closing balances go to the balance sheet.

docs.title: 9.2 The receipts and payments account
docs.text:
The receipts and payments account is a summary of the cash book for the year, classified under suitable heads. It begins with the opening balance of cash and bank, lists all receipts on the debit side and all payments on the credit side, and ends with the closing balance. Its features:

  • It records cash transactions only, actual receipts and payments, whatever period they relate to: subscriptions received for last year and next year are included along with this year's.
  • It includes both capital and revenue items: the purchase of furniture and the payment of salaries appear side by side.
  • It does not include non-cash items such as depreciation, outstanding expenses or accrued income.
  • Its balance is the cash and bank balance, a debit (or, for an overdraft, a credit).

Many small organisations publish only this account. It shows where the cash came from and where it went, but it does not show whether the year's income covered the year's expenses, because it mixes capital with revenue and one year with another. That is the job of the income and expenditure account.

docs.title: 9.3 The income and expenditure account
docs.text:
The income and expenditure account is prepared on the accrual basis, like a profit and loss account. It includes only revenue items relating to the current year: incomes on the credit side and expenses on the debit side, after adjusting for outstanding and prepaid amounts, accruals and depreciation. The balance is a surplus (credit side larger) or deficit (debit side larger), transferred to the capital fund.

Point Receipts and payments account Income and expenditure account Nature Summary of the cash book; a real account Equivalent of the profit and loss account; a nominal account Basis Cash basis Accrual basis Items Capital and revenue Revenue only Period Receipts and payments of any year Income and expenditure of the current year only Non-cash items Not included Included (depreciation, outstanding, accrued) Opening balance Cash and bank balance None Closing balance Cash and bank balance Surplus or deficit Sides Receipts debit, payments credit Expenditure debit, income credit

Table 9.2. The two accounts compared.

docs.title: 9.4 Special items
docs.text:
Several items are peculiar to non-profit organisations, and their treatment as capital or revenue decides what goes into the income and expenditure account.

  • Subscriptions are periodic payments by members. They are the main revenue item. Only the subscriptions for the current year are income: those received for past years are not, and those received in advance are a liability; subscriptions due but not received are an asset (Section 9.5).
  • Entrance (admission) fees are paid once by new members. Being recurring in nature for the organisation (some new members join every year), they are commonly treated as revenue; some organisations capitalise them, wholly or partly, under their own rules. Follow the organisation's stated policy.
  • Life membership fees are paid once in place of annual subscriptions for life. They are usually capitalised (added to the capital fund or kept in a life membership fund), because they relate to many future years.
  • Donations without any condition are revenue if small and regular; a large, non-recurring donation may be capitalised. A specific donation, given for a stated purpose (a building, a prize, a tournament), is always capital and is credited to a separate fund.
  • Legacies (amounts left by will) are capital receipts, credited to the capital fund.
  • Sale of old assets is a capital receipt. The asset's book value is removed, and any profit or loss on sale goes to the income and expenditure account. The sale of old newspapers and similar scrap is a small revenue receipt.
  • Grants from government or other bodies are revenue if for running expenses, capital if for buying assets.
  • Honorarium is a payment to a person who is not an employee (a visiting coach, an honorary secretary): a revenue expense.

docs.title: 9.5 Subscriptions
docs.text:
Subscriptions received during a year usually include amounts for three periods: arrears of the previous year, the current year, and advances for the next year. The income for the current year is found by adjustment:

₹ Subscriptions received during the year (from receipts and payments account) Less: Subscriptions outstanding at the start of the year (received this year) Less: Subscriptions received in advance at the end of the year (for next year) Add: Subscriptions outstanding at the end of the year (for this year, not received) Add: Subscriptions received in advance at the start of the year (for this year, received last year) Subscriptions income for the current year

Table 9.3. Adjusting subscriptions received to subscriptions income.

The same result is obtained by preparing a subscriptions account, as Example 9.1 shows.

Example 9.1 Subscriptions income

Greenfield Sports Club received ₹85,000 as subscriptions during 2025-26. Of this, ₹4,000 was for 2024-25 and ₹3,000 for 2026-27. Subscriptions outstanding on 1 April 2025 were ₹4,000, and on 31 March 2026 ₹5,000 was outstanding for 2025-26. There were no advances on 1 April 2025.

Particulars ₹ Subscriptions received in 2025-26 85,000 Less: For 2024-25 (arrears received) (4,000) Less: For 2026-27 (received in advance) (3,000) Received for 2025-26 78,000 Add: Outstanding for 2025-26 5,000 Subscriptions income for 2025-26 83,000

Subscriptions Account

Particulars ₹ Particulars ₹ To Balance b/d (outstanding, 1 April 2025) 4,000 By Receipts and Payments A/c 85,000 To Income and Expenditure A/c (balancing figure) 83,000 By Balance c/d (outstanding, 31 March 2026) 5,000 To Balance c/d (received in advance) 3,000 Total 90,000 Total 90,000

In the balance sheet at 31 March 2026, the ₹5,000 outstanding is an asset and the ₹3,000 received in advance is a liability.

docs.title: 9.6 The opening capital fund
docs.text: When the capital fund at the start of the year is not given, it is found from a balance sheet at the start of the year (often called the opening statement of affairs): capital fund = assets − liabilities, both at the start of the year. Remember to include opening cash, outstanding and accrued items as well as fixed assets and investments.

docs.title: 9.7 A complete example
docs.text:
Example 9.2 Final accounts of Greenfield Sports Club

Receipts and Payments Account of Greenfield Sports Club for the year ended 31 March 2026

Receipts ₹ Payments ₹ To Balance b/d (cash) 12,000 By Salaries 36,000 To Subscriptions 85,000 By Rent 12,000 To Entrance fees 10,000 By Sports equipment purchased 30,000 To Donations (general) 15,000 By Electricity 6,500 To Sale of old equipment 2,500 By Tournament expenses 14,000 To Interest on investments 3,000 By Printing and stationery 3,500 To Locker rent 4,000 By Investments purchased (31 March 2026) 20,000 To Donations for tournament fund 20,000 By Balance c/d (cash) 29,500 Total 1,51,500 Total 1,51,500

Additional information

  1. On 1 April 2025 the club had: sports equipment ₹50,000; 10% investments ₹60,000; subscriptions outstanding ₹4,000; salaries outstanding ₹2,000; cash ₹12,000.
  2. Subscriptions as in Example 9.1: ₹4,000 of the receipts is for 2024-25, ₹3,000 for 2026-27, and ₹5,000 is outstanding for 2025-26.
  3. Salaries of ₹3,000 are outstanding on 31 March 2026; the payments include the ₹2,000 outstanding from last year.
  4. The equipment sold had a book value of ₹4,000.
  5. Depreciate sports equipment by 10% on its closing book value.
  6. Entrance fees and general donations are treated as revenue.
  7. Tournament expenses are to be met from the tournament fund.

Step 1: opening capital fund.

Opening balance sheet, 1 April 2025 ₹ Sports equipment 50,000 Investments 60,000 Subscriptions outstanding 4,000 Cash 12,000 Total assets 1,26,000 Less: Salaries outstanding 2,000 Capital fund 1,24,000

Step 2: workings.

  • Subscriptions income = ₹83,000 (Example 9.1).
  • Salaries = 36,000 − 2,000 (last year's) + 3,000 (this year's outstanding) = ₹37,000.
  • Interest: 10% × 60,000 = ₹6,000 earned on the investments held all year; ₹3,000 received, so ₹3,000 is accrued. (The new investments were bought on the last day and earn nothing this year.)
  • Loss on sale of equipment = book value 4,000 − proceeds 2,500 = ₹1,500.
  • Sports equipment = 50,000 − 4,000 + 30,000 = ₹76,000; depreciation 10% = ₹7,600; closing book value ₹68,400.
  • Tournament fund = 20,000 received − 14,000 spent = ₹6,000.

Income and Expenditure Account for the year ended 31 March 2026

Expenditure ₹ ₹ Income ₹ ₹ To Salaries 36,000 By Subscriptions 85,000 Less: For 2024-25 2,000 Less: For 2024-25 4,000 34,000 Less: For 2026-27 3,000 Add: Outstanding 3,000 37,000 78,000 To Rent 12,000 Add: Outstanding for 2025-26 5,000 83,000 To Electricity 6,500 By Entrance fees 10,000 To Printing and stationery 3,500 By Donations 15,000 To Depreciation on equipment 7,600 By Interest on investments 3,000 To Loss on sale of equipment 1,500 Add: Accrued 3,000 6,000 To Surplus (transferred to capital fund) 49,900 By Locker rent 4,000 1,18,000 1,18,000

Check: income 83,000 + 10,000 + 15,000 + 6,000 + 4,000 = ₹1,18,000; expenditure 37,000 + 12,000 + 6,500 + 3,500 + 7,600 + 1,500 = ₹68,100; surplus ₹49,900.

Balance Sheet of Greenfield Sports Club as at 31 March 2026

Liabilities ₹ ₹ Assets ₹ ₹ Capital fund 1,24,000 Sports equipment 50,000 Add: Surplus 49,900 1,73,900 Less: Sold 4,000 Tournament fund 20,000 Add: Purchased 30,000 Less: Tournament expenses 14,000 6,000 76,000 Subscriptions received in advance 3,000 Less: Depreciation 7,600 68,400 Salaries outstanding 3,000 Investments (60,000 + 20,000) 80,000 Interest accrued 3,000 Subscriptions outstanding 5,000 Cash 29,500 1,85,900 1,85,900

Check: liabilities 1,73,900 + 6,000 + 3,000 + 3,000 = ₹1,85,900; assets 68,400 + 80,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 + 29,500 = ₹1,85,900.

Notice what the income and expenditure account leaves out: the purchase of equipment and investments (capital payments), the sale proceeds of equipment (a capital receipt; only the loss appears), and everything to do with the tournament fund (a specific fund kept separate from general income). Notice also what it puts in that the receipts and payments account lacks: depreciation, the loss on sale, outstanding salaries, accrued interest and outstanding subscriptions.

docs.title: 9.8 Specific funds
docs.text:
A specific fund is created when money is received for a particular purpose: a building fund, a prize fund, a tournament fund. The receipts are credited to the fund, not to income. Expenses met from the fund are debited to it, not to the income and expenditure account. The balance of the fund is shown on the liabilities side of the balance sheet. If the fund has been invested in securities, the income from those investments is also credited to the fund, and the investments are shown separately on the assets side.

If the expenses on the purpose exceed the fund, the excess is charged to the income and expenditure account (or, if the organisation's rules say so, shown as a debit balance to be made good from future receipts).

Caution

Do not take specific donations or the expenses met from them to the income and expenditure account. Doing so would overstate both income and expenditure and, if they did not match, would distort the surplus. A specific fund is held for its purpose, much as a trust is held for its beneficiaries.

docs.title: 9.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Non-profit organisations serve members or the public; their accounts use the terms capital fund, surplus and deficit, and the surplus is retained, not distributed.
  • The receipts and payments account summarises the cash book: cash basis, capital and revenue items, any year, starting and ending with cash.
  • The income and expenditure account is on the accrual basis: revenue items of the current year only, including non-cash items; its balance is the surplus or deficit.
  • Subscriptions income = received − arrears of past years − advances for next year + outstanding for this year + advances received last year for this year.
  • Life membership fees, legacies and specific donations are capital; entrance fees and general donations are usually revenue, according to the organisation's policy.
  • The opening capital fund is the excess of opening assets over opening liabilities.
  • Specific funds are shown on the liabilities side, less the expenses met from them.

docs.title: 9.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A society received ₹1,20,000 as subscriptions in 2025-26, including ₹6,000 for 2024-25 and ₹4,000 for 2026-27. Subscriptions of ₹7,000 for 2025-26 were outstanding at the year end, and ₹2,500 for 2025-26 had been received in advance during 2024-25. Find the subscriptions income for 2025-26.

Answer

1,20,000 − 6,000 − 4,000 + 7,000 + 2,500 = ₹1,19,500.

Exercise 2

Classify as capital or revenue for a club: (a) life membership fees; (b) annual subscriptions; (c) a legacy of ₹2,00,000; (d) sale of old newspapers; (e) a donation for building a pavilion; (f) honorarium to a visiting coach.

Answer

(a) capital; (b) revenue; (c) capital; (d) revenue; (e) capital (specific fund); (f) revenue expense.

Exercise 3

On 1 April 2025 a library had books ₹1,50,000, furniture ₹40,000, cash ₹18,000, subscriptions outstanding ₹3,000, and rent outstanding ₹5,000. Find its capital fund.

Answer

Assets: 1,50,000 + 40,000 + 18,000 + 3,000 = ₹2,11,000. Liabilities: ₹5,000. Capital fund = ₹2,06,000.

Exercise 4

A club's prize fund stood at ₹50,000 on 1 April 2025, invested in 8% bonds. During the year interest of ₹4,000 was received on the bonds, donations of ₹10,000 were received for the fund, and prizes of ₹12,000 were awarded. Show the prize fund in the balance sheet at 31 March 2026.

Answer Liabilities ₹ ₹ Prize fund 50,000 Add: Interest on prize fund investments 4,000 Add: Donations 10,000 64,000 Less: Prizes awarded 12,000 52,000

On the assets side, the prize fund investments (8% bonds) are shown at ₹50,000.

Exercise 5

Stationery used during the year must be found from: stock of stationery on 1 April 2025 ₹2,000; paid for stationery during the year ₹15,000; creditors for stationery on 1 April 2025 ₹1,500 and on 31 March 2026 ₹2,500; stock of stationery on 31 March 2026 ₹3,000. Compute the amount for the income and expenditure account.

Answer

Purchases of stationery for the year = paid 15,000 − opening creditors 1,500 + closing creditors 2,500 = ₹16,000. Consumption = opening stock 2,000 + purchases 16,000 − closing stock 3,000 = ₹15,000.

Exercise 6

Why can the receipts and payments account not show whether a club's activities were self-supporting during the year?

Answer

Because it is on the cash basis and mixes capital with revenue and one year with another. It includes capital payments (new equipment) and receipts (legacies, specific donations), receipts for past and future years, and leaves out depreciation and unpaid expenses. Only the income and expenditure account, which matches the year's revenue income with the year's revenue expenses, shows whether there was a surplus or a deficit.
