docs.title: Chapter 13: Analysis of Financial Statements
docs.text:
Comparative and common-size statements, trends, and the main accounting ratios

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. State the purpose of financial statement analysis and name its main tools.
  2. Prepare comparative and common-size statements and a simple trend analysis.
  3. Compute and interpret liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability ratios.
  4. Compute the working capital cycle and break return on equity into its parts.
  5. Explain the limitations of ratio analysis.

docs.title: 13.1 Why analyse financial statements
docs.text:
Financial statements are full of figures, but figures by themselves say little. Is a profit of ₹2,62,500 good? It depends on the size of the business, on what it earned last year, on what similar businesses earn, and on how much capital was needed to earn it. Financial statement analysis is the process of relating figures to one another, across years and across businesses, to judge the performance and position of an enterprise.

Different users look for different things (Chapter 1). A supplier asks whether the business can pay its bills next month (liquidity). A lender asks whether it can carry its debt and pay interest year after year (solvency). Managers ask how efficiently assets are used (activity). Owners and investors ask how much the business earns on their money (profitability).

The main tools are:

  • comparative statements (horizontal analysis), which set the figures of two or more years side by side with the changes;
  • common-size statements (vertical analysis), which express each item as a percentage of a total;
  • trend analysis, which expresses each year's figures as an index of a base year;
  • ratio analysis, which relates two figures that have a meaningful connection;
  • cash flow analysis (Chapter 12).

Throughout this chapter the figures of one company, Meridian Ltd, are used.

Example 13.1 The data: Meridian Ltd

Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended 31 March

Particulars 2026 (₹) 2025 (₹) Revenue from operations (all credit) 20,00,000 16,00,000 Less: Cost of goods sold 12,00,000 10,00,000 Gross profit 8,00,000 6,00,000 Less: Operating expenses 4,00,000 3,20,000 Operating profit (earnings before interest and tax, EBIT) 4,00,000 2,80,000 Less: Finance costs 50,000 50,000 Profit before tax 3,50,000 2,30,000 Less: Tax at 25% 87,500 57,500 Profit after tax 2,62,500 1,72,500

Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026

Equity and liabilities ₹ Assets ₹ Equity share capital (1,00,000 shares of ₹10) 10,00,000 Property, plant and equipment 14,00,000 Reserves and surplus 3,50,000 Inventories 3,00,000 10% Debentures 5,00,000 Trade receivables 4,00,000 Trade payables 3,00,000 Cash and cash equivalents 1,50,000 Other current liabilities 1,50,000 Prepaid expenses 50,000 Total 23,00,000 Total 23,00,000

At 31 March 2025: inventories ₹2,00,000; trade receivables ₹3,00,000; trade payables ₹2,50,000. All purchases are on credit.

docs.title: 13.2 Comparative statements
docs.text:
A comparative statement shows the figures of two (or more) years side by side, with the absolute change and the percentage change:

\[ \text{Percentage change} = \frac{\text{Current year} - \text{Previous year}}{\text{Previous year}} \times 100 \]

Example 13.2 Comparative statement of profit and loss of Meridian Ltd

Particulars 2025 (₹) 2026 (₹) Change (₹) Change (%) Revenue from operations 16,00,000 20,00,000 4,00,000 25.00 Cost of goods sold 10,00,000 12,00,000 2,00,000 20.00 Gross profit 6,00,000 8,00,000 2,00,000 33.33 Operating expenses 3,20,000 4,00,000 80,000 25.00 Operating profit (EBIT) 2,80,000 4,00,000 1,20,000 42.86 Finance costs 50,000 50,000 0 0.00 Profit before tax 2,30,000 3,50,000 1,20,000 52.17 Tax 57,500 87,500 30,000 52.17 Profit after tax 1,72,500 2,62,500 90,000 52.17

Reading. Revenue grew by 25%, but cost of goods sold grew by only 20%, so gross profit grew by a third. Operating expenses grew in step with revenue. Because finance costs did not change, the growth in operating profit was magnified further down: profit after tax rose by 52%. This magnifying effect of fixed costs is called leverage.

docs.title: 13.3 Common-size statements
docs.text:
A common-size statement expresses every item as a percentage of a common base: revenue from operations for the statement of profit and loss, and total assets (or total of equity and liabilities) for the balance sheet. It removes the effect of size, so that a company can be compared with a larger or smaller one, or with itself in years of different size.

Example 13.3 Common-size statement of profit and loss of Meridian Ltd

Particulars 2025 (% of revenue) 2026 (% of revenue) Revenue from operations 100.00 100.00 Cost of goods sold 62.50 60.00 Gross profit 37.50 40.00 Operating expenses 20.00 20.00 Operating profit (EBIT) 17.50 20.00 Finance costs 3.13 2.50 Profit before tax 14.38 17.50 Tax 3.59 4.38 Profit after tax 10.78 13.13

(Percentages are rounded to two decimals; for 2025, 50,000 ÷ 16,00,000 = 3.125% and so on.)

Reading. Out of every ₹100 of revenue, the company kept ₹13.13 as profit after tax in 2026, against ₹10.78 in 2025. The improvement came from a lower cost of goods sold (62.5% to 60%) and from finance costs being spread over a larger revenue.

docs.title: 13.4 Trend analysis
docs.text:
For a longer run of years, each figure is expressed as an index of a base year, set at 100:

\[ \text{Trend index} = \frac{\text{Figure for the year}}{\text{Figure for the base year}} \times 100 \] Year ended 31 March 2023 2024 2025 2026 Revenue of Meridian Ltd (₹) 12,00,000 13,80,000 16,00,000 20,00,000 Trend index (2023 = 100) 100.0 115.0 133.3 166.7

Table 13.1. Trend of revenue, with 2023 as the base year.

Revenue has grown every year, and the growth has accelerated: 15 points in the first year, about 18 in the second and about 33 in the third. A trend is most informative when related items are compared: if receivables were growing much faster than revenue, for example, it would suggest that credit control was weakening.

docs.title: 13.5 Ratio analysis
docs.text:
A ratio relates two figures that have a meaningful connection. It may be expressed as a pure ratio (2:1), as a percentage (40%), as a number of times (4.8 times) or as a number of days. Ratios are usually grouped into four families.

Figure 13.1 The four families of ratios. Accounting ratios fall into four families: liquidity (current and quick ratios), solvency (debt-equity, proprietary ratio, interest coverage), activity (inventory, receivables, payables and asset turnover) and profitability (gross and net profit ratios, operating ratio, ROCE, ROE, EPS and P/E).

Caution

A ratio means nothing on its own. It must be compared: with the same business in earlier years, with other businesses in the same industry, or with a target. A current ratio of 2:1 may be comfortable for a manufacturer and excessive for a supermarket that sells for cash and turns its stock over every few days.

docs.title: 13.6 Liquidity ratios
docs.text:
Liquidity ratios measure the ability to meet short-term obligations as they fall due.

Current ratio

\[ \text{Current ratio} = \frac{\text{Current assets}}{\text{Current liabilities}} \]

Meridian: current assets = 3,00,000 + 4,00,000 + 1,50,000 + 50,000 = ₹9,00,000; current liabilities = 3,00,000 + 1,50,000 = ₹4,50,000. Current ratio = 9,00,000 ÷ 4,50,000 = 2:1. A ratio of about 2:1 is often quoted as a rough benchmark for a manufacturing business; too low a ratio signals difficulty in paying debts, too high a ratio may mean idle funds.

Quick (liquid or acid-test) ratio

\[ \text{Quick ratio} = \frac{\text{Current assets} - \text{Inventories} - \text{Prepaid expenses}}{\text{Current liabilities}} \]

Inventories and prepaid expenses are excluded because they cannot quickly be turned into cash. Meridian: quick assets = 9,00,000 − 3,00,000 − 50,000 = ₹5,50,000. Quick ratio = 5,50,000 ÷ 4,50,000 = 1.22:1. A quick ratio of about 1:1 is often taken as satisfactory.

docs.title: 13.7 Solvency ratios
docs.text:
Solvency ratios measure the ability to meet long-term obligations and the balance between owners' funds and borrowed funds.

Debt-equity ratio

\[ \text{Debt-equity ratio} = \frac{\text{Long-term debt}}{\text{Shareholders' funds}} \]

Meridian: shareholders' funds = 10,00,000 + 3,50,000 = ₹13,50,000; long-term debt = ₹5,00,000. Debt-equity = 5,00,000 ÷ 13,50,000 = 0.37:1. A low ratio means the business relies mainly on owners' funds and is safe for lenders; a high ratio means more risk, but also more leverage for the owners when business is good.

Proprietary ratio

\[ \text{Proprietary ratio} = \frac{\text{Shareholders' funds}}{\text{Total assets}} \]

Meridian: 13,50,000 ÷ 23,00,000 = 0.59 (59% of the assets are financed by the owners).

Interest coverage ratio

\[ \text{Interest coverage} = \frac{\text{Profit before interest and tax}}{\text{Interest on long-term debt}} \]

Meridian: 4,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = 8 times. Operating profit could fall to one-eighth of its present level before the company could not meet its interest from profit.

docs.title: 13.8 Activity (turnover) ratios
docs.text:
Activity ratios measure how efficiently the business uses its assets. Averages of opening and closing balances are used where both are available.

Inventory turnover ratio

\[ \text{Inventory turnover} = \frac{\text{Cost of goods sold}}{\text{Average inventory}} \]

Meridian: average inventory = (2,00,000 + 3,00,000) ÷ 2 = ₹2,50,000. Inventory turnover = 12,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 4.8 times, so goods are held on average for 365 ÷ 4.8 = 76 days before being sold.

Trade receivables turnover ratio and average collection period

\[ \text{Receivables turnover} = \frac{\text{Credit revenue from operations}}{\text{Average trade receivables}}, \qquad \text{Collection period} = \frac{365}{\text{Receivables turnover}} \]

Meridian: average receivables = (3,00,000 + 4,00,000) ÷ 2 = ₹3,50,000. Turnover = 20,00,000 ÷ 3,50,000 = 5.71 times; collection period = 365 ÷ 5.714 = 64 days. If the company's credit terms are 45 days, customers are paying late.

Trade payables turnover ratio and average payment period

\[ \text{Payables turnover} = \frac{\text{Credit purchases}}{\text{Average trade payables}}, \qquad \text{Payment period} = \frac{365}{\text{Payables turnover}} \]

Credit purchases = cost of goods sold + closing inventory − opening inventory = 12,00,000 + 3,00,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹13,00,000. Average payables = (2,50,000 + 3,00,000) ÷ 2 = ₹2,75,000. Turnover = 13,00,000 ÷ 2,75,000 = 4.73 times; payment period = 365 ÷ 4.727 = 77 days.

Total asset turnover

\[ \text{Asset turnover} = \frac{\text{Revenue from operations}}{\text{Total assets}} \]

Meridian: 20,00,000 ÷ 23,00,000 = 0.87 times: each rupee of assets generated 87 paise of revenue.

docs.title: The working capital (operating) cycle
docs.text:
The time between paying for goods and receiving cash from customers is the working capital cycle:

\[ \text{Cycle} = \text{Inventory days} + \text{Collection days} - \text{Payment days} \]

Meridian: 76 + 64 − 77 = 63 days. For 63 days, on average, the company has paid for goods without yet being paid for them, and must finance that gap. Shortening the collection period would shorten the cycle and release cash.

docs.title: 13.9 Profitability ratios
docs.text:
Gross profit ratio

\[ \text{Gross profit ratio} = \frac{\text{Gross profit}}{\text{Revenue from operations}} \times 100 \]

Meridian: 8,00,000 ÷ 20,00,000 × 100 = 40%.

Operating ratio and operating profit ratio

\[ \text{Operating ratio} = \frac{\text{Cost of goods sold} + \text{Operating expenses}}{\text{Revenue from operations}} \times 100 \]

Meridian: (12,00,000 + 4,00,000) ÷ 20,00,000 × 100 = 80%. The operating profit ratio is the complement: 100 − 80 = 20% (4,00,000 ÷ 20,00,000).

Net profit ratio

\[ \text{Net profit ratio} = \frac{\text{Profit after tax}}{\text{Revenue from operations}} \times 100 \]

Meridian: 2,62,500 ÷ 20,00,000 × 100 = 13.13%.

Return on capital employed (ROCE)

\[ \text{ROCE} = \frac{\text{Profit before interest and tax}}{\text{Capital employed}} \times 100 \]

Capital employed = shareholders' funds + long-term debt = 13,50,000 + 5,00,000 = ₹18,50,000 (equivalently, total assets − current liabilities = 23,00,000 − 4,50,000). ROCE = 4,00,000 ÷ 18,50,000 × 100 = 21.62%. This is the return on all the long-term funds in the business, whoever provided them. Because it exceeds the 10% interest on the debentures, borrowing has increased the return to the shareholders.

Return on equity (ROE)

\[ \text{ROE} = \frac{\text{Profit after tax}}{\text{Shareholders' funds}} \times 100 \]

Meridian: 2,62,500 ÷ 13,50,000 × 100 = 19.44%.

Earnings per share (EPS) and price-earnings ratio

\[ \text{EPS} = \frac{\text{Profit after tax} - \text{Preference dividend}}{\text{Number of equity shares}}, \qquad \text{P/E ratio} = \frac{\text{Market price per share}}{\text{EPS}} \]

Meridian has no preference shares: EPS = 2,62,500 ÷ 1,00,000 = ₹2.625. If its shares were quoted at ₹31.50, the P/E ratio would be 31.50 ÷ 2.625 = 12 times: investors would be paying twelve rupees for each rupee of annual earnings.

docs.title: Breaking down return on equity
docs.text:
Return on equity can be split into three ratios, a method often called the DuPont analysis:

\[ \text{ROE} = \frac{\text{Profit after tax}}{\text{Revenue}} \times \frac{\text{Revenue}}{\text{Total assets}} \times \frac{\text{Total assets}}{\text{Shareholders' funds}} \]

The three factors are the net profit margin (profitability), the asset turnover (efficiency) and the equity multiplier (financial leverage). For Meridian: 13.125% × 0.8696 × 1.7037 = 19.44%, which agrees with the direct calculation. A company can raise its ROE by earning more on each sale, by using its assets harder, or by borrowing more; the breakdown shows which it is doing.

docs.title: 13.10 The ratios of Meridian Ltd at a glance
docs.text:
Ratio Formula Meridian Ltd, 2026 Current ratio Current assets ÷ current liabilities 2:1 Quick ratio Quick assets ÷ current liabilities 1.22:1 Debt-equity ratio Long-term debt ÷ shareholders' funds 0.37:1 Proprietary ratio Shareholders' funds ÷ total assets 0.59 Interest coverage EBIT ÷ interest 8 times Inventory turnover COGS ÷ average inventory 4.8 times (76 days) Receivables turnover Credit revenue ÷ average receivables 5.71 times (64 days) Payables turnover Credit purchases ÷ average payables 4.73 times (77 days) Asset turnover Revenue ÷ total assets 0.87 times Gross profit ratio Gross profit ÷ revenue 40% Operating ratio (COGS + operating expenses) ÷ revenue 80% Net profit ratio Profit after tax ÷ revenue 13.13% ROCE EBIT ÷ capital employed 21.62% ROE Profit after tax ÷ shareholders' funds 19.44% EPS Earnings for equity ÷ number of equity shares ₹2.625

Table 13.2. Summary of the ratios of Meridian Ltd.

Key idea

Read the ratios together, not one by one. Meridian Ltd is liquid (current ratio 2:1, quick ratio above 1), lightly geared (debt-equity 0.37) and comfortably able to pay interest (8 times). It is profitable and improving (net margin up from 10.78% to 13.13%, ROCE 21.6%). Its weak point is the collection of receivables (64 days), which lengthens its working capital cycle.

docs.title: 13.11 Limitations of ratio analysis
docs.text:
Ratios are powerful but must be used with care:

  • They are only as good as the statements. Ratios inherit every estimate, choice of method and error in the accounts, and they can be affected by window dressing (Chapter 14).
  • Historical cost. Assets at old costs make returns look higher in an old business than in a new one with the same performance.
  • Different accounting policies (depreciation methods, inventory valuation) make comparisons between businesses less reliable.
  • A balance sheet is a snapshot. Year-end balances may not be typical of the year, especially in a seasonal business.
  • No absolute standards. Rules of thumb such as 2:1 are rough guides; what is normal varies by industry.
  • Ratios ignore what is not in the accounts: the quality of management, the state of the market, technological change.
  • Inflation distorts comparisons across years.

Ratios raise questions; they rarely answer them by themselves. Their proper use is to direct attention to the areas that need a closer look.

docs.title: 13.12 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Financial statement analysis relates figures across items, years and businesses. Its tools are comparative statements, common-size statements, trend analysis, ratios and cash flow analysis.
  • Liquidity: current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) and quick ratio (excluding inventories and prepaid expenses).
  • Solvency: debt-equity ratio, proprietary ratio and interest coverage.
  • Activity: inventory, receivables and payables turnover (and the corresponding days), asset turnover; the working capital cycle is inventory days + collection days − payment days.
  • Profitability: gross profit ratio, operating ratio, net profit ratio, ROCE, ROE, EPS and P/E. ROE = net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier.
  • Ratios must be compared with the past, with other firms or with targets, and their limitations kept in mind.

docs.title: 13.13 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Current assets are ₹6,00,000, of which inventories are ₹2,20,000 and prepaid expenses ₹20,000. Current liabilities are ₹3,00,000. Compute the current ratio and the quick ratio.

Answer

Current ratio = 6,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 2:1. Quick assets = 6,00,000 − 2,20,000 − 20,000 = ₹3,60,000; quick ratio = 3,60,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 1.2:1.

Exercise 2

Revenue ₹12,00,000; gross profit 25% of revenue; opening inventory ₹1,00,000; closing inventory ₹1,40,000. Find the inventory turnover ratio and the number of days' inventory held.

Answer

Cost of goods sold = 12,00,000 × 75% = ₹9,00,000. Average inventory = (1,00,000 + 1,40,000) ÷ 2 = ₹1,20,000. Turnover = 9,00,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 7.5 times; days = 365 ÷ 7.5 = 48.7 days (about 49 days).

Exercise 3

A company's EBIT is ₹6,00,000, interest on 12% debentures is ₹1,20,000, tax is at 25%, and shareholders' funds are ₹20,00,000. Find the interest coverage ratio, the profit after tax, ROCE and ROE.

Answer

Interest coverage = 6,00,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 5 times. Debentures = 1,20,000 ÷ 12% = ₹10,00,000. Profit before tax = 6,00,000 − 1,20,000 = 4,80,000; tax 1,20,000; profit after tax ₹3,60,000. Capital employed = 20,00,000 + 10,00,000 = ₹30,00,000; ROCE = 20%. ROE = 3,60,000 ÷ 20,00,000 = 18%.

Exercise 4

Credit sales for the year are ₹7,30,000; trade receivables were ₹90,000 at the start and ₹1,10,000 at the end. Find the receivables turnover and the average collection period. If the credit period allowed is 30 days, comment.

Answer

Average receivables = ₹1,00,000. Turnover = 7,30,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = 7.3 times; collection period = 365 ÷ 7.3 = 50 days. Customers take 50 days against 30 allowed: credit control needs attention.

Exercise 5

State the effect (increase, decrease, no change) on a current ratio of 2:1 of: (a) paying a creditor in cash; (b) buying inventory on credit; (c) selling a fixed asset for cash; (d) collecting cash from a debtor.

Answer

Take current assets 2,00,000 and current liabilities 1,00,000, and a transaction of ₹20,000. (a) 1,80,000 ÷ 80,000 = 2.25: increase. (b) 2,20,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 1.83: decrease. (c) 2,20,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = 2.2: increase. (d) one current asset replaces another: no change. When the ratio is above 1, paying off a current liability with a current asset raises it, and adding equal amounts to both lowers it.

Exercise 6

Two companies each have ROE of 18%. Company P has a net margin of 6%, asset turnover of 2 and an equity multiplier of 1.5. Company Q has a net margin of 18%, asset turnover of 0.5 and an equity multiplier of 2. Verify the ROEs and contrast the two businesses.

Answer

P: 6% × 2 × 1.5 = 18%. Q: 18% × 0.5 × 2 = 18%. P earns thin margins on a high volume of sales with little borrowing, like a retailer; Q earns high margins on a large asset base and uses more debt, like a capital-intensive manufacturer. The same ROE hides very different businesses and risks.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Bank Reconciliation and Bills of Exchange
docs.text:
Agreeing the cash book with the bank, and accounting for written promises to pay

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain why the bank balance in the cash book differs from the balance in the bank statement.
  2. Prepare a bank reconciliation statement, starting from either balance, for a favourable balance and for an overdraft.
  3. Prepare an adjusted cash book and reconcile it with the bank statement.
  4. Define a bill of exchange and a promissory note and name their parties.
  5. Calculate the due date of a bill, including days of grace.
  6. Journalise the main transactions in bills in the books of the drawer and the drawee: retaining, discounting, endorsing and dishonour.

docs.title: 5.1 Two records of the same account
docs.text:
A business that keeps money in a bank has two records of that money. The business keeps one, in the bank column of its cash book (Chapter 4). The bank keeps the other, in its own books, and sends the customer a copy as a bank statement (traditionally a pass book). Both record the same deposits and the same cheques, so one might expect their balances to agree. On any given date they usually do not.

There is also a reversal of sides to keep in mind. In the business's cash book, money in the bank is an asset: a debit balance. In the bank's books, the same money is owed by the bank to the customer, a liability of the bank: a credit balance. So a favourable balance appears as a debit in the cash book and as a credit in the bank statement. An overdraft, when the business has withdrawn more than it deposited, appears as a credit in the cash book and a debit in the bank statement.

A bank reconciliation statement is a statement prepared on a date to explain the difference between the two balances, item by item, so that both records are shown to be correct (or the errors are found).

docs.title: 5.2 Causes of the difference
docs.text:
The causes fall into three groups.

Timing differences, where both records will agree in time:

  • Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment. The business credits its cash book when it issues the cheque. The bank pays it only when the payee presents it, which may be days later.
  • Cheques deposited but not yet credited (not yet cleared). The business debits its cash book when it deposits a cheque. The bank credits the account only when the cheque has been collected from the other bank.

Items recorded by the bank but not yet known to the business:

  • Bank charges and fees debited by the bank.
  • Interest credited on a deposit, or debited on an overdraft or loan.
  • Direct deposits by customers into the business's account, and amounts collected by the bank on the business's behalf (dividends, interest on investments).
  • Payments made by the bank under standing instructions, such as insurance premiums, loan instalments or utility bills.
  • Cheques deposited and dishonoured, which the bank reverses.

Errors, either in the cash book (a wrong amount, a receipt entered as a payment) or by the bank.

Key idea

Timing differences need no entry in the books: they will disappear on their own. Items the bank has recorded that the business has not yet recorded must be entered in the cash book, because they are real transactions of the business.

docs.title: 5.3 Preparing a bank reconciliation statement
docs.text:
Start with one balance and adjust it, item by item, to arrive at the other. For each item ask: has this item made the balance I am starting from larger or smaller than the balance I am working towards? If it has made the starting balance smaller, add it back; if larger, deduct it.

Starting from a favourable (debit) balance in the cash book and working towards the balance in the bank statement:

Item Effect on the bank statement balance compared with the cash book Adjustment Cheques issued but not yet presented Bank balance is higher (bank has not yet paid) Add Cheques deposited but not yet credited Bank balance is lower (bank has not yet credited) Deduct Bank charges debited by the bank Bank balance is lower Deduct Interest credited by the bank Bank balance is higher Add Direct deposits and collections by the bank Bank balance is higher Add Payments by the bank under standing instructions Bank balance is lower Deduct Cheque deposited and dishonoured Bank balance is lower Deduct

Table 5.1. Adjustments when starting from a favourable cash book balance.

When the starting point is the bank statement instead, every adjustment is reversed. When the balance is an overdraft, think in terms of the overdraft: an item that makes the bank's overdraft larger than the cash book's is added to the cash book overdraft, and so on. The worked examples show each case.

Example 5.1 Reconciliation starting from the cash book

On 31 March 2026 the bank column of the cash book of Nair Enterprises showed a debit balance of ₹48,500. Comparing the cash book with the bank statement revealed:

(a) Cheques of ₹12,400 issued to suppliers had not yet been presented for payment.

(b) Cheques of ₹9,600 deposited on 30 and 31 March had not yet been credited by the bank.

(c) Bank charges of ₹350 had been debited by the bank.

(d) Interest of ₹1,200 had been credited by the bank.

(e) A customer had deposited ₹5,000 directly into the business's account.

(f) The bank had paid an insurance premium of ₹3,600 under a standing instruction.

(g) A cheque of ₹2,000 from a customer, deposited in March, had been dishonoured; the bank statement showed the reversal but the cash book did not.

Bank Reconciliation Statement of Nair Enterprises as at 31 March 2026

Particulars ₹ ₹ Balance as per cash book (debit) 48,500 Add: (a) Cheques issued but not yet presented 12,400 (d) Interest credited by the bank 1,200 (e) Direct deposit by a customer 5,000 18,600 67,100 Less: (b) Cheques deposited but not yet credited 9,600 (c) Bank charges 350 (f) Insurance premium paid by the bank 3,600 (g) Cheque dishonoured 2,000 15,550 Balance as per bank statement (credit) 51,550

Check: 48,500 + 18,600 − 15,550 = 51,550.

docs.title: 5.4 The adjusted cash book
docs.text:
In practice, a careful accountant first brings the cash book up to date by recording the items that the bank has entered and the business has not: charges, interest, direct deposits, standing-instruction payments, dishonoured cheques and any errors in the cash book. The corrected balance is the true bank balance of the business, and it is this figure that goes into the balance sheet. The reconciliation statement that follows then contains only the timing differences (and any bank errors).

Example 5.2 Adjusted cash book and reconciliation (same data)

Adjusted Cash Book (bank column) as at 31 March 2026

Particulars ₹ Particulars ₹ To Balance b/d (unadjusted) 48,500 By Bank charges A/c 350 To Interest A/c 1,200 By Insurance A/c 3,600 To Customer (direct deposit) 5,000 By Customer (cheque dishonoured) 2,000 By Balance c/d (adjusted) 48,750 Total 54,700 Total 54,700

Bank Reconciliation Statement as at 31 March 2026

Particulars ₹ Balance as per adjusted cash book 48,750 Add: Cheques issued but not yet presented 12,400 61,150 Less: Cheques deposited but not yet credited 9,600 Balance as per bank statement 51,550

Both methods arrive at ₹51,550. The balance sheet shows the bank balance at ₹48,750, the adjusted cash book figure, because the uncleared cheques and unpresented cheques are the business's own transactions, correctly recorded.

Caution

Do not show the bank statement balance in the balance sheet. It is the bank's record, which lags behind the business's own record by the timing differences. The figure for the balance sheet is the adjusted cash book balance.

docs.title: 5.5 Reconciling an overdraft
docs.text:
When the business has an overdraft, the cash book shows a credit balance and the bank statement a debit balance. Work with the overdraft as a positive amount and ask, for each item, whether it makes the bank's overdraft larger or smaller than the cash book's.

Example 5.3 Reconciliation of an overdraft

On 31 March 2026 the cash book of Pillai & Co showed an overdraft of ₹25,000. On examination:

(a) Cheques of ₹6,000 issued had not been presented.

(b) Cheques of ₹4,500 deposited had not been credited.

(c) The bank had charged interest on the overdraft of ₹800.

(d) The bank had collected a dividend of ₹1,500 on the firm's behalf.

Particulars ₹ ₹ Overdraft as per cash book 25,000 Add: (b) Cheques deposited but not credited (bank overdraft is larger) 4,500 (c) Interest on overdraft charged by the bank 800 5,300 30,300 Less: (a) Cheques issued but not presented (bank has not yet paid them) 6,000 (d) Dividend collected by the bank 1,500 7,500 Overdraft as per bank statement 22,800

Reasoning: the bank has not yet paid the cheques issued, so its overdraft is smaller by ₹6,000; it has not yet credited the cheques deposited, so its overdraft is larger by ₹4,500; interest charged increases the overdraft; the dividend collected reduces it. 25,000 + 5,300 − 7,500 = ₹22,800.

docs.title: Starting from the bank statement
docs.text: A reconciliation can equally begin with the bank statement balance and arrive at the cash book balance; each adjustment is simply reversed. Starting from the bank statement balance of ₹51,550 in Example 5.1, one would deduct the unpresented cheques (12,400), interest (1,200) and direct deposit (5,000), and add the uncleared cheques (9,600), charges (350), insurance (3,600) and dishonoured cheque (2,000): 51,550 − 18,600 + 15,550 = ₹48,500, the cash book balance.

docs.title: 5.6 Bills of exchange and promissory notes
docs.text:
When goods are sold on credit, the seller relies on the buyer's word to pay. A bill of exchange turns that word into a written document that can be enforced in law and that the seller can use before the due date to raise money.

In India, bills of exchange, promissory notes and cheques are negotiable instruments governed by the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. In general terms:

  • A bill of exchange is an instrument in writing containing an unconditional order, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer of the instrument.
  • A promissory note is an instrument in writing containing an unconditional undertaking, signed by the maker, to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer of the instrument.
  • A cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand.

The essential difference is that a bill contains an order (the seller orders the buyer to pay), while a promissory note contains a promise (the buyer promises to pay). A bill must be accepted by the person on whom it is drawn before it binds him; a note binds its maker from the start.

docs.title: The parties to a bill
docs.text:
• The drawer is the person who writes (draws) the bill: usually the seller or creditor.
  • The drawee is the person on whom the bill is drawn and who is ordered to pay: usually the buyer or debtor. Once he has signed his acceptance on it, he is called the acceptor.
  • The payee is the person to whom the money is to be paid: the drawer himself, or a person to whom the drawer has passed the bill (an endorsee), or a bank that has discounted it.
Figure 5.1 The parties to a bill of exchange. The drawer (seller) sends goods and a bill to the drawee (buyer), who accepts it and returns it; the drawer keeps, discounts or endorses the bill, and on the due date the drawee pays the payee, who may be the drawer, a bank or an endorsee.

In the drawer's books an accepted bill is an asset called Bills Receivable (B/R); in the drawee's books it is a liability called Bills Payable (B/P).

docs.title: 5.7 Term and due date
docs.text:
A bill may be payable on demand (at sight) or after a stated period (a time bill), such as "three months after date" or "sixty days after sight". The period is the term of the bill.

For a time bill, the law adds three days of grace to the end of the term. The date of maturity (due date) is the date on which the term ends plus three days. The main rules for counting are:

  • A term stated in months ends on the same date of the month in which it ends. If that month has no such date, the term ends on the last day of that month.
  • A term stated in days excludes the date of the bill and counts the following days.
  • If the date of maturity is a public holiday, the bill falls due on the preceding business day.

Example 5.4 Calculating due dates

Bill Term ends Add 3 days of grace Date of maturity Dated 1 January 2026, at three months after date 1 April 2026 +3 days 4 April 2026 Dated 10 March 2026, at 60 days after date 9 May 2026 +3 days 12 May 2026 Dated 31 January 2026, at one month after date 28 February 2026 (no 31 February) +3 days 3 March 2026 Dated 15 August 2025, at two months after date 15 October 2025 +3 days 18 October 2025

For the 60-day bill: March has 31 days, so 21 days remain after 10 March (11 to 31 March); April adds 30 days (total 51); 9 more days in May make 60, so the term ends on 9 May.

docs.title: 5.8 What the holder can do with a bill
docs.text:
Once a bill has been accepted, its holder (the drawer, to begin with) has four choices:

  1. Retain it till maturity and present it to the drawee for payment on the due date.
  2. Discount it with a bank: hand it to the bank before maturity and receive the amount of the bill less a charge called discount, which is interest for the unexpired period. The bank then collects from the drawee.
  3. Endorse it to a creditor in settlement of a debt, by signing it over. The creditor (endorsee) collects from the drawee.
  4. Send it to the bank for collection: the bank holds it and collects the amount on the due date for a small fee.

If the drawee fails to pay on the due date, the bill is dishonoured. The holder usually has the dishonour formally recorded by a notary public, who charges a fee called noting charges; this provides legal evidence of dishonour. Whoever holds the bill at that time pays the noting charges and recovers them, along with the amount of the bill, from the person who passed the bill to him, and ultimately from the drawee. On dishonour, the drawee's debt to the drawer revives as an ordinary debt.

docs.title: 5.9 Journal entries for bills
docs.text:
The entries follow the ordinary rules of debit and credit. Bills Receivable is an asset; Bills Payable is a liability.

Example 5.5 Bill discounted and later dishonoured

On 1 January 2026 Anil sold goods for ₹20,000 to Bharat and drew on him a bill at three months, which Bharat accepted. On 4 January Anil discounted the bill with his bank at 12% per annum, the bank charging discount for three months. On the due date the bill was dishonoured, and the bank paid noting charges of ₹100.

Discount = 20,000 × 12/100 × 3/12 = ₹600. Due date: 4 April 2026.

Journal of Anil (drawer)

Date 2026 Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) Jan 1 Bharat ... Dr 20,000 To Sales A/c 20,000 (Being goods sold on credit) Jan 1 Bills Receivable A/c ... Dr 20,000 To Bharat 20,000 (Being Bharat's acceptance received for three months) Jan 4 Bank A/c ... Dr 19,400 Discount on Bills A/c ... Dr 600 To Bills Receivable A/c 20,000 (Being the bill discounted at 12% p.a.) Apr 4 Bharat ... Dr 20,100 To Bank A/c 20,100 (Being the discounted bill dishonoured; bank paid noting charges ₹100)

Journal of Bharat (drawee)

Date 2026 Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) Jan 1 Purchases A/c ... Dr 20,000 To Anil 20,000 (Being goods bought on credit) Jan 1 Anil ... Dr 20,000 To Bills Payable A/c 20,000 (Being acceptance given to Anil) Apr 4 Bills Payable A/c ... Dr 20,000 Noting Charges A/c ... Dr 100 To Anil 20,100 (Being our acceptance dishonoured and noting charges payable)

After the dishonour, Bharat again owes Anil ₹20,100 as an ordinary debt, and Anil has repaid the bank. The discount of ₹600 remains Anil's expense. Bharat does not record the discounting at all: it is a matter between Anil and his bank.

The entries for the other choices, for the same bill of ₹20,000, are summarised below.

Event Drawer's books Drawee's books Bill retained and honoured at maturity Bank Dr 20,000; To Bills Receivable 20,000 Bills Payable Dr 20,000; To Bank 20,000 Bill endorsed to Chetan, a creditor of the drawer Chetan Dr 20,000; To Bills Receivable 20,000 No entry Endorsed bill honoured No entry Bills Payable Dr 20,000; To Bank 20,000 Endorsed bill dishonoured, noting ₹100 paid by Chetan Drawee Dr 20,100; To Chetan 20,100 Bills Payable Dr 20,000; Noting Charges Dr 100; To Drawer 20,100 Retained bill dishonoured, noting ₹100 paid by drawer Drawee Dr 20,100; To Bills Receivable 20,000; To Bank 100 Bills Payable Dr 20,000; Noting Charges Dr 100; To Drawer 20,100 Bill sent to bank for collection Bills Sent for Collection Dr 20,000; To Bills Receivable 20,000; on collection, Bank Dr; To Bills Sent for Collection No entry until payment, then as for honour

Table 5.2. Entries for the main events in the life of a bill of ₹20,000.

Note

Bills of exchange are less common in everyday trade than they once were; many payments are now made electronically. Cheques, however, are bills of exchange, and the ideas of this section (endorsement, dishonour, the drawer's liability) apply to them too. Banks also continue to discount trade bills as a form of short-term finance.

docs.title: 5.10 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The cash book and the bank statement record the same account from opposite sides, and their balances differ because of timing differences, items recorded only by the bank, and errors.
  • A bank reconciliation statement starts from one balance and adds or deducts each difference to arrive at the other. Unpresented cheques and bank credits make the bank balance higher; uncleared cheques, bank charges, standing-instruction payments and dishonoured cheques make it lower.
  • The adjusted cash book records the bank-originated items; its balance is the figure for the balance sheet, and only timing differences remain to be reconciled.
  • For an overdraft, reason in terms of whether each item makes the bank's overdraft larger or smaller.
  • A bill of exchange is an unconditional written order to pay, accepted by the drawee; a promissory note is an unconditional written promise to pay. The parties to a bill are the drawer, the drawee and the payee.
  • The date of maturity of a time bill is the end of its term plus three days of grace, brought forward if it falls on a public holiday.
  • The holder may retain, discount, endorse or send a bill for collection. On dishonour, the drawee's debt revives with the noting charges.

docs.title: 5.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

On 31 March 2026 the cash book of Kaur Traders showed a bank balance of ₹36,200. Cheques issued but not presented ₹8,400; cheques deposited but not credited ₹5,700; bank charges ₹250; interest credited ₹900; a customer paid ₹3,000 directly into the bank. Prepare the bank reconciliation statement.

Answer Particulars ₹ ₹ Balance as per cash book 36,200 Add: Cheques not presented 8,400 Interest credited 900 Direct deposit 3,000 12,300 48,500 Less: Cheques not credited 5,700 Bank charges 250 5,950 Balance as per bank statement 42,550

Exercise 2

For the data of Exercise 1, find the adjusted cash book balance that should appear in the balance sheet.

Answer

36,200 + 900 + 3,000 − 250 = ₹39,850. Check: 39,850 + 8,400 − 5,700 = 42,550, the bank statement balance.

Exercise 3

The bank statement of a firm shows an overdraft of ₹18,000 on 31 March 2026. Cheques issued but not presented ₹4,000; cheques deposited but not credited ₹2,500; interest on overdraft debited by the bank ₹600, not in the cash book. Find the overdraft as per the cash book.

Answer

Start from the bank overdraft of ₹18,000. The unpresented cheques make the cash book overdraft larger (the cash book has already deducted them): add 4,000. The uncleared deposits make the cash book overdraft smaller (the cash book has already added them): deduct 2,500. The interest makes the bank overdraft larger than the cash book's: deduct 600. Overdraft as per cash book = 18,000 + 4,000 − 2,500 − 600 = ₹18,900.

Check from the cash book side: 18,900 − 4,000 + 2,500 + 600 = 18,000.

Exercise 4

Find the date of maturity of: (a) a bill dated 5 May 2025 at 90 days after date; (b) a bill dated 30 November 2025 at three months after date.

Answer

(a) Days remaining in May after the 5th: 26; June 30 (56); July 31 (87); 3 more days in August make 90, so the term ends on 3 August 2025. Adding 3 days of grace: 6 August 2025.

(b) Three months after 30 November is 30 February, which does not exist, so the term ends on the last day of February, 28 February 2026. Adding 3 days: 3 March 2026.

Exercise 5

Mohan sold goods for ₹15,000 to Sohan and drew a bill at two months, which Sohan accepted. Mohan endorsed the bill to his creditor Rohan. At maturity the bill was dishonoured and Rohan paid noting charges of ₹50. Journalise in Mohan's books.

Answer Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) Sohan ... Dr 15,000 To Sales A/c 15,000 Bills Receivable A/c ... Dr 15,000 To Sohan 15,000 Rohan ... Dr 15,000 To Bills Receivable A/c 15,000 Sohan ... Dr 15,050 To Rohan 15,050

On dishonour Mohan becomes liable to Rohan again for the bill and the noting charges, and Sohan becomes liable to Mohan for the same amount.

Exercise 6

A bill of ₹30,000 with four months to run is discounted at 9% per annum. How much does the drawer receive?

Answer

Discount = 30,000 × 9/100 × 4/12 = ₹900. The drawer receives 30,000 − 900 = ₹29,100.

docs.title: Chapter 12: The Cash Flow Statement
docs.text:
Where the cash came from and where it went: operating, investing and financing activities

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain why profit and cash differ and why users need a cash flow statement.
  2. Define cash and cash equivalents.
  3. Classify cash flows as operating, investing or financing.
  4. Compute cash flows from operating activities by the direct method and by the indirect method.
  5. Prepare a complete cash flow statement from two balance sheets and additional information.
  6. Read the pattern of a company's cash flows.

docs.title: 12.1 Profit is not cash
docs.text:
A business can be profitable and still run out of cash. Suppose a trader doubles his sales in a year by giving customers three months' credit and building up a large stock. His profit rises, but the cash from the extra sales has not yet come in, and the cash spent on stock is tied up on the shelves. If a supplier or a bank demands payment, he may be unable to pay, however good his profit looks. Many businesses that fail are profitable on paper.

The difference arises because profit is measured on the accrual basis (Chapter 1): revenue is recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, and non-cash items such as depreciation are deducted. Cash moves on its own timetable. Neither the statement of profit and loss nor the balance sheet tells a reader directly how much cash the business generated from its operations, how much it spent on new assets, or how it raised the money.

The cash flow statement answers those questions. It shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, classified into three activities. Companies other than certain small companies are required to present one with their financial statements; the relevant standards are AS 3 and, for companies following Ind AS, Ind AS 7 (based on IAS 7), which agree on the main principles.

Users rely on it to judge:

  • the business's ability to generate cash from its operations;
  • its ability to pay its debts, interest and dividends;
  • its need for outside finance;
  • the quality of its profit: a profit that is regularly turned into cash is more reliable than one that is not.

docs.title: 12.2 Cash and cash equivalents
docs.text:
Cash comprises cash on hand and demand deposits with banks. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value. An investment normally qualifies as a cash equivalent only when it has a short maturity, of, say, three months or less from the date of acquisition. Shares are generally not cash equivalents, because their value can change.

Movements between cash and cash equivalents (depositing cash in a two-month deposit, for instance) are not cash flows: they are part of the business's cash management.

docs.title: 12.3 The three activities
docs.text:
Figure 12.1 The three activities of the cash flow statement. Cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities together make up the net change in cash; for Lotus Ltd (Example 12.2) operating activities brought in ₹1,91,000, investing activities used ₹1,49,000 and financing activities netted to zero, so cash rose by ₹42,000 from ₹18,000 to ₹60,000.

Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities of the business, and other activities that are not investing or financing. Examples:

  • cash receipts from the sale of goods and services, royalties, fees and commissions;
  • cash payments to suppliers of goods and services;
  • cash payments to and on behalf of employees;
  • payments of income tax, unless they can be specifically identified with investing or financing.

Investing activities are the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and of investments not included in cash equivalents. Examples:

  • payments to buy property, plant and equipment and intangible assets;
  • receipts from the sale of such assets;
  • payments to buy, and receipts from selling, shares and debentures of other entities;
  • loans made to others and their repayment.

Financing activities change the size and composition of the owners' capital and the borrowings of the business. Examples:

  • proceeds from issuing shares;
  • proceeds from issuing debentures and raising loans;
  • repayments of borrowings, redemption of debentures and preference shares, buy-back of shares;
  • for a non-financial business, interest and dividends paid.

docs.text: Some important transactions involve no cash: buying a building by issuing shares to the seller, converting debentures into shares. They are left out of the cash flow statement, but disclosed in the notes so that users are aware of them.

docs.title: 12.4 Operating cash flow: direct and indirect methods
docs.text:
Cash flows from operating activities can be reported in two ways.

The direct method lists the major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments: cash received from customers, cash paid to suppliers, cash paid to employees and for expenses, tax paid. Each is found by adjusting the corresponding revenue or expense for the change in the related receivable or payable.

The indirect method starts with the profit before tax and adjusts it for (a) non-cash items such as depreciation, (b) items that belong to investing or financing activities, such as a profit or loss on sale of fixed assets and interest expense, and (c) changes in working capital (inventories, receivables, payables).

Both methods give the same figure for net cash from operating activities. The direct method shows more about the sources and uses of cash and is encouraged by the standards; the indirect method is far more common in practice because it is easier to prepare from the financial statements and it shows why profit and cash differ.

Example 12.1 Operating cash flow by the direct method

A trading business provides: sales (all on credit) ₹5,00,000; trade receivables at the start ₹40,000 and at the end ₹55,000; purchases (all on credit) ₹3,00,000; trade payables at the start ₹30,000 and at the end ₹38,000; operating expenses (excluding depreciation) ₹80,000; outstanding expenses at the start ₹5,000 and at the end ₹3,000; income tax paid ₹20,000.

Particulars Working ₹ Cash received from customers 5,00,000 + 40,000 − 55,000 4,85,000 Cash paid to suppliers 3,00,000 + 30,000 − 38,000 (2,92,000) Cash paid for operating expenses 80,000 + 5,000 − 3,000 (82,000) Cash generated from operations 1,11,000 Income tax paid (20,000) Net cash from operating activities 91,000

Receivables rose by ₹15,000, so customers paid ₹15,000 less than the sales. Payables rose by ₹8,000, so suppliers were paid ₹8,000 less than the purchases. Outstanding expenses fell by ₹2,000, so ₹2,000 more was paid than the expense charged.

Key idea

For working capital: an increase in a current asset uses cash (deduct it); an increase in a current liability saves cash (add it). Decreases work the other way round.

docs.title: 12.6 Reading a cash flow statement
docs.text:
The signs of the three sections tell a story about the business.

Operating Investing Financing A typical reading Positive Negative Negative A healthy, mature business: its operations pay for new assets and for returns to lenders and owners Positive Negative Positive A growing business: operations generate cash, but expansion needs more, raised from lenders or owners Negative Negative Positive A young or struggling business living on outside finance; sustainable only for a time Negative Positive Negative or positive A business selling assets to survive or to repay debt; a warning sign if it lasts

Table 12.3. Patterns of cash flow.

Lotus Ltd generated ₹1,91,000 from operations, more than its profit after tax of ₹1,20,000, mainly because depreciation of ₹60,000 is not a cash cost. It spent heavily on new plant (₹2,10,000), paying for it partly from operations and partly from asset sales; it raised ₹1,00,000 from new shares and used the same amount to repay debentures, pay interest and pay a dividend. It ended the year with more cash than it started. That is the profile of a sound business that is investing for growth.

A useful single figure is free cash flow: net cash from operating activities less capital expenditure (here 1,91,000 − 2,10,000 = −₹19,000). A negative figure in a year of heavy investment is not alarming in itself, but a business whose free cash flow is negative year after year depends on outside finance.

docs.title: 12.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Profit and cash differ because of accruals, non-cash items and working capital; the cash flow statement explains the change in cash and cash equivalents.
  • Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments with insignificant risk of change in value, normally maturing within three months.
  • Operating activities are the main revenue-producing activities; investing activities are the purchase and sale of long-term assets and investments; financing activities change capital and borrowings.
  • For non-financial businesses, interest and dividends paid are financing; interest and dividends received are investing; tax paid is operating.
  • The direct method lists gross receipts and payments; the indirect method adjusts profit before tax for non-cash items, investing and financing items and working capital changes. Both give the same answer.
  • Increases in current assets use cash; increases in current liabilities save cash.
  • The pattern of signs of the three sections, and free cash flow, show whether a business funds itself or depends on outside money.

docs.title: 12.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each as operating, investing or financing for a manufacturing company: (a) cash paid to suppliers; (b) purchase of machinery; (c) issue of debentures; (d) dividend received on shares held; (e) interest paid on a bank loan; (f) income tax paid; (g) sale of an old building; (h) buy-back of own shares.

Answer

(a) operating; (b) investing; (c) financing; (d) investing; (e) financing; (f) operating; (g) investing; (h) financing.

Exercise 2

Profit before tax ₹2,40,000; depreciation ₹50,000; profit on sale of land ₹20,000; interest expense ₹15,000; increase in inventories ₹30,000; decrease in receivables ₹12,000; decrease in payables ₹8,000; tax paid ₹55,000. Find net cash from operating activities.

Answer

Operating profit before working capital changes = 2,40,000 + 50,000 − 20,000 + 15,000 = ₹2,85,000. Working capital: −30,000 + 12,000 − 8,000 = −₹26,000. Cash generated = ₹2,59,000. Less tax paid ₹55,000: ₹2,04,000.

Exercise 3

Machinery (net) was ₹4,00,000 at the start of the year and ₹4,80,000 at the end. Depreciation for the year was ₹45,000. A machine with a book value of ₹25,000 was sold for ₹32,000. Find the cash paid for new machinery and the cash flow from investing activities relating to machinery.

Answer

Purchases = closing 4,80,000 + depreciation 45,000 + book value sold 25,000 − opening 4,00,000 = ₹1,50,000. Investing cash flow = −1,50,000 + 32,000 = −₹1,18,000. (The profit on sale of ₹7,000 is deducted in the operating section.)

Exercise 4

Provision for tax was ₹40,000 at the start and ₹55,000 at the end of the year; the tax charged in the statement of profit and loss was ₹70,000. How much tax was paid?

Answer

Tax paid = 40,000 + 70,000 − 55,000 = ₹55,000.

Exercise 5

A company's net cash from operating activities has been negative for three years, while its profit has been positive. Suggest two reasons and say why a lender should be concerned.

Answer

Possible reasons: sales are growing on long credit, so receivables are rising faster than collections; inventory is building up, perhaps because goods are not selling; or revenue is being recognised aggressively. A lender should be concerned because interest and repayments must be paid in cash; a business whose operations consume cash must keep borrowing or selling assets to pay its lenders, and its reported profit may not be of good quality.

Exercise 6

Cash sales ₹1,20,000; credit sales ₹3,80,000; receivables rose from ₹60,000 to ₹75,000 during the year. Compute the cash received from customers.

Answer

Cash received = cash sales 1,20,000 + credit sales 3,80,000 + opening receivables 60,000 − closing receivables 75,000 = ₹4,85,000.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Company Accounts
docs.text:
Share capital, the issue and forfeiture of shares, debentures, and the format of a company's financial statements

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Describe the main features of a company and how its accounts differ from those of a sole trader or partnership.
  2. Explain the categories of share capital and the kinds of shares.
  3. Journalise the issue of shares at par and at a premium, payable in instalments, including over-subscription.
  4. Journalise the forfeiture and reissue of shares.
  5. Distinguish debentures from shares and record their issue.
  6. Present a company's balance sheet and statement of profit and loss in the vertical format, with notes on share capital and reserves.

docs.title: 11.1 The company
docs.text:
A company is an association of persons formed and registered under company law. Its main features are:

  • Separate legal entity. The company is a legal person distinct from its members. It owns property, makes contracts, sues and is sued in its own name. The business entity concept of Chapter 1 is, for a company, a fact of law.
  • Limited liability. In a company limited by shares, a member's liability is limited to the amount unpaid on his shares. If the company fails, its creditors cannot reach the members' private property.
  • Perpetual succession. The company continues to exist whatever happens to its members; shares change hands, members die, but the company goes on until it is wound up according to law.
  • Transferable shares. The shares of a public company are, in general, freely transferable; those of a private company are subject to restrictions in its articles.
  • Separation of ownership and management. The members (shareholders) own the company, but it is managed by a board of directors whom they elect. This separation is why company accounts are so closely regulated: the owners depend on accounts prepared by the managers.

Companies may be private or public, and public companies may be listed on a stock exchange. Company law requires every company to keep proper books of account, to prepare financial statements in a prescribed form that give a true and fair view and comply with the notified accounting standards, to have them audited, and to file them with the registrar. Listed companies have further disclosure duties under securities regulation. The details of these requirements change from time to time; this chapter describes them in general terms.

The ledger of a company is kept by the same double-entry rules as any other. What is distinctive is the owners' side of the balance sheet. Instead of a single capital account per owner, there is share capital, divided into many units called shares, and the profits kept in the business are shown separately as reserves and surplus.

docs.title: 11.2 Share capital
docs.text:
The capital of a company is divided into shares of a fixed amount, called the nominal (face or par) value, such as ₹10 or ₹100 each. Share capital is described at several levels:

  • Authorised (nominal or registered) capital: the maximum amount of share capital the company is permitted to issue, as stated in its memorandum of association. It can be increased by following the procedure laid down in law.
  • Issued capital: the part of the authorised capital that has been offered for subscription.
  • Subscribed capital: the part of the issued capital that has actually been taken up (applied for and allotted).
  • Called-up capital: the part of the subscribed capital that the company has asked shareholders to pay so far.
  • Paid-up capital: the part of the called-up capital that shareholders have actually paid. The amount called up but not paid is calls in arrears; it is deducted from called-up capital.

Any part of subscribed capital not yet called is uncalled capital. A company may decide that part of its uncalled capital will be called only in the event of winding up; this is reserve capital.

Figure 11.1 The categories of share capital. Five nested layers of share capital: authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up, each a part of the one above.

docs.title: Kinds of shares
docs.text:
• Preference shares carry a preferential right to a dividend at a fixed rate, and to repayment of capital on winding up, before the equity shareholders. They may be cumulative (unpaid dividends accumulate and must be paid before any equity dividend) or non-cumulative; participating (sharing in surplus profits beyond the fixed dividend) or non-participating; redeemable (repaid after a period) or irredeemable as the law permits; convertible into equity shares or not.
  • Equity shares are all shares that are not preference shares. Equity shareholders bear the residual risk: they receive dividends only after preference dividends, and capital only after all creditors and preference shareholders have been paid. In return, they have voting rights and the benefit of all remaining profits.

docs.title: 11.3 The issue of shares
docs.text:
A company invites the public (or a selected group) to subscribe for shares, receives applications with application money, allots shares to the applicants (asking for allotment money), and later makes one or more calls for the balance. The amounts payable on application, on allotment and on each call are stated in the offer.

Shares may be issued:

  • at par, at their nominal value;
  • at a premium, at more than their nominal value. The premium is not share capital; it is credited to a separate Securities Premium Account, which company law allows to be used only for specified purposes, such as issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses or the expenses and discount of issues of shares and debentures, and buying back the company's own shares.
  • at a discount, below nominal value. Company law generally prohibits this, apart from limited exceptions; it is not dealt with here.

The accounts used in the books of the company are: Share Application Account, Share Allotment Account, Share First Call Account (and further call accounts), Share Capital Account, Securities Premium Account, and Bank. The application, allotment and call accounts are temporary accounts that collect the amounts due and received; each should be closed when all money has been received.

docs.title: 11.4 Forfeiture and reissue
docs.text:
If a shareholder fails to pay an allotment or call, the directors may, after due notice and as the articles permit, forfeit the shares: the shareholder loses the shares and the money already paid on them. On forfeiture:

  • Share Capital Account is debited with the amount called up on the forfeited shares (not their full nominal value, unless fully called);
  • the allotment or call accounts are credited with the amounts unpaid;
  • Share Forfeiture (Forfeited Shares) Account is credited with the amount already received on those shares;
  • if the shares were issued at a premium and the premium has not been received, Securities Premium Account is debited with the unpaid premium; a premium already received is not touched.

Forfeited shares may be reissued at any price, but the price, plus the amount already credited to Share Forfeiture Account for them, must at least equal the amount credited to share capital as paid up. Any discount on reissue is debited to Share Forfeiture Account. After reissue, the balance remaining in Share Forfeiture Account on the reissued shares is a capital profit and is transferred to Capital Reserve.

Example 11.1 Issue at a premium, forfeiture and reissue

Sunrise Ltd has an authorised capital of ₹10,00,000 in equity shares of ₹10 each. It issues 50,000 equity shares at ₹12 per share (a premium of ₹2), payable:

docs.title: Over-subscription
docs.text:
When applications exceed the shares offered, the directors may reject some applications outright (refunding their money), allot shares pro rata (in proportion) to the rest, or combine the two. Excess application money from applicants who receive fewer shares than they applied for is usually kept and adjusted towards the allotment money due from them, with any amount beyond that refunded.

Suppose Sunrise Ltd had received applications for 60,000 shares and allotted the 50,000 shares pro rata to all applicants. Application money received = 60,000 × ₹3 = ₹1,80,000. Of this, 50,000 × ₹3 = ₹1,50,000 is needed on application; the excess of ₹30,000 is adjusted towards allotment.

docs.title: 11.6 The financial statements of a company
docs.text:
Company law prescribes the form and content of a company's balance sheet and statement of profit and loss (in India, in a schedule to the Companies Act, 2013, with separate divisions for companies following Ind AS and those following the other Accounting Standards). The financial statements of a company include:

  1. a balance sheet at the end of the year;
  2. a statement of profit and loss for the year;
  3. a cash flow statement for the year (Chapter 12), subject to exemptions for certain small companies;
  4. a statement of changes in equity, where applicable (for companies following Ind AS);
  5. notes, including the significant accounting policies and the details behind the figures on the face of the statements.

Both main statements are presented in vertical form, with figures for the current and the previous year side by side, and with the details placed in numbered notes. The outline below follows the general structure for companies that do not follow Ind AS; companies following Ind AS use similar headings with some differences in terms (for example, "Equity" with "Equity share capital" and "Other equity" in place of "Shareholders' funds").

docs.title: 11.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A company is a separate legal entity with limited liability, perpetual succession and transferable shares, managed by directors on behalf of shareholders; its accounts are regulated by company law and standards.
  • Share capital is authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up; calls in arrears are deducted from called-up capital. Shares are equity or preference.
  • Application, allotment and call accounts collect the money due on shares; a premium is credited to Securities Premium Account, whose uses are restricted by law.
  • On forfeiture, share capital is debited with the amount called up, unpaid calls are credited, and the amount received is credited to Share Forfeiture Account. On reissue, any discount is met from the forfeiture balance, and the remaining balance on reissued shares goes to Capital Reserve.
  • Debentures are borrowings; their interest is a charge against profit.
  • A company presents a vertical balance sheet (shareholders' funds, non-current liabilities, current liabilities; non-current and current assets) and a statement of profit and loss ending in profit for the period and earnings per share, with details in notes.

Exercise 5

Why is the premium received on an issue of shares not treated as profit available for dividend?

Answer

The premium is part of the capital contributed by shareholders, not a profit earned from operations. Treating it as distributable profit would return capital to shareholders in the guise of dividends, to the detriment of creditors who rely on the company's capital. Company law therefore requires it to be kept in Securities Premium Account and used only for specified capital purposes.

A company's profit after tax is ₹12,60,000. It has 4,20,000 equity shares and no preference shares. Find its earnings per share. How would the answer change if it also had preference shares with an annual dividend of ₹1,50,000?

EPS = 12,60,000 ÷ 4,20,000 = ₹3.00. With preference shares, the preference dividend is deducted first: (12,60,000 − 1,50,000) ÷ 4,20,000 = 11,10,000 ÷ 4,20,000 = ₹2.64 (to two decimals).

docs.title: Chapter 7: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
docs.text:
Spreading the cost of assets over their lives, and setting amounts aside for losses and for the future

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain what depreciation is, why it is charged and what causes it.
  2. Compute depreciation by the straight line and written down value methods and compare them.
  3. Record depreciation by charging it to the asset account and through a provision for depreciation account, including part-year charges and the sale of an asset.
  4. Explain what a provision is and account for bad debts and a provision for doubtful debts.
  5. Explain what a reserve is, name the main kinds of reserve, and distinguish a provision from a reserve.

docs.title: 7.1 What depreciation is
docs.text:
A delivery van bought for ₹8,00,000 will serve a business for several years and then be sold for a fraction of its cost or scrapped. Its cost is not an expense of the year in which it was bought, because it helps to earn revenue in every year of its use. Nor can it be ignored, because by the end of its life the van will have been used up. The accounting answer is to spread the cost, less whatever is expected to be recovered at the end, over the years of use. The part charged to each year is depreciation.

Depreciation is best understood as a process of allocation, not of valuation. It allocates the cost of an asset to the periods that benefit from it, in keeping with the matching concept. The book value of an asset after depreciation (cost less accumulated depreciation) is the part of its cost not yet charged to profit; it is not an estimate of what the asset could be sold for.

Depreciation applies to tangible fixed assets with limited lives: buildings, plant and machinery, furniture, vehicles, computers. Land normally has an unlimited life and is not depreciated. The equivalent process for intangible assets such as patents is called amortisation, and for natural resources such as mines and quarries, depletion.

docs.title: Causes of depreciation
docs.text:
• Wear and tear from use: machines wear out, vehicles run up kilometres.
  • Passage of time: some assets, such as a lease or a patent, expire after a fixed period whether used or not.
  • Obsolescence: a newer, better or cheaper asset makes the old one uneconomic before it wears out; computers are a common example.
  • Depletion: a wasting asset such as a mine is used up as its contents are extracted.
  • Accidents: damage that permanently reduces the asset's service.

docs.title: Why depreciation must be charged
docs.text:
1. To find the true profit. The asset is used up in earning revenue, so part of its cost is an expense of each year. Leaving it out overstates profit.
  2. To show a fair financial position. Showing a ten-year-old machine at its original cost would overstate the assets.
  3. To keep capital intact. Profit measured after depreciation can be withdrawn without eating into the capital invested in assets.
  4. To comply with law and standards. Accounting standards on property, plant and equipment, and company law, require depreciation to be charged.

Tax law also allows a deduction for depreciation, but it has its own rates and rules, which often differ from those used in the financial statements.

docs.title: 7.2 The amount to be depreciated
docs.text:
Three figures decide depreciation:

  • Cost: the purchase price plus all costs needed to bring the asset to working condition: freight, installation, trial runs, import duties and non-refundable taxes.
  • Residual (scrap or salvage) value: the amount expected to be recovered at the end of the asset's useful life, net of disposal costs.
  • Useful life: the period over which the asset is expected to be used by the business, in years or in units of output.

The depreciable amount is cost less residual value. Under the accounting standards the residual value and useful life are estimates that should be reviewed periodically, and the method should reflect the pattern in which the asset's benefits are consumed. Company law also lays down indicative useful lives for classes of assets; the business may use different estimates where it can justify them.

docs.title: 7.3 The straight line method
docs.text:
Under the straight line method (also called the fixed instalment or original cost method), the same amount of depreciation is charged every year:

\[ \text{Annual depreciation} = \frac{\text{Cost} - \text{Residual value}}{\text{Useful life in years}} \]

The rate is the annual depreciation as a percentage of cost. The book value falls by equal amounts each year and reaches the residual value at the end of the useful life.

docs.title: 7.4 The written down value method
docs.text:
Under the written down value method (also called the diminishing balance or reducing balance method), a fixed percentage is applied each year to the book value at the start of the year, that is, to the cost less all depreciation already charged. Because the book value falls each year, so does the depreciation. The charge is highest in the first year, when the asset is new and most productive and repairs are lowest, and falls as the asset ages and repairs rise; the total of depreciation plus repairs is therefore roughly even over the asset's life.

Under this method the book value never reaches zero. The rate that would bring cost \(C\) down to residual value \(S\) in \(n\) years is

\[ r = 1 - \left(\frac{S}{C}\right)^{1/n} \]

which for a ₹2,00,000 asset with a residual value of ₹20,000 after 5 years is \(1 - 0.1^{0.2} = 0.369\), or about 36.9%. In practice a round rate is usually chosen.

Example 7.1 The two methods compared

A machine is bought on 1 April 2025 for ₹1,80,000; installation costs ₹20,000. Its useful life is 5 years and its residual value ₹20,000. Compute depreciation (a) by the straight line method and (b) by the written down value method at 20% per annum. The year ends on 31 March.

Cost = 1,80,000 + 20,000 = ₹2,00,000.

(a) Straight line. Annual depreciation = (2,00,000 − 20,000) ÷ 5 = ₹36,000, a rate of 18% on cost.

docs.title: 7.5 Recording depreciation
docs.text:
There are two ways to record depreciation in the books.

Method 1: charging depreciation to the asset account. Each year:

Entry Dr Cr For the year's depreciation Depreciation A/c Asset A/c To close the depreciation account Profit and Loss A/c Depreciation A/c

The asset account then shows the book value. Its weakness is that the original cost of the asset disappears from the ledger.

Method 2: creating a provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account. Each year:

Entry Dr Cr For the year's depreciation Depreciation A/c (or Profit and Loss A/c directly) Provision for Depreciation A/c To close the depreciation account Profit and Loss A/c Depreciation A/c

The asset account stays at cost, and the provision account accumulates the total depreciation. The balance sheet shows the asset at cost less accumulated depreciation, which tells the reader both how much was spent and how much of it has been used up. This is the method used by companies.

docs.title: Part-year depreciation
docs.text: An asset bought or sold during the year is depreciated only for the months it was held, unless the business has a stated policy of charging a full year's depreciation in the year of purchase and none in the year of sale.

docs.title: Sale of an asset
docs.text:
When an asset is sold, depreciation is first charged up to the date of sale. The book value on that date is compared with the sale proceeds: an excess of proceeds is a profit on sale and a shortfall a loss on sale, both taken to the profit and loss account.

docs.title: 7.6 Provisions
docs.text:
A provision is an amount charged against profit to cover a known liability or an expected loss whose amount cannot be determined exactly. Its key features are that it is a charge against profit (it must be made whether there is a profit or not) and that it relates to something that has already happened or is already known.

Common examples are the provision for depreciation (Section 7.5), the provision for doubtful debts, the provision for repairs and renewals, and the provision for taxation. Under the accounting standards, a provision in the strict sense is a liability of uncertain timing or amount, recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable, and the amount can be reliably estimated; the term is also used in everyday practice for allowances that reduce an asset, such as the provision for doubtful debts.

docs.title: Bad debts and the provision for doubtful debts
docs.text:
Some customers who buy on credit never pay. A debt that is certainly irrecoverable (the customer is insolvent or cannot be traced) is a bad debt: it is written off by debiting Bad Debts Account and crediting the customer, and Bad Debts is charged to the profit and loss account.

Other debts are doubtful: they may or may not be paid. Prudence requires that the expected loss be provided for now, in the year in which the sales were made. A provision for doubtful debts is created, usually as a percentage of the debtors outstanding at the year end (after writing off bad debts), based on past experience or a review of individual accounts. In the balance sheet the provision is deducted from debtors.

Each year the provision is adjusted to the new required figure. The charge to the profit and loss account is:

\[ \text{Charge} = \text{Bad debts written off} + \text{New provision required} - \text{Existing provision} \]

If the result is negative, the excess provision is written back as a credit to the profit and loss account.

Example 7.4 Provision for doubtful debts over two years

Sen Traders' year ends on 31 March. It maintains a provision for doubtful debts of 5% of debtors.

  • 2024-25: bad debts written off ₹3,000; debtors at the year end, after writing off bad debts, ₹1,80,000. There was no provision before.
  • 2025-26: bad debts written off ₹5,000; debtors at the year end, after writing off bad debts, ₹2,10,000.

Bad debts are transferred to the provision account.

2024-25. Required provision = 5% × 1,80,000 = ₹9,000. Charge to profit and loss = 3,000 + 9,000 − 0 = ₹12,000.

2025-26. Required provision = 5% × 2,10,000 = ₹10,500. Charge = 5,000 + 10,500 − 9,000 = ₹6,500.

Provision for Doubtful Debts Account
