docs.title: 7.7 Reserves
docs.text:
A reserve is an amount set aside out of profits, not to meet a known liability or loss, but to strengthen the financial position of the business, to provide for unknown contingencies, to finance expansion, or to equalise dividends. A reserve is an appropriation of profit, not a charge against it: it is made only when there is a profit, after the profit has been found. It belongs to the owners and is shown in the balance sheet with capital (for a company, under "Reserves and surplus").

The main kinds:

  • Revenue reserves are created out of revenue profits and can be used for any purpose, including paying dividends.
    • A general reserve is not earmarked for any purpose.
    • A specific reserve is set aside for a stated purpose: a dividend equalisation reserve, a debenture redemption reserve, a reserve for replacement of assets.
  • Capital reserves arise from capital profits, such as a profit on the sale of a fixed asset or on the reissue of forfeited shares (Chapter 11), or a premium received on the issue of shares (which company law treats as a separate securities premium). They are generally not available for distribution as dividend.
  • A secret (hidden) reserve arises when assets are deliberately understated or liabilities overstated, so that the reserve does not appear in the balance sheet. Deliberately creating hidden reserves conflicts with the aim of a true and fair view, and modern standards and company law do not permit it in published accounts.

A reserve fund is a reserve whose amount has been invested outside the business, for example in government securities, so that the cash will be available when needed.

Example 7.5 Transfer to a general reserve

A sole trader's net profit for 2025-26 is ₹2,00,000. He decides to transfer 20% of the profit to a general reserve before crediting the rest to his capital.

Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) Profit and Loss A/c ... Dr 40,000 To General Reserve A/c 40,000 (Being 20% of the profit transferred to general reserve) Profit and Loss A/c ... Dr 1,60,000 To Capital A/c 1,60,000 (Being the balance of profit transferred to capital)

The general reserve of ₹40,000 is shown on the liabilities side of the balance sheet next to capital. Both still belong to the owner; the reserve simply keeps that part of the profit in the business.

Point Provision Reserve Nature A charge against profit An appropriation of profit Purpose To meet a known liability or expected loss To strengthen the position or meet future needs When made Whether there is a profit or a loss Only out of profit Effect on profit Reduces the profit Does not reduce the profit; it divides it Balance sheet Deducted from the asset concerned, or shown as a liability Shown with capital (reserves and surplus) Required by Prudence, accounting standards Decision of the owners, or law in particular cases Available for dividend No Revenue reserves yes; capital reserves generally no

Table 7.2. Provisions and reserves compared.

Caution

Do not confuse a reserve with cash. A reserve is a part of the owners' claim on the assets; it is on the liabilities side of the balance sheet and does not mean that a matching sum of money is sitting in the bank. Only a reserve fund is backed by specific investments.

docs.title: 7.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Depreciation allocates the cost of a fixed asset, less its residual value, over its useful life. It is caused by wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence and depletion, and must be charged to find true profit and a fair position.
  • Straight line: (cost − residual value) ÷ life, the same each year. Written down value: a fixed rate on the opening book value, falling each year and never reaching zero.
  • Depreciation is recorded either by crediting the asset account or by crediting a provision for depreciation account, which keeps the asset at cost. Assets bought or sold during the year are depreciated for the months held; on sale, book value is compared with proceeds to find the profit or loss.
  • A provision is a charge against profit for a known liability or expected loss. The charge for doubtful debts is bad debts + new provision − old provision.
  • A reserve is an appropriation of profit to strengthen the business. Reserves are revenue (general or specific) or capital; secret reserves are not permitted in published accounts.

docs.title: 7.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A vehicle costs ₹6,00,000, has a useful life of 8 years and a residual value of ₹40,000. Find the annual depreciation and the rate on cost under the straight line method.

Answer

(6,00,000 − 40,000) ÷ 8 = ₹70,000 a year. Rate = 70,000 ÷ 6,00,000 × 100 = 11.67% on cost.

Exercise 2

A computer system costing ₹1,50,000 is depreciated at 30% per annum on the written down value. Find the depreciation for each of the first three years and the book value at the end of the third year.

Answer

Year 1: 30% × 1,50,000 = ₹45,000; book value ₹1,05,000. Year 2: 30% × 1,05,000 = ₹31,500; book value ₹73,500. Year 3: 30% × 73,500 = ₹22,050; book value ₹51,450. Check: 1,50,000 − (45,000 + 31,500 + 22,050) = 51,450.

Exercise 3

Furniture costing ₹50,000 was bought on 1 July 2025. Depreciation is 10% per annum on cost, and the year ends on 31 March. What is the depreciation for 2025-26?

Answer

The furniture is held for 9 months (July to March): 50,000 × 10% × 9/12 = ₹3,750.

Exercise 4

A machine bought on 1 April 2023 for ₹80,000 is depreciated at 15% per annum by the written down value method. It is sold on 31 March 2026 for ₹45,000 after charging that year's depreciation. Find the profit or loss on sale.

Answer

2023-24: 12,000, book value 68,000. 2024-25: 10,200, book value 57,800. 2025-26: 8,670, book value 49,130. Sale proceeds 45,000: loss ₹4,130.

Exercise 5

The provision for doubtful debts at 1 April 2025 was ₹6,000. During 2025-26 bad debts of ₹4,500 were written off. Debtors at 31 March 2026 (after writing off) were ₹1,40,000, and the provision is to be 4%. Find the charge to the profit and loss account and the net debtors in the balance sheet.

Answer

New provision = 4% × 1,40,000 = ₹5,600. Charge = 4,500 + 5,600 − 6,000 = ₹4,100. Net debtors = 1,40,000 − 5,600 = ₹1,34,400.

Exercise 6

State whether each is a provision or a reserve: (a) amount set aside for expected repairs to a building already damaged; (b) 10% of profit kept aside to finance future expansion; (c) amount set aside for depreciation of machinery; (d) profit on the sale of land kept aside and not distributed.

Answer

(a) provision (an expected cost of a known event); (b) reserve (general or specific revenue reserve); (c) provision; (d) capital reserve.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietor
docs.text:
From the trial balance to the trading account, the profit and loss account and the balance sheet

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain the purpose of the trading account, the profit and loss account and the balance sheet.
  2. Prepare a trading account and compute the cost of goods sold and the gross profit.
  3. Prepare a profit and loss account and find the net profit.
  4. Classify assets and liabilities and prepare a balance sheet.
  5. Make the common year-end adjustments, showing each in both places it affects.
  6. Prepare complete final accounts from a trial balance with adjustments.

docs.title: 8.1 The final accounts
docs.text:
At the end of the accounting year the trial balance (Chapter 3) lists every balance in the ledger. It proves arithmetic, but it does not answer the two questions every owner asks: how much profit did I make? and what is my business worth on paper? The final accounts (or financial statements) answer them.

For a sole proprietor carrying on trade, the final accounts are:

  1. the trading account, which finds the gross profit from buying and selling goods;
  2. the profit and loss account, which deducts the other expenses, adds other incomes, and finds the net profit;
  3. the balance sheet, which shows the assets, liabilities and capital at the end of the year.

The first two are usually prepared together as the trading and profit and loss account. They are accounts: they form part of the double-entry system, since the revenue and expense balances are closed by transfer to them. The balance sheet is a statement, not an account: it lists the balances that remain open and are carried into the next year.

Figure 8.1 From the trial balance to the final accounts. The trial balance, together with the year-end adjustments, feeds three statements: the trading account (finding gross profit), the profit and loss account (finding net profit, which goes to capital) and the balance sheet (the position at the year end).

The dividing line between the statements is the distinction between revenue items and capital items (Chapter 1). Revenue items (sales, purchases, expenses, incomes) describe what happened during the year and go to the trading and profit and loss account. Capital items (assets, liabilities, capital, drawings) describe the position at the year end and go to the balance sheet.

docs.title: 8.2 The trading account
docs.text:
The trading account compares the net sales of the year with the cost of goods sold (cost of sales). Its main items are:

  • Debit side: opening stock; purchases less purchases returns; direct expenses, those incurred in buying goods and bringing them to a saleable condition: carriage inwards (freight inwards), wages (for a trading concern, wages of those who handle the goods), import duty, dock charges, and for a manufacturer, factory power, fuel and factory rent.
  • Credit side: sales less sales returns; closing stock.

The balance is the gross profit (credit side larger) or gross loss (debit side larger), which is carried down to the profit and loss account.

The cost of goods sold can also be computed directly:

\[ \text{Cost of goods sold} = \text{Opening stock} + \text{Net purchases} + \text{Direct expenses} - \text{Closing stock} \] \[ \text{Gross profit} = \text{Net sales} - \text{Cost of goods sold} \]

Example 8.1 A trading account

From the following for the year ended 31 March 2026, prepare a trading account: opening stock ₹20,000; purchases ₹1,50,000; purchases returns ₹5,000; carriage inwards ₹3,000; wages ₹12,000; sales ₹2,40,000; sales returns ₹8,000; closing stock ₹30,000.

Trading Account for the year ended 31 March 2026

Particulars ₹ ₹ Particulars ₹ ₹ To Opening stock 20,000 By Sales 2,40,000 To Purchases 1,50,000 Less: Sales returns 8,000 2,32,000 Less: Purchases returns 5,000 1,45,000 By Closing stock 30,000 To Carriage inwards 3,000 To Wages 12,000 To Gross profit c/d 82,000 2,62,000 2,62,000

Cost of goods sold = 20,000 + 1,45,000 + 3,000 + 12,000 − 30,000 = ₹1,50,000. Gross profit = 2,32,000 − 1,50,000 = ₹82,000, which is 82,000 ÷ 2,32,000 = 35.3% of net sales.

Caution

Closing stock does not normally appear in the trial balance, because it is found by counting and valuing the goods on hand at the year end (at the lower of cost and net realisable value). It is given as an adjustment and appears twice: on the credit side of the trading account and as an asset in the balance sheet. If closing stock does appear in the trial balance (because purchases have already been adjusted for it), it goes to the balance sheet only.

docs.title: 8.3 The profit and loss account
docs.text:
The profit and loss account starts with the gross profit and deducts the indirect expenses, those not directly connected with buying or making goods, and adds any other incomes. The expenses are usually grouped as:

  • Administrative (office) expenses: office salaries, office rent, lighting, printing and stationery, postage, telephone, insurance, audit fees, depreciation of office assets.
  • Selling and distribution expenses: salespeople's salaries and commission, advertising, carriage outwards, delivery van expenses, bad debts, discount allowed.
  • Financial expenses: interest on loans, bank charges.
  • Other losses: loss by fire not covered by insurance, loss on sale of assets.

The incomes include discount received, commission received, rent received, interest earned, and profit on sale of assets.

The balance is the net profit (credit side larger) or net loss, which is transferred to the capital account.

Tip

Carriage inwards (on purchases) is a direct expense and goes to the trading account; carriage outwards (on sales) is a selling expense and goes to the profit and loss account. Wages go to the trading account; salaries to the profit and loss account. "Wages and salaries" given together are usually taken to the trading account unless the question says otherwise.

docs.title: Closing entries
docs.text:
The transfer of balances to the trading and profit and loss account is made by closing entries in the journal:

Entry Dr Cr Transfer opening stock, purchases, direct expenses, sales returns Trading A/c Each of those accounts Transfer sales, purchases returns Sales A/c, Purchases Returns A/c Trading A/c Record closing stock Closing Stock A/c Trading A/c Transfer gross profit Trading A/c Profit and Loss A/c Transfer indirect expenses and losses Profit and Loss A/c Each expense account Transfer other incomes Each income account Profit and Loss A/c Transfer net profit Profit and Loss A/c Capital A/c Transfer drawings Capital A/c Drawings A/c

Table 8.1. Closing entries.

After these entries, every revenue and expense account is closed, and only the asset, liability and capital accounts remain open: precisely the items in the balance sheet.

docs.title: 8.4 The balance sheet
docs.text:
The balance sheet shows the financial position on the last day of the year. Its items are classified so that a reader can judge the solvency and liquidity of the business.

Assets

  • Non-current (fixed) assets are held for long-term use, not for sale: land, buildings, plant and machinery, furniture, vehicles. Intangible assets such as goodwill and patents are also non-current. Long-term investments are shown separately.
  • Current assets are cash and assets expected to be turned into cash, sold or used up within a year: stock, debtors, bills receivable, short-term investments, prepaid expenses, accrued income, cash at bank and in hand.

Liabilities

  • Capital, adjusted for the year's profit and drawings.
  • Non-current (long-term) liabilities are due after more than a year: long-term loans.
  • Current liabilities are due within a year: creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft, outstanding expenses, income received in advance.

The items may be arranged in order of liquidity (most liquid assets and most urgent liabilities first) or in order of permanence (fixed assets and capital first). The arrangement is called marshalling. Companies follow a prescribed order (Chapter 11); for a sole trader either is acceptable, provided it is followed consistently. This book uses the order of permanence.

docs.title: 8.5 Year-end adjustments
docs.text:
The trial balance records transactions as they were entered during the year. Some of them belong partly to another year, and some events of the year have not been recorded at all. Under the accrual basis and the matching concept, these must be adjusted before the final accounts are prepared. Every adjustment has two effects, one in the trading or profit and loss account and one in the balance sheet, because it is a double entry.

Adjustment Journal entry Effect 1 Effect 2 Closing stock Closing Stock Dr; To Trading A/c Credit side of trading account Current asset Outstanding expense (incurred, not paid) Expense Dr; To Outstanding Expense Added to the expense Current liability Prepaid expense (paid in advance) Prepaid Expense Dr; To Expense Deducted from the expense Current asset Accrued income (earned, not received) Accrued Income Dr; To Income Added to the income Current asset Income received in advance Income Dr; To Income Received in Advance Deducted from the income Current liability Depreciation Depreciation Dr; To Asset Debit of profit and loss account Deducted from the asset Further bad debts Bad Debts Dr; To Debtors Added to bad debts Deducted from debtors Provision for doubtful debts Profit and Loss Dr; To Provision New provision less old, added to bad debts Deducted from debtors Interest on capital Interest on Capital Dr; To Capital Debit of profit and loss account Added to capital Interest on drawings Capital Dr; To Interest on Drawings Credit of profit and loss account Deducted from capital Goods taken by the owner Drawings Dr; To Purchases Deducted from purchases Added to drawings Interest on loan outstanding Interest on Loan Dr; To Outstanding Interest Debit of profit and loss account Added to the loan (or shown as a liability)

Table 8.2. The common adjustments and their two effects.

Key idea

An item given in the trial balance appears once in the final accounts. An item given as an adjustment (outside the trial balance) appears twice, because the trial balance does not yet contain either side of its entry.

docs.title: 8.7 The vertical form
docs.text:
The horizontal (T-shaped) form above follows the double-entry structure of the accounts. Many businesses, and all companies, present their results in a vertical form, one figure below another, which is easier to read and to compare across years. Example 8.2 in vertical form begins:

The figures are the same; only the layout changes. Chapter 11 presents the vertical format prescribed for companies.

docs.title: 8.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The final accounts of a sole trader are the trading account (gross profit), the profit and loss account (net profit) and the balance sheet (financial position).
  • Cost of goods sold = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses − closing stock; gross profit = net sales − cost of goods sold.
  • Indirect expenses (administrative, selling, financial) and other incomes go to the profit and loss account; net profit is added to capital.
  • Closing entries transfer all revenue and expense balances; only asset, liability and capital accounts remain for the balance sheet.
  • Assets are non-current or current; liabilities are capital, long-term or current; they are marshalled by liquidity or permanence.
  • Each adjustment appears twice, once in the trading or profit and loss account and once in the balance sheet; items in the trial balance appear once.

docs.title: 8.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Compute the cost of goods sold and the gross profit: opening stock ₹45,000; purchases ₹2,80,000; purchases returns ₹6,000; freight inwards ₹9,000; closing stock ₹52,000; sales ₹3,90,000; sales returns ₹10,000.

Answer

Cost of goods sold = 45,000 + (2,80,000 − 6,000) + 9,000 − 52,000 = ₹2,76,000. Net sales = 3,90,000 − 10,000 = ₹3,80,000. Gross profit = 3,80,000 − 2,76,000 = ₹1,04,000.

Exercise 2

State where each item appears in the final accounts: (a) carriage outwards; (b) bank overdraft; (c) discount allowed; (d) prepaid rent; (e) wages; (f) drawings; (g) accrued interest; (h) goodwill.

Answer

(a) profit and loss account, debit (selling expense); (b) balance sheet, current liability; (c) profit and loss account, debit; (d) balance sheet, current asset (and deducted from rent in the profit and loss account if given as an adjustment); (e) trading account, debit; (f) balance sheet, deducted from capital; (g) balance sheet, current asset (and added to interest income if an adjustment); (h) balance sheet, non-current (intangible) asset.

Exercise 3

From the trial balance of Nisha Stores at 31 March 2026, prepare the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet. Debit balances: opening stock ₹15,000; purchases ₹85,000; wages ₹6,000; rent ₹9,000; salaries ₹18,000; debtors ₹25,000; furniture ₹20,000; cash ₹8,000; drawings ₹6,000. Credit balances: capital ₹50,000; sales ₹1,30,000; creditors ₹12,000. Adjustments: closing stock ₹22,000; rent prepaid ₹1,000; salaries outstanding ₹2,000; depreciation on furniture 10%; the sales include ₹4,000 received in advance for goods to be supplied in April 2026.

Answer

Trial balance totals: debit ₹1,92,000; credit ₹1,92,000.

Trading and Profit and Loss Account for the year ended 31 March 2026

Exercise 4

Pass the adjustment entries: (a) rent received includes ₹2,500 for the next year; (b) interest on investments ₹1,800 has accrued; (c) insurance of ₹12,000 was paid on 1 October 2025 for one year (year ends 31 March).

Answer

(a) Rent Received A/c Dr 2,500; To Rent Received in Advance A/c 2,500.

(b) Accrued Interest A/c Dr 1,800; To Interest on Investments A/c 1,800.

(c) Six months (April to September 2026) are prepaid: 12,000 × 6/12 = 6,000. Prepaid Insurance A/c Dr 6,000; To Insurance A/c 6,000.

Exercise 5

A proprietor's capital is ₹2,00,000. Interest on capital at 6% is to be allowed. Show the effect on net profit and on closing capital, and explain the result.

Answer

Interest on capital = 6% × 2,00,000 = ₹12,000. It is debited to the profit and loss account (net profit falls by ₹12,000) and credited to capital (capital rises by ₹12,000). Since the net profit is also credited to capital, the closing capital is unchanged. For a sole trader, interest on capital only shows how much of the profit is a return on the money invested; it matters more in partnerships (Chapter 10), where it changes how profit is shared.

Exercise 6

The trial balance shows debtors ₹60,000, bad debts ₹1,200 and a provision for doubtful debts of ₹2,500. Adjustments: write off a further ₹1,000 as bad, and create a provision of 5% on debtors. Show the entries in the profit and loss account and the balance sheet.

Answer

Debtors after further bad debts: 60,000 − 1,000 = ₹59,000. New provision: 5% × 59,000 = ₹2,950. Charge to profit and loss = 1,200 + 1,000 + 2,950 − 2,500 = ₹2,650. Balance sheet: debtors 60,000 − 1,000 − 2,950 = ₹56,050.

docs.title: Textbooks
docs.text:
The following are widely used textbooks that cover the ground of this book in more depth, with many more exercises. Editions are revised regularly; any recent edition will serve.

  1. Frank Wood and Alan Sangster, Frank Wood's Business Accounting, Volume 1, Pearson. A long-established British textbook on double entry and final accounts; Volume 2 continues with partnership and company accounts.
  2. Jerry J. Weygandt, Paul D. Kimmel and Donald E. Kieso, Financial Accounting (also published in an IFRS edition), Wiley. A comprehensive introductory text with an international outlook.
  3. Charles T. Horngren, Gary L. Sundem, John A. Elliott and Donna Philbrick, Introduction to Financial Accounting, Pearson. A classic introduction with emphasis on the use of financial statements.
  4. S. N. Maheshwari and S. K. Maheshwari, Financial Accounting, Vikas Publishing House. A standard Indian textbook covering the topics of this book with Indian practice.
  5. T. S. Grewal, Double Entry Book Keeping, Sultan Chand & Sons. A long-used Indian text with extensive practice in journal, ledger and final accounts.
  6. National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT), Financial Accounting (Class XI) and Accountancy (Class XII), New Delhi. Freely available school textbooks that cover the basic principles, accounts of non-profit organisations, partnership and company accounts, and the analysis of financial statements.
  7. OpenStax, Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting, Rice University, 2019. A free, openly licensed introductory textbook.

docs.text:
1. IFRS Foundation, Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting (2018), and the texts of IFRS and IAS, published by the IFRS Foundation.
  2. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, the texts of the Accounting Standards (AS) and Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), and its guidance notes and study material.
  3. Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Government of India, the Companies Act, 2013, its schedules (including the format of financial statements) and the rules and notifications made under it.

docs.title: How to use these sources
docs.text: For more practice in the mechanics of recording and final accounts, the textbooks by Wood and Sangster, Maheshwari and Grewal are the most useful. For the use and analysis of financial statements, Horngren and Weygandt are good next steps. For the exact wording of a standard, a legal format or an ethical requirement, always go to the official source, and check that you are reading the version currently in force.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The main terms of the book, with the chapter in which each is explained

docs.title: A
docs.text: Accounting The process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, interpreting and communicating financial information about an organisation to its users. (Chapter 1) Accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital; true after every transaction because every transaction has two aspects. (Chapter 2) Accounting period The interval, usually a year, for which results are measured and financial statements prepared. (Chapter 1) Accounting standards Authoritative statements of how particular transactions and events are to be recognised, measured, presented and disclosed, such as IFRS, Ind AS and AS. (Chapter 1) Accrual basis Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, whether or not cash has been received or paid. (Chapter 1) Accrued income Income earned during the period but not yet received; a current asset. (Chapter 8) Appropriation account In a partnership, the account that divides net profit among the partners through interest on capital, salaries and shares of profit. (Chapter 10) Asset A resource owned or controlled by the business from which future benefits are expected. (Chapter 1) Audit trail A record, kept by accounting software, of who entered or changed each transaction, when, and what was changed. (Chapter 14) Authorised capital The maximum share capital that a company is permitted to issue. (Chapter 11)

docs.title: B
docs.text: Bad debt An amount owed by a customer that is certainly irrecoverable and is written off as an expense. (Chapter 7) Balance sheet A statement of the assets, liabilities and capital of a business at a date. (Chapters 2 and 8) Bank reconciliation statement A statement explaining the difference between the bank balance in the cash book and the balance in the bank statement on a date. (Chapter 5) Bill of exchange An unconditional written order, signed by the drawer, directing the drawee to pay a certain sum to a certain person or to the bearer; it binds the drawee once accepted. (Chapter 5) Bookkeeping The recording part of accounting: keeping the journal, cash book and ledger. (Chapter 1) Business entity concept The principle that the business is accounted for separately from its owner. (Chapter 1)

docs.title: C
docs.text: Calls in arrears Amounts called up on shares but not yet paid by shareholders. (Chapter 11) Capital The owner's claim on the assets of the business; assets less liabilities. (Chapter 2) Capital employed The long-term funds used in a business: shareholders' funds plus long-term debt, or total assets less current liabilities. (Chapter 13) Capital expenditure Spending that brings benefit for more than one year and creates or improves an asset. (Chapter 1) Capital fund In a non-profit organisation, the excess of assets over liabilities; the equivalent of capital. (Chapter 9) Capital reserve A reserve created out of capital profits, such as the profit on reissue of forfeited shares; generally not available for dividend. (Chapters 7 and 11) Cash equivalents Short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value. (Chapter 12) Cash flow statement A statement of the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents, classified into operating, investing and financing activities. (Chapter 12) Chart of accounts The organised list of all ledger accounts of a business, usually coded and grouped. (Chapter 14) Compensating errors Errors that cancel each other out, leaving the trial balance in agreement. (Chapter 6) Contra entry An entry in the cash book that affects both the cash and the bank columns; it is not posted to the ledger. (Chapter 4) Cost of goods sold Opening stock plus net purchases plus direct expenses minus closing stock. (Chapter 8) Credit note A document sent to a customer stating that his account has been credited, usually for goods returned. (Chapter 4) Current assets Cash and assets expected to be realised, sold or used up within a year. (Chapter 8) Current liabilities Liabilities due for settlement within a year. (Chapter 8) Current ratio Current assets divided by current liabilities. (Chapter 13)

docs.title: D
docs.text: Debentures Long-term borrowings of a company in the form of written acknowledgements of debt, usually carrying fixed interest. (Chapter 11) Debit and credit The left and right sides of an account. Increases in assets, expenses and drawings are debits; increases in liabilities, capital and revenue are credits. (Chapters 2 and 3) Debit note A document sent to a supplier stating that his account has been debited, usually for goods returned to him. (Chapter 4) Debt-equity ratio Long-term debt divided by shareholders' funds. (Chapter 13) Depreciation The systematic allocation of the cost of a fixed asset, less its residual value, over its useful life. (Chapter 7) Discounting a bill Obtaining cash from a bank for a bill before its maturity, less a charge called discount. (Chapter 5) Double entry The principle that every transaction is recorded with equal debits and credits. (Chapter 3) Drawings Money or goods taken out of the business by the owner for personal use. (Chapter 1)

docs.title: E
docs.text: Earnings per share Profit after tax less preference dividend, divided by the number of equity shares. (Chapters 11 and 13) Equity shares Shares that are not preference shares; their holders bear the residual risk and have voting rights. (Chapter 11) Error of principle Recording a transaction in the wrong class of account, such as treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure. (Chapter 6)

docs.title: F
docs.text: Final accounts The trading account, the profit and loss account and the balance sheet prepared at the end of the year. (Chapter 8) Forfeiture of shares Cancellation of shares for non-payment of allotment or calls, the shareholder losing the money already paid. (Chapter 11)

docs.title: G
docs.text: Going concern concept The assumption that the business will continue to operate for the foreseeable future. (Chapter 1) Goodwill The value of a business beyond its separate net assets, arising from reputation, location, customers and staff. (Chapter 10) Gross profit Net sales less the cost of goods sold. (Chapter 8)

docs.title: H
docs.text: Historical cost concept The principle that assets are recorded at the price paid to acquire them. (Chapter 1)

docs.title: I
docs.text: IFRS International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board. (Chapter 1) Imprest system A method of keeping petty cash in which the amount spent is reimbursed each period, restoring a fixed float. (Chapter 4) Ind AS Indian Accounting Standards converged with IFRS, applicable to specified classes of companies. (Chapter 1) Income and expenditure account The accrual-basis statement of a non-profit organisation's revenue income and expenses for the year; its balance is a surplus or deficit. (Chapter 9) Interest coverage ratio Profit before interest and tax divided by interest. (Chapter 13)

docs.title: J
docs.text: Journal The book of original entry in which transactions are first recorded in date order, with debits, credits and a narration. (Chapter 3)

docs.title: L
docs.text: Ledger The book containing all the accounts of a business. (Chapter 3) Liability An amount owed by the business to outsiders. (Chapter 1)

docs.title: M
docs.text: Matching concept The principle that expenses are recognised in the same period as the revenue they help to earn. (Chapter 1) Materiality The principle that items which could influence users' decisions must be shown accurately and separately, while immaterial items may be treated simply. (Chapter 1)

docs.title: N
docs.text: Net profit Gross profit plus other incomes less indirect expenses. (Chapter 8) Net realisable value The estimated selling price less the costs needed to complete and sell. (Chapter 1) Noting charges The fee paid to a notary public for recording the dishonour of a bill. (Chapter 5)

docs.title: O
docs.text: Operating activities The principal revenue-producing activities of a business, and other activities that are not investing or financing. (Chapter 12) Outstanding expense An expense incurred during the period but not yet paid; a current liability. (Chapter 8)

docs.title: P
docs.text: Paid-up capital Called-up share capital less calls in arrears. (Chapter 11) Partnership deed The written agreement setting out the terms of a partnership. (Chapter 10) Petty cash book The book in which small cash payments are recorded, usually on the imprest system. (Chapter 4) Posting Transferring entries from the books of original entry to the ledger accounts. (Chapter 3) Prepaid expense An expense paid in advance for a later period; a current asset. (Chapter 8) Promissory note An unconditional written promise, signed by the maker, to pay a certain sum to a certain person or to the bearer. (Chapter 5) Provision An amount charged against profit to cover a known liability or expected loss whose amount cannot be determined exactly. (Chapter 7) Prudence Caution in judgement under uncertainty, so that assets and income are not overstated and liabilities and expenses are not understated. (Chapter 1)

docs.title: Q
docs.text: Quick ratio Current assets less inventories and prepaid expenses, divided by current liabilities. (Chapter 13)

docs.title: R
docs.text: Receipts and payments account A summary of the cash book of a non-profit organisation, on the cash basis. (Chapter 9) Rectification The correction of errors by means of entries, without erasing. (Chapter 6) Reserve An amount appropriated out of profit to strengthen the business or for a future purpose. (Chapter 7) Return on capital employed Profit before interest and tax as a percentage of capital employed. (Chapter 13) Revenue expenditure Spending whose benefit is used up within the year; an expense. (Chapter 1)

docs.title: S
docs.text: Sacrificing ratio The ratio in which old partners give up their shares of profit to a new partner. (Chapter 10) Securities premium The excess of the issue price of shares over their nominal value, kept in a separate account whose uses are restricted by law. (Chapter 11) Straight line method Charging the same amount of depreciation every year: (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life. (Chapter 7) Subsidiary books Books of original entry for particular kinds of transaction: purchases, sales, returns, cash and petty cash books, and the journal proper. (Chapter 4) Suspense account A temporary account holding the difference in a trial balance until the errors are found. (Chapter 6)

docs.title: T
docs.text: Trade discount A reduction in list price given to traders; deducted on the invoice and not recorded in the books. (Chapter 3) Trading account The account that compares net sales with the cost of goods sold to find gross profit. (Chapter 8) Trial balance A list of the balances of all ledger accounts, in debit and credit columns, prepared to check arithmetical accuracy. (Chapter 3)

docs.title: W
docs.text: Window dressing Arranging transactions around the year end so that the financial statements look better than the underlying position. (Chapter 14) Working capital cycle The time between paying suppliers and receiving cash from customers: inventory days plus collection days minus payment days. (Chapter 13) Written down value method Charging depreciation at a fixed percentage of the book value at the start of each year. (Chapter 7)

docs.title: Chapter 3: Double Entry: Journal, Ledger and Trial Balance
docs.text:
Recording every transaction twice, posting it to accounts and checking the arithmetic

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain the principle of double entry and the form of an account.
  2. Classify accounts and apply the rules of debit and credit, both in the modern form and in the traditional form.
  3. Record transactions in the journal with correct narrations, including compound and opening entries.
  4. Post journal entries to ledger accounts and balance the accounts.
  5. Prepare a trial balance and explain what it does and does not prove.

docs.title: 3.1 Accounts and double entry
docs.text:
An account is a record, kept under one heading, of all the transactions that affect one item: one account for cash, one for each customer, one for rent, one for sales, and so on. The collection of all the accounts of a business is the ledger.

Each account has two sides. The left side is the debit side (Dr) and the right side is the credit side (Cr). Drawn in its simplest form, an account looks like the letter T, which is why it is often called a T-account:

Dr: Date Particulars ₹ Cr: Date Particulars ₹ debit entries credit entries

Table 3.1. The form of a ledger account.

The words debit and credit mean nothing more than left and right. They do not mean good or bad, and "credit" in accounting does not mean the same as credit in a bank statement seen from the customer's side.

Double entry is the principle that every transaction is recorded in at least two accounts, with a debit in one and an equal credit in another, so that the total of all debits always equals the total of all credits. It follows from the accounting equation (Chapter 2): every transaction keeps the equation in balance, and recording the increases and decreases on the sides laid down by the equation keeps the debits equal to the credits.

Key idea

For every debit there is an equal credit. If the debits and credits of a transaction do not agree, the entry is wrong.

docs.title: 3.2 The rules of debit and credit
The modern (accounting equation) approach
docs.text:
The accounting equation gives the rules directly, as Chapter 2 showed. Accounts are grouped into five types, and the side on which each type increases is fixed:

Type of account Examples Increase Decrease Normal balance Assets Cash, bank, debtors, inventory, furniture, machinery Debit Credit Debit Expenses and losses Purchases, wages, rent, salaries, discount allowed Debit Credit Debit Drawings Drawings Debit Credit Debit Liabilities Creditors, loans, outstanding expenses Credit Debit Credit Capital Capital Credit Debit Credit Revenue and gains Sales, commission received, discount received Credit Debit Credit

Table 3.2. The modern rules of debit and credit.

To journalise a transaction with this approach, ask three questions: Which accounts are affected? What type is each? Does each increase or decrease? The answers fix the debit and the credit.

docs.title: The traditional approach
docs.text:
An older approach, still widely taught, classifies accounts into three kinds and gives each kind a rule:

  • Personal accounts are accounts of persons and organisations. They are natural (an individual such as Ravi), artificial (a firm, company, bank or club such as Mehta & Co or State Bank) or representative (an account that stands for persons, such as Outstanding Salaries, which represents the employees who are owed salary, or Prepaid Insurance, which represents the insurer). Capital and drawings are personal accounts of the owner.
  • Real accounts are accounts of things owned: tangible (cash, furniture, machinery, buildings, inventory) or intangible (goodwill, patents, trademarks).
  • Nominal accounts are accounts of expenses, losses, incomes and gains (rent, salaries, commission received, interest earned).
Kind of account Rule Personal Debit the receiver, credit the giver Real Debit what comes in, credit what goes out Nominal Debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains

Table 3.3. The traditional ("golden") rules of debit and credit.

The two approaches always give the same entry. When a business pays rent in cash, the modern approach says: rent (an expense) increases, so debit Rent; cash (an asset) decreases, so credit Cash. The traditional approach says: Rent is nominal, an expense, so debit it; Cash is real and goes out, so credit it.

Caution

Purchases and Sales are not assets. Goods are recorded in separate accounts according to the direction of movement: goods bought for resale are debited to Purchases Account, goods sold are credited to Sales Account, goods returned by customers are debited to Sales Returns (Returns Inward) Account and goods returned to suppliers are credited to Purchases Returns (Returns Outward) Account. The value of goods still unsold is found by counting at the end of the period (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 3.3 Source documents and vouchers
docs.text:
Every entry in the books should rest on evidence. The documents that provide it are called source documents: cash memos for cash sales, invoices (bills) for credit sales and purchases, receipts for money received, cheque counterfoils and bank pay-in slips, debit notes and credit notes for returns, salary sheets, and so on.

From a source document, an accounting voucher is often prepared inside the business: a written instruction that names the accounts to be debited and credited, the amount and the narration, signed by the person who prepares it and by the person who authorises it. Vouchers are numbered in sequence and kept on file. In accounting software (Chapter 14), entering a voucher is the way every transaction is recorded.

docs.title: 3.4 The journal
docs.text:
The journal is the book of original entry, in which transactions are first recorded in the order of their dates. Each record is called a journal entry, and the act of recording is called journalising. The journal shows, for each transaction, the accounts debited and credited, the amounts and a short explanation called the narration.

Date Particulars L.F. Dr (₹) Cr (₹) Year, month, day Name of account debited ... Dr Amount To Name of account credited Amount (Being the narration)

Table 3.4. The form of the journal. L.F. is the ledger folio, the page of the ledger to which the entry is posted.

The debit account is written first, close to the left, followed by "Dr". The credit account is written on the next line, set in a little and preceded by "To". The narration, beginning "Being ...", follows in brackets.

Example 3.1 Journalising the transactions of Sharma Electricals

Vikram Sharma starts an electrical goods shop, Sharma Electricals, in April 2025. Its transactions are:

Date Transaction Apr 1 Started business with cash ₹2,00,000 Apr 2 Deposited ₹1,20,000 in the bank Apr 3 Bought goods on credit from Mehta & Co ₹80,000 Apr 5 Bought office equipment, paying by cheque ₹30,000 Apr 8 Sold goods on credit to Gupta Stores ₹45,000 Apr 10 Cash sales ₹25,000 Apr 12 Paid Mehta & Co by cheque ₹50,000 Apr 15 Received cash from Gupta Stores ₹30,000 Apr 18 Cash purchases ₹12,000 Apr 20 Paid rent in cash ₹8,000 Apr 25 Withdrew cash for personal use ₹4,000 Apr 28 Received commission in cash ₹3,000 Apr 30 Paid salaries by cheque ₹10,000 Apr 30 Paid electricity bill in cash ₹2,000

Journal of Sharma Electricals

Dr 30,000 To Bank A/c 30,000 (Being office equipment bought by cheque) Apr 8 Gupta Stores ... Dr 45,000 To Sales A/c 45,000 (Being goods sold on credit) Apr 10 Cash A/c ... Dr 25,000 To Sales A/c 25,000 (Being cash sales) Apr 12 Mehta & Co ... Dr 50,000 To Bank A/c 50,000 (Being payment made by cheque) Apr 15 Cash A/c ... Dr 30,000 To Gupta Stores 30,000 (Being cash received from a customer) Apr 18 Purchases A/c ... Dr 12,000 To Cash A/c 12,000 (Being goods bought for cash) Apr 20 Rent A/c ... Dr 8,000 To Cash A/c 8,000 (Being rent paid) Apr 25 Drawings A/c ... Dr 4,000 To Cash A/c 4,000 (Being cash withdrawn for personal use) Apr 28 Cash A/c ... Reasoning for three of the entries.

  • Apr 3. Purchases (goods for resale, an expense) increase: debit. Mehta & Co, a creditor (liability; traditionally the giver), increases: credit.
  • Apr 8. Gupta Stores becomes a debtor (asset; traditionally the receiver): debit. Sales (revenue) increase: credit.
  • Apr 25. Drawings reduce the owner's capital: debit Drawings. Cash goes out: credit Cash.

docs.title: Compound entries
docs.text: When a transaction affects more than two accounts, or when several transactions of the same kind on the same date are recorded together, a single compound entry with more than one debit or more than one credit is used. The total of the debits must still equal the total of the credits.

docs.title: The opening entry
docs.text: A business that continues from one year to the next starts the new year's books with an opening entry, which brings in the balances of the assets and liabilities at the end of the previous year. Assets are debited, liabilities are credited, and the capital (the excess of assets over liabilities) is credited.

docs.title: Discounts
docs.text:
A trade discount is a reduction in the list price given by a seller to a trader who buys for resale, usually for buying in quantity. It is deducted on the invoice and is not recorded in the books: the purchase or sale is recorded at the net amount. A cash discount is an allowance for prompt payment. It is recorded: the seller debits Discount Allowed (an expense) and the buyer credits Discount Received (a gain).

Example 3.2 Opening, compound and other special entries

(a) On 1 April 2025 the balances of a business were: cash ₹15,000; bank ₹60,000; inventory ₹40,000; debtors ₹25,000; furniture ₹30,000; creditors ₹35,000; bank loan ₹50,000. Capital = (15,000 + 60,000 + 40,000 + 25,000 + 30,000) − (35,000 + 50,000) = 1,70,000 − 85,000 = ₹85,000.

(b) Received a cheque for ₹29,400 from a customer, Patil, in full settlement of ₹30,000.

(c) The owner took goods costing ₹2,000 for personal use.

(d) Goods costing ₹1,500 were distributed as free samples.

(e) Bought goods with a list price of ₹20,000 on credit from Khan Bros, less 10% trade discount.

(f) Goods costing ₹5,000 were destroyed by fire; the insurance company admitted a claim for ₹3,000.

Date 2025 Particulars L.F. Dr (₹) Cr (₹) (a) Apr 1 Cash A/c ... Dr 15,000 Bank A/c ... Dr 60,000 Inventory A/c ... Dr 40,000 Debtors A/c ... Dr 25,000 Furniture A/c ... Dr 30,000 To Creditors A/c 35,000 To Bank Loan A/c 50,000 To Capital A/c 85,000 (Being balances brought forward from the previous year) (b) Bank A/c ... Dr 29,400 Discount Allowed A/c ... Dr 600 To Patil 30,000 (Being cheque received in full settlement, discount allowed) (c) Drawings A/c ... Dr 2,000 To Purchases A/c 2,000 (Being goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use) (d) Advertisement A/c ... Dr 1,500 To Purchases A/c 1,500 (Being goods distributed as free samples) (e) Purchases A/c ... Dr 18,000 To Khan Bros 18,000 (Being goods bought at list price ₹20,000 less 10% trade discount) (f) Insurance Claim A/c ... Dr 3,000 Loss by Fire A/c ... Dr 2,000 To Purchases A/c 5,000 (Being goods destroyed by fire and claim admitted)

Notes: in (c), (d) and (f) the goods leave the business other than by sale, so they are taken out of Purchases at cost. In (e) the trade discount of ₹2,000 does not appear anywhere. In (f) the part of the loss not covered by insurance is a loss of the business; the insurance claim is an asset until the money is received.

docs.title: 3.6 The ledger: posting and balancing
docs.text: The journal records transactions in date order, but it does not tell you how much cash there is or how much Gupta Stores owes. For that, each journal entry is transferred to the accounts it names. This transfer is called posting, and the book of accounts is the ledger, the principal book of the accounting system.

docs.title: How to post
docs.text:
For each journal entry:

  1. In the account that is debited, write on the debit side the date, "To" and the name of the account credited, and the amount.
  2. In the account that is credited, write on the credit side the date, "By" and the name of the account debited, and the amount.
  3. Write the page number of the ledger account in the L.F. column of the journal, and the journal page in the J.F. column of the account, so that every entry can be traced both ways.

The name written in each account is that of the other account in the entry. Reading Cash Account, a line "To Sales A/c 25,000" tells you that cash came in from sales.

docs.title: How to balance an account
docs.text:
At the end of a period each account is balanced:

  1. Add both sides.
  2. Write the difference on the lighter side as "By Balance c/d" (credit side) or "To Balance c/d" (debit side), so that both sides have the same total.
  3. Write the totals on the same line on both sides.
  4. Bring the balance down on the opposite side at the start of the next period as "To Balance b/d" or "By Balance b/d".

An account whose debit side is larger has a debit balance; one whose credit side is larger has a credit balance. Assets, expenses and drawings normally have debit balances; liabilities, capital and revenue normally have credit balances.

Example 3.3 Ledger of Sharma Electricals

The journal entries of Example 3.1 are posted below. The main accounts are shown in full.

Cash Account

Bank Account

Date Particulars ₹ Date Particulars ₹ Apr 2 To Cash A/c 1,20,000 Apr 5 By Office Equipment A/c 30,000 Apr 12 By Mehta & Co 50,000 Apr 30 By Salaries A/c 10,000 Apr 30 By Balance c/d 30,000 1,20,000 1,20,000 May 1 To Balance b/d 30,000

docs.title: 3.7 The trial balance
docs.text:
When all the accounts have been balanced, their balances are listed in a statement called the trial balance: debit balances in one column and credit balances in another. Because every transaction was recorded with equal debits and credits, the two columns should have the same total.

The trial balance has three uses:

  1. It checks the arithmetical accuracy of the journal and the ledger. If the totals disagree, an error has certainly been made.
  2. It summarises the ledger on a single page.
  3. It is the starting point for the final accounts (Chapter 8).

There are two ways to prepare it. The balances method, used here and in practice, lists the balance of each account. The totals method lists the total of the debit side and the total of the credit side of each account; it also agrees, but it is longer and less useful for preparing final accounts.

Example 3.4 Trial balance of Sharma Electricals

Trial Balance of Sharma Electricals as at 30 April 2025

Name of account L.F. Debit balance (₹) Credit balance (₹) Cash 1,12,000 Bank 30,000 Capital 2,00,000 Purchases 92,000 Mehta & Co (creditor) 30,000 Office Equipment 30,000 Gupta Stores (debtor) 15,000 Sales 70,000 Rent 8,000 Drawings 4,000 Commission Received 3,000 Salaries 10,000 Electricity 2,000 Total 3,03,000 3,03,000

Debit total: 1,12,000 + 30,000 + 92,000 + 30,000 + 15,000 + 8,000 + 4,000 + 10,000 + 2,000 = ₹3,03,000. Credit total: 2,00,000 + 30,000 + 70,000 + 3,000 = ₹3,03,000. The trial balance agrees.

Figure 3.1 The accounting cycle. The accounting cycle: a transaction and its source document are recorded in the journal, posted to the ledger and summarised in the trial balance; after adjustments the final accounts are prepared, and the cycle begins again in the next period.

docs.title: What the trial balance does not prove
docs.text:
A trial balance that agrees shows only that total debits equal total credits. It does not prove that the books are correct. Several kinds of error leave it in agreement:

  • Errors of omission: a transaction left out completely (neither debit nor credit recorded).
  • Errors of commission of certain kinds: posting to the wrong account of the same class, such as debiting Gupta Stores instead of Gupta Traders.
  • Errors of principle: recording a transaction in the wrong class of account, such as debiting the purchase of furniture to Purchases.
  • Compensating errors: two errors of equal amount on opposite sides that cancel each other.
  • Errors of original entry: a wrong amount entered in the book of original entry, then posted correctly on both sides.

Chapter 6 deals with the location and correction of errors, including those that the trial balance cannot reveal.

Example 3.5 Preparing a trial balance from a list of balances

The following balances were taken from the books of Leela Traders on 31 March 2026: Capital ₹1,50,000; Purchases ₹2,10,000; Sales ₹3,05,000; Debtors ₹42,000; Creditors ₹36,000; Wages ₹28,000; Rent ₹24,000; Machinery ₹90,000; Bank ₹19,000; Cash ₹6,000; Drawings ₹18,000; Discount received ₹2,000; Opening inventory ₹30,000; Bank loan ₹40,000; Interest on loan ₹4,000; Sales returns ₹5,000; Purchases returns ₹3,000; Commission received ₹10,000; Salaries ₹30,000; Furniture ₹40,000.

Opening inventory is an asset at the start of the year, so it is a debit. Sales returns reduce sales, so they are a debit; purchases returns reduce purchases, so they are a credit.

docs.title: 3.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • An account records all transactions affecting one item; its left side is the debit side and its right side the credit side. The ledger is the book of all the accounts.
  • Double entry records every transaction with equal debits and credits.
  • Modern rules: assets, expenses and drawings increase on the debit side; liabilities, capital and revenue increase on the credit side. Traditional rules: personal, debit the receiver and credit the giver; real, debit what comes in and credit what goes out; nominal, debit expenses and losses and credit incomes and gains.
  • The journal records transactions in date order with a narration. Compound entries have more than one debit or credit; the opening entry brings forward last year's balances. Trade discount is not recorded; cash discount is.
  • Posting transfers each journal entry to the debit of one account and the credit of another. Accounts are balanced at the end of each period.
  • The trial balance lists all the balances; equal totals prove arithmetical accuracy but not the absence of errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry or compensating errors.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Partnership Accounts
docs.text:
Capital and current accounts, the appropriation of profit, and an introduction to admitting a partner

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Describe a partnership and the main contents of a partnership deed.
  2. State the usual rules that apply when the deed is silent.
  3. Maintain partners' capital accounts under the fixed and the fluctuating capital methods.
  4. Prepare a profit and loss appropriation account, including interest on capital, interest on drawings and salaries.
  5. Compute interest on drawings by the product method and the average period method.
  6. Explain goodwill, the new profit-sharing ratio and the sacrificing ratio, and record the admission of a partner who brings a premium.

docs.title: 10.1 Partnerships and the deed
docs.text:
A sole proprietor eventually meets limits: of capital, of skill, of time. One answer is to join with others. A partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all of them or by any of them acting for all. The persons are individually called partners and collectively a firm. In India the general law of partnership is the Indian Partnership Act, 1932; there is also a separate form, the limited liability partnership, governed by its own law, which is not covered here.

The essential features of an ordinary partnership are:

  • an agreement, oral or written, between two or more persons;
  • a business carried on with a view to sharing profits;
  • mutual agency: each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners for the business of the firm;
  • unlimited liability: partners are liable jointly and severally for the debts of the firm, to the full extent of their private assets.

Law may set an upper limit on the number of partners; check the current rules where it matters.

docs.title: The partnership deed
docs.text:
The agreement is best put in writing, in a document called the partnership deed. A deed typically states:

  • the name and address of the firm and the nature of its business;
  • the names of the partners and the capital each contributes;
  • the profit-sharing ratio;
  • whether interest on capital is allowed and at what rate;
  • whether interest on drawings is charged and at what rate;
  • salaries or commission payable to partners;
  • the rate of interest on loans by partners to the firm;
  • how the accounts are kept and audited;
  • the rules for the admission, retirement or death of a partner, including the valuation of goodwill;
  • the method of settling disputes.

docs.title: 10.2 When the deed is silent
docs.text:
If the partners have not agreed on a matter, the law fills the gap. Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, unless the partners have agreed otherwise:

Matter Rule in the absence of agreement Sharing of profits and losses Equally Interest on capital Not allowed Interest on drawings Not charged Salary or commission to a partner Not allowed Interest on a loan advanced by a partner Allowed at 6% per annum, as a charge against profit

Table 10.1. The usual rules when the partnership agreement is silent.

Example 10.1 No agreement on the sharing of profit

Xavier and Yusuf are partners with capitals of ₹2,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. On 1 April 2025 Xavier also lent the firm ₹50,000. There is no deed. The profit for 2025-26 before any interest is ₹1,23,000. Xavier wants profit shared in the capital ratio; Yusuf wants interest on capital at 10% and a salary of ₹2,000 a month. Settle the dispute.

With no agreement, neither claim succeeds: profits are shared equally, and no interest on capital or salary is allowed. Xavier is, however, entitled to interest on his loan at 6% per annum.

Particulars ₹ Profit before interest 1,23,000 Less: Interest on Xavier's loan (6% × 50,000) 3,000 Profit to be shared 1,20,000 Xavier's share (1/2) 60,000 Yusuf's share (1/2) 60,000

Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit (like interest on a bank loan), so it is deducted before the profit is divided.

docs.title: 10.3 Partners' capital accounts
docs.text:
Each partner has a capital account. There are two ways to maintain it.

Fixed capital method. Each partner has two accounts. The capital account records only the capital introduced or withdrawn by agreement; its balance stays the same from year to year unless capital is permanently changed. All the routine items (interest on capital, salary, share of profit, drawings, interest on drawings) go to a separate current account, whose balance changes every year and may be debit or credit.

Fluctuating capital method. Each partner has only a capital account, and all the items above go into it, so its balance changes every year.

Point Fixed capital method Fluctuating capital method Number of accounts per partner Two: capital and current One: capital Capital balance Unchanged unless capital is added or withdrawn Changes every year Profit, salary, interest, drawings Recorded in the current account Recorded in the capital account Balance Capital always credit; current may be debit Normally credit Interest on capital Easy: on the fixed balance Needs care: on a changing balance

Table 10.2. Fixed and fluctuating capitals.

docs.title: 10.4 The profit and loss appropriation account
docs.text:
A partnership prepares its trading and profit and loss account exactly as a sole trader does (Chapter 8). The net profit is then divided among the partners in a separate profit and loss appropriation account. The items in it are not expenses of the firm; they are ways of dividing the profit among the partners according to the deed.

Figure 10.1 The profit and loss appropriation account. The net profit from the profit and loss account, plus interest on drawings, less interest on capital, partners' salaries, commission and transfers to reserve, gives the divisible profit, which is shared in the profit-sharing ratio and credited to the partners' current or capital accounts. Debit side Credit side Interest on capital Net profit brought down from profit and loss account Salaries and commission to partners Interest on drawings Transfer to reserve Profit shared among partners (balancing figure)

Table 10.3. The contents of the profit and loss appropriation account.

Caution

Keep charges and appropriations apart. Charges against profit, such as interest on a partner's loan, rent paid to a partner for premises, and salaries of employees, go to the profit and loss account and must be paid whether there is a profit or not. Appropriations, such as interest on capital and partners' salaries, go to the appropriation account and are made only out of profit. If the profit is not enough to cover them in full, the deed decides; a common rule is that the available profit is divided in the ratio of the appropriations.

docs.title: 10.5 Interest on capital and on drawings
docs.text:
Interest on capital compensates partners who have invested more than others. It is computed at the agreed rate on the opening capital, adjusted for any additional capital introduced or capital withdrawn during the year, for the period it was in the business.

Interest on drawings compensates the firm, and thus the other partners, when a partner withdraws money in advance of his share of profit. It is computed at the agreed rate for the period from the date of each drawing to the end of the year. The product method multiplies each drawing by the months it was outstanding:

\[ \text{Interest on drawings} = \frac{\text{Sum of (drawing} \times \text{months outstanding)} \times \text{Rate}}{12 \times 100} \]

When equal amounts are drawn at regular intervals, the average period method is quicker: interest is charged on the total drawings for the average period. For drawings made evenly through the year (or, in an exam, when the dates are not given), the average period is taken as six months. For equal monthly drawings at the start of each month, it is 6.5 months; at the end of each month, 5.5 months.

Example 10.2 Interest on drawings by the product method

A partner made these drawings in the year ended 31 March 2026: ₹10,000 on 1 June 2025, ₹6,000 on 1 October 2025 and ₹8,000 on 1 January 2026. Interest on drawings is charged at 10% per annum.

Date Amount (₹) Months to 31 March Product (₹) 1 June 2025 10,000 10 1,00,000 1 October 2025 6,000 6 36,000 1 January 2026 8,000 3 24,000 Total 24,000 1,60,000

Interest = 1,60,000 × 10/100 × 1/12 = ₹1,333 (to the nearest rupee).

docs.title: 10.6 A complete example
docs.text:
Example 10.3 Appropriation account and current accounts

Arjun and Bina are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3:2. Their fixed capitals on 1 April 2025 were Arjun ₹3,00,000 and Bina ₹2,00,000. The deed provides:

  • interest on capital at 8% per annum;
  • a salary to Bina of ₹4,000 a month;
  • interest on drawings at 6% per annum.

During 2025-26 Arjun drew ₹30,000 and Bina ₹24,000, evenly through the year. The net profit for the year, before any of the above, was ₹2,40,000. The current accounts had no opening balances.

Workings

  • Interest on capital: Arjun 8% × 3,00,000 = ₹24,000; Bina 8% × 2,00,000 = ₹16,000.
  • Salary to Bina: 4,000 × 12 = ₹48,000.
  • Interest on drawings (average period 6 months): Arjun 30,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹900; Bina 24,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹720.
  • Divisible profit = 2,40,000 + 900 + 720 − 24,000 − 16,000 − 48,000 = ₹1,53,620.
  • Arjun's share = 1,53,620 × 3/5 = ₹92,172; Bina's share = 1,53,620 × 2/5 = ₹61,448.

Profit and Loss Appropriation Account for the year ended 31 March 2026

Particulars ₹ ₹ Particulars ₹ ₹ To Interest on capital: Arjun 24,000 By Profit and Loss A/c (net profit) 2,40,000 Bina 16,000 40,000 By Interest on drawings: Arjun 900 To Salary to Bina 48,000 Bina 720 1,620 To Profit transferred: Arjun (3/5) 92,172 Bina (2/5) 61,448 1,53,620 2,41,620 2,41,620

Partners' Current Accounts

Particulars Arjun (₹) Bina (₹) Particulars Arjun (₹) Bina (₹) To Drawings 30,000 24,000 By Interest on capital 24,000 16,000 To Interest on drawings 900 720 By Salary 48,000 To Balance c/d 85,272 1,00,728 By Share of profit 92,172 61,448 Total 1,16,172 1,25,448 Total 1,16,172 1,25,448 By Balance b/d 85,272 1,00,728

The capital accounts stay at ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000. In the balance sheet, the partners' interest is shown as capital (₹5,00,000) plus current account balances (₹1,86,000).

Under the fluctuating capital method, the same items would go into the capital accounts, whose closing balances would be Arjun 3,00,000 + 85,272 = ₹3,85,272 and Bina 2,00,000 + 1,00,728 = ₹3,00,728.

Check. The total credited to the partners (24,000 + 16,000 + 48,000 + 92,172 + 61,448 = ₹2,41,620) less the interest on drawings charged to them (₹1,620) equals the firm's net profit of ₹2,40,000.

Key idea

Interest on capital, salaries and interest on drawings do not change the total profit going to the partners; they change only how it is divided. In Example 10.3 the partners together receive exactly ₹2,40,000 net, whatever the rates in the deed.

docs.title: 10.7 Changes in a partnership: an overview
docs.text:
A partnership changes whenever a partner joins, retires or dies, or the partners change their profit-sharing ratio. Each change ends the old agreement and begins a new one, so the firm must settle the rights of the partners up to that date. This is called the reconstitution of the firm. A full treatment belongs to a second course; the main ideas are:

  • Goodwill. A successful firm is worth more than the sum of its separate assets, because of its reputation, location, customers and staff. This extra value is goodwill. An incoming partner who will share in future profits that the old partners' efforts made possible should compensate them for their share of goodwill. A simple method of valuing it is the average profits method: goodwill = average profit of a number of past years × an agreed number of years' purchase.
  • New and sacrificing ratios. When a partner joins, the old partners give up (sacrifice) part of their shares. The sacrificing ratio is each old partner's old share minus his new share. Compensation for goodwill is shared by the old partners in the sacrificing ratio. When a partner retires, the remaining partners gain his share, in the gaining ratio.
  • Revaluation. Assets and liabilities are revalued at the date of the change, and the resulting profit or loss belongs to the old partners in their old ratio. It is recorded in a revaluation account.
  • Accumulated profits and reserves in the books at the date of the change also belong to the old partners in their old ratio.

Example 10.4 Admission of a partner with a premium for goodwill

Arjun and Bina (ratio 3:2, fixed capitals) admit Chirag on 1 April 2026 for a one-fifth share of future profits. Chirag brings ₹1,50,000 as capital and his share of goodwill in cash. Goodwill is valued at one year's purchase of the average profit of the last three years, which were ₹1,60,000, ₹2,00,000 and ₹2,40,000. Arjun and Bina will share the remaining four-fifths in their old ratio.

Goodwill. Average profit = (1,60,000 + 2,00,000 + 2,40,000) ÷ 3 = ₹2,00,000. Goodwill = 2,00,000 × 1 = ₹2,00,000. Chirag's share = 1/5 × 2,00,000 = ₹40,000.

New ratio. Arjun 3/5 × 4/5 = 12/25; Bina 2/5 × 4/5 = 8/25; Chirag 1/5 = 5/25. New ratio 12:8:5.

Sacrificing ratio. Arjun 3/5 − 12/25 = 15/25 − 12/25 = 3/25; Bina 2/5 − 8/25 = 10/25 − 8/25 = 2/25. Sacrificing ratio 3:2, the same as the old ratio, because the old partners keep their old ratio between themselves.

Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) Bank A/c ... Dr 1,90,000 To Chirag's Capital A/c 1,50,000 To Premium for Goodwill A/c 40,000 (Being capital and premium for goodwill brought in by Chirag) Premium for Goodwill A/c ... Dr 40,000 To Arjun's Current A/c 24,000 To Bina's Current A/c 16,000 (Being the premium shared by the old partners in the sacrificing ratio 3:2)

Arjun receives 3/5 × 40,000 = ₹24,000 and Bina 2/5 × 40,000 = ₹16,000. (With fluctuating capitals the premium would be credited to their capital accounts.)

docs.title: 10.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A partnership is an agreement to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of the partners for all; partners have mutual agency and unlimited liability. The deed records the terms.
  • Without agreement: profits shared equally; no interest on capital, no interest on drawings, no salary; interest on partners' loans at 6% per annum.
  • Under the fixed capital method, capital accounts stay constant and current accounts take profits, salaries, interest and drawings; under the fluctuating method, all go to the capital account.
  • The appropriation account divides net profit: add interest on drawings; deduct interest on capital, salaries, commission and reserves; share the balance in the agreed ratio.
  • Interest on drawings is computed by products or by the average period. Charges (loan interest, rent to a partner) go to the profit and loss account; appropriations go to the appropriation account.
  • On admission, the incoming partner compensates the old partners for goodwill in the sacrificing ratio; assets are revalued and reserves distributed in the old ratio.

docs.title: 10.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Priya and Qadir share profits 2:1. Capitals: Priya ₹4,00,000, Qadir ₹2,00,000. Interest on capital is 5%; Qadir gets a salary of ₹30,000 a year. Net profit is ₹1,20,000. Prepare the appropriation account.

Answer

Interest on capital: Priya ₹20,000, Qadir ₹10,000. Salary to Qadir ₹30,000. Divisible profit = 1,20,000 − 20,000 − 10,000 − 30,000 = ₹60,000: Priya 2/3 = ₹40,000, Qadir 1/3 = ₹20,000.

Particulars ₹ Particulars ₹ To Interest on capital: Priya 20,000 By Net profit 1,20,000 To Interest on capital: Qadir 10,000 To Salary to Qadir 30,000 To Share of profit: Priya 40,000 To Share of profit: Qadir 20,000 Total 1,20,000 Total 1,20,000

Exercise 2

A partner withdrew ₹5,000 at the beginning of every month during the year ended 31 March 2026. Interest on drawings is 9% per annum. Compute the interest.

Answer

Total drawings ₹60,000; average period for drawings at the start of each month = 6.5 months. Interest = 60,000 × 9/100 × 6.5/12 = ₹2,925.

By products: the drawings are outstanding for 12, 11, ..., 1 months, a total of 78 months, so the product is 5,000 × 78 = 3,90,000, and 3,90,000 × 9/100 × 1/12 = 2,925.

Exercise 3

In Exercise 1, suppose the net profit was only ₹45,000 and the deed says interest on capital and salary are appropriations. How is the profit divided?

Answer

The appropriations due are interest 20,000 + 10,000 and salary 30,000, a total of ₹60,000, more than the profit of ₹45,000. Dividing the profit in the ratio of the appropriations (20,000 : 10,000 : 30,000 = 2 : 1 : 3): Priya interest 45,000 × 2/6 = ₹15,000; Qadir interest 45,000 × 1/6 = ₹7,500; Qadir salary 45,000 × 3/6 = ₹22,500. Nothing is left to share in the profit-sharing ratio.

Exercise 4

Mona and Nita share profits 5:3. They admit Ojas for a 1/4 share, which he takes 1/8 from each. Find the new ratio and the sacrificing ratio.

Answer

Mona: 5/8 − 1/8 = 4/8; Nita: 3/8 − 1/8 = 2/8; Ojas: 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8. New ratio 4:2:2 = 2:1:1. Sacrificing ratio = 1/8 : 1/8 = 1:1.

Exercise 5

Distinguish between interest on a partner's capital and interest on a partner's loan.

Answer

Interest on capital is an appropriation of profit, allowed only if the deed provides for it and only out of profit; it is debited to the appropriation account. Interest on a loan is a charge against profit, payable whether or not there is a profit (at 6% per annum if not agreed); it is debited to the profit and loss account and credited to the partner's loan account.

Exercise 6

The average profit of a firm for the last four years is ₹90,000. Goodwill is valued at two years' purchase. A new partner joins for a 1/6 share and brings his share of goodwill in cash. How much does he bring?

Answer

Goodwill = 90,000 × 2 = ₹1,80,000. New partner's share = 1/6 × 1,80,000 = ₹30,000.
