docs.title: Preface
docs.text: How this book is organised and how to get the most from it

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
Accounting is often called the language of business. Every business, however small, has to answer the same questions: what does it own, what does it owe, did it make a profit last year, and can it pay its bills next month? Accounting is the discipline that answers them, and financial accounting is the part of it that produces the reports a business shows to the outside world.

This book teaches financial accounting from the beginning. It starts with the purpose of accounting and the ideas on which it rests, moves through the mechanics of recording (the accounting equation, double entry, the journal, the ledger and the trial balance), and then builds up, chapter by chapter, to complete financial statements for a sole trader, a non-profit organisation, a partnership and a company. The last three chapters show how those statements are read and used: the cash flow statement, the analysis of financial statements through ratios, and the use of accounting software together with the ethical duties of the people who prepare accounts.

Every chapter is built around fully worked numerical examples. Journal entries, ledger accounts, cash books, reconciliation statements and financial statements are all laid out as tables, in the form in which you would draw them on paper, and every total in them has been checked. The amounts are in Indian rupees (₹), written with the Indian grouping of digits (₹1,00,000 is one lakh rupees; ₹10,00,000 is ten lakh).

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The book is written for a reader who has never studied accounting before. It suits:

  • a student in a first university course in accounting or commerce, or in the final years of school;
  • a student of management, economics, law or engineering who needs to read financial statements;
  • a person who runs, or plans to run, a small business and wants to understand the books that an accountant keeps for it;
  • anyone preparing for a professional course who wants a careful grounding in the basics.

No background beyond school arithmetic is assumed. Percentages, fractions and simple interest are the only mathematics used, and each is shown in full where it occurs.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
Part of the book Chapters What you learn Foundations 1 to 2 Why accounting exists, who uses it, the concepts and standards behind it, and the accounting equation Recording 3 to 5 Double entry, the journal, the ledger, the trial balance, subsidiary books, the cash book, bank reconciliation and bills of exchange Correcting and adjusting 6 to 7 Finding and correcting errors; depreciation, provisions and reserves Reporting 8 to 11 Final accounts of a sole proprietor, of a non-profit organisation, of a partnership and of a company Using the reports 12 to 14 The cash flow statement, ratio analysis, accounting software and ethics

Table P.1. The five parts of the book.

The chapters are meant to be read in order. Chapters 1 to 4 are the foundation for everything else: a reader who is comfortable with the journal, the ledger and the trial balance will find every later chapter an extension of the same few ideas.

docs.title: How each chapter is built
docs.text:
Every chapter follows the same plan:

  • Learning outcomes at the top tell you what you should be able to do when you finish.
  • Numbered sections explain each idea, first in plain words and then precisely.
  • Worked examples show every step of a calculation or a set of entries. Work through them with a pencil before moving on.
  • Boxes pick out what matters most: a key idea to remember, a note that adds detail, and a caution that warns of a common mistake.
  • A summary collects the main points.
  • Exercises follow, each with its answer folded underneath. Try each exercise on paper before you open the answer.
  • A short quiz at the end lets you check your understanding; it can be answered on the page.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
Accounting is learned by doing. Reading a journal entry is easy; writing one from a description of a transaction is the skill that counts. For each chapter:

  1. Read the explanation once, without stopping to memorise.
  2. Rework every worked example on paper, covering the solution and comparing only when you have finished.
  3. Attempt the exercises, then open the answers. Where your answer differs, find the step at which it went wrong.
  4. Take the quiz. If you miss a question, reread the section it comes from.

Keep a notebook with ruled columns, or use a spreadsheet, and lay out your answers in the same tables as the book. The habit of neat columns and checked totals is half of good accounting.

docs.title: A note on laws and standards
docs.text: Accounting is shaped by law and by accounting standards, and both change. Company law, tax law and the standards issued by standard-setting bodies are revised from time to time, and the details differ from country to country. This book explains the principles, which change slowly, and describes the legal and regulatory setting only in general terms. Where a rule depends on the current law (a rate of tax, a limit, a required format), check the latest official text before relying on it in practice.

docs.title: Conventions in the examples
docs.text:
• The financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March, as it does for most businesses in India. "2025-26" means the year from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026.
  • Names of businesses and people in the examples are invented.
  • Goods and services tax and other indirect taxes are left out of most examples so that the accounting principle is not hidden by tax entries; Chapter 4 explains briefly where tax columns are added in practice.
  • In ledger accounts, "To" introduces an entry on the debit side and "By" an entry on the credit side, as is customary.
  • "Dr" means debit and "Cr" means credit; "A/c" means account; "b/d" means brought down and "c/d" carried down.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Rectification of Errors
docs.text:
Finding mistakes in the books and correcting them without erasing anything

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Classify errors as errors of omission, commission, principle and compensating errors.
  2. Say which errors affect the agreement of the trial balance and which do not.
  3. Use practical techniques to locate errors.
  4. Rectify errors at each stage: before the trial balance, after it through a suspense account, and after the final accounts.
  5. Prepare a suspense account and compute the effect of errors on profit.

docs.title: 6.1 Why errors need a method
docs.text:
Errors creep into every set of books: a figure is copied wrongly, a total is added wrongly, a posting goes to the wrong account or is forgotten. Accounting has two firm rules about them. First, an error is never erased or overwritten: a clean record of what was done, and of how it was corrected, is part of the evidence on which the accounts rest. Second, an error is corrected by an entry, so that the correction itself passes through double entry and leaves a trail. This process is called rectification.

To rectify an error you need to know three things: what entry was made, what entry should have been made, and therefore what entry will turn the first into the second.

Key idea

Rectifying entry = correct entry − wrong entry. Write down the wrong entry and the correct entry side by side; the rectifying entry is whatever must be added to the accounts to move them from the first to the second.

docs.title: 6.2 Kinds of errors
docs.text:
Figure 6.1 Classification of errors. Accounting errors divide into clerical errors (omission, commission and compensating) and errors of principle. Complete omissions, compensating errors and errors of principle leave the trial balance in agreement; partial omissions and most errors of commission do not.

Errors of omission. A transaction is left out of the books. A complete omission (the transaction is not recorded at all, in neither the book of original entry nor the ledger) does not affect the trial balance. A partial omission (the transaction is recorded in one account but not the other, for example entered in the sales book and posted to the customer but omitted from the total posted to Sales Account) does.

Errors of commission. A transaction is recorded, but wrongly: a wrong amount, a posting to the wrong side, a posting to the wrong account of the right class, a wrong total (casting) or a wrong balance carried forward. Most errors of commission affect the trial balance; a posting to the wrong account of the right class and on the right side does not.

Errors of principle. A transaction is recorded in the wrong class of account, because an accounting principle has been misapplied: capital expenditure treated as revenue expenditure (furniture debited to Purchases or to Repairs), or a revenue receipt treated as capital. The debit and credit are both made, so the trial balance agrees, but profit and the balance sheet are both wrong.

Compensating errors. Two or more errors cancel one another: a debit overstated by ₹100 in one account and a credit overstated by ₹100 in another. The trial balance agrees despite both errors.

Error Example Trial balance agrees? Complete omission A credit purchase not recorded at all Yes Partial omission Sale posted to customer but not to Sales No Wrong amount in book of original entry Sale of ₹5,400 entered as ₹4,500 in sales book and posted from there Yes Wrong amount in posting ₹5,400 in sales book posted to customer as ₹4,500 No Wrong side Payment to a creditor debited to Cash No Wrong account, same class Sale to Gupta Traders debited to Gupta Stores Yes Wrong casting Purchases book undercast by ₹1,000 No Principle Purchase of machinery debited to Purchases Yes Compensating Sales overcast ₹500 and Wages overcast ₹500 Yes

Table 6.1. Common errors and their effect on the trial balance.

The distinction that matters for rectification is between two-sided errors, which affect both a debit and a credit equally (and so leave the trial balance in agreement), and one-sided errors, which affect only one account (and so make the trial balance disagree).

docs.title: 6.3 Locating errors
docs.text:
When a trial balance does not agree, the error must be found before final accounts can be relied on. Useful techniques:

  1. Re-add the trial balance, and check that every balance has been brought into it on the correct side.
  2. Halve the difference. If the difference is ₹840, look for an item of ₹420: an amount posted to the wrong side creates a difference of twice the amount.
  3. Divide the difference by 9. If it divides exactly, suspect a transposition (₹540 written as ₹450 gives a difference of 90) or a slide (₹540 written as ₹54 gives a difference of 486). Both differences are multiples of 9.
  4. Look for the exact difference. An omitted balance or an unposted item may be exactly the amount of the difference.
  5. Check the totals of the subsidiary books and their postings, then the balancing of each ledger account.
  6. Check the postings from the books of original entry to the ledger, item by item, ticking each one.

If the error still cannot be found and the final accounts must be prepared, the difference is placed temporarily in a suspense account (Section 6.5).

docs.title: 6.4 Rectification at different stages
docs.text: How an error is rectified depends on when it is found.

docs.title: Before the trial balance is prepared
docs.text:
• A two-sided error is rectified by a journal entry that debits one account and credits another.
  • A one-sided error affects only one account, so it is corrected by an entry in that account alone, with an explanation. No journal entry is possible, because there is no second account to make it in. For example, if the sales book was undercast by ₹500, Sales Account is credited with ₹500 ("By undercasting of the sales book for May").

Example 6.1 Rectification before the trial balance

Rectify the following errors found before the trial balance was drawn up.

(a) A credit purchase of ₹4,000 from Lal was entered in the sales book.

(b) Repairs to machinery of ₹1,200 were debited to Machinery Account.

(c) The sales returns book was overcast by ₹300.

(d) ₹750 received from Verma was credited to Varma's account.

(e) Cash paid to Iqbal, ₹2,600, was posted to his account as ₹6,200.

Error Wrong entry Correct entry Rectification (a) Lal Dr 4,000; Sales Cr 4,000 Purchases Dr 4,000; Lal Cr 4,000 Journal: Purchases A/c Dr 4,000; Sales A/c Dr 4,000; To Lal 8,000 (b) Machinery Dr 1,200 Repairs Dr 1,200 Journal: Repairs A/c Dr 1,200; To Machinery A/c 1,200 (c) Sales Returns Dr 300 too much One-sided: credit Sales Returns A/c ₹300 ("By overcasting of sales returns book") (d) Varma Cr 750 Verma Cr 750 Journal: Varma Dr 750; To Verma 750 (e) Iqbal Dr 6,200 Iqbal Dr 2,600 One-sided: credit Iqbal's account ₹3,600 ("By excess posting")

In (a), Lal's account was wrongly debited ₹4,000 and should have been credited ₹4,000, so it needs a credit of ₹8,000; Sales must lose its wrong credit (debit ₹4,000) and Purchases must receive its missing debit (₹4,000).

docs.title: After the trial balance, through a suspense account
docs.text: Once the trial balance has been prepared with the difference placed in a suspense account, every error can be rectified by a journal entry: for a one-sided error, the suspense account takes the place of the missing second account. When all the errors have been found and rectified, the suspense account is left with no balance.

docs.title: After the final accounts
docs.text: If the error is found only after the final accounts have been prepared and the books closed, the nominal accounts (revenue and expense accounts) for that year have already been closed by transfer to the profit and loss account. Correcting them in the new year would distort the new year's profit. So in the rectifying entry, every nominal account is replaced by a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account (sometimes called Prior Period Items Account). The balance of that account, which is the correction of the previous year's profit, is transferred to capital.

docs.title: 6.5 The suspense account
docs.text:
Example 6.2 Rectification through a suspense account

The trial balance of Joshi & Co on 31 March 2026 did not agree. The difference was placed in a suspense account, and the final accounts were drafted showing a net profit of ₹42,000. The following errors were later discovered:

(a) The sales book was overcast by ₹1,000.

(b) Furniture bought for ₹8,000 was debited to Purchases Account.

(c) A credit sale of ₹2,500 to Mohan was not recorded at all.

(d) A payment of ₹1,800 to Sohan, a creditor, was posted to his account as ₹1,080.

(e) A discount of ₹300 allowed to Ram was credited to his account but not debited to Discount Allowed Account.

(f) Wages of ₹1,500 paid for installing a new machine were debited to Wages Account.

(g) Goods of ₹600 returned by Gopal, a customer, were entered in the purchases returns book.

(h) The purchases book was undercast by ₹2,000.

Pass rectifying entries, prepare the suspense account and find the corrected net profit.

Analysis.

Error One- or two-sided Effect on the trial balance (a) One-sided (Sales overstated) Credit side too high by 1,000 (b) Two-sided, principle None (c) Two-sided, complete omission None (d) One-sided (Sohan debited 720 too little) Debit side too low by 720 (e) One-sided (discount not debited) Debit side too low by 300 (f) Two-sided, principle None (g) Two-sided, wrong book None (h) One-sided (Purchases understated) Debit side too low by 2,000

The debit side was short by 1,000 + 720 + 300 + 2,000 = ₹4,020, so the suspense account was opened with a debit balance of ₹4,020.

Journal (rectifying entries)

Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) (a) Sales A/c ... Dr 1,000 To Suspense A/c 1,000 (Being the overcasting of the sales book corrected) (b) Furniture A/c ... Dr 8,000 To Purchases A/c 8,000 (Being furniture wrongly debited to Purchases) (c) Mohan ... Dr 2,500 To Sales A/c 2,500 (Being an unrecorded credit sale now recorded) (d) Sohan ... Dr 720 To Suspense A/c 720 (Being ₹1,800 posted as ₹1,080 corrected) (e) Discount Allowed A/c ... Dr 300 To Suspense A/c 300 (Being discount allowed not posted to its account) (f) Machinery A/c ... Dr 1,500 To Wages A/c 1,500 (Being installation wages capitalised) (g) Sales Returns A/c ... Dr 600 Purchases Returns A/c ... Dr 600 To Gopal 1,200 (Being return inwards wrongly entered in the purchases returns book) (h) Purchases A/c ... Dr 2,000 To Suspense A/c 2,000 (Being the undercasting of the purchases book corrected)

For (g): the wrong entry debited Gopal ₹600 and credited Purchases Returns ₹600; the correct entry debits Sales Returns ₹600 and credits Gopal ₹600. Gopal therefore needs a credit of ₹1,200, and Purchases Returns must lose its wrong credit.

Suspense Account

Particulars ₹ Particulars ₹ To Difference in trial balance 4,020 By Sales A/c (a) 1,000 By Sohan (d) 720 By Discount Allowed A/c (e) 300 By Purchases A/c (h) 2,000 Total 4,020 Total 4,020

The suspense account is closed: all the errors have been found.

Effect on profit. Only errors that touch a revenue or expense account change the profit.

Error Effect on net profit ₹ (a) Sales reduced Decrease (1,000) (b) Purchases reduced Increase 8,000 (c) Sales increased Increase 2,500 (d) Personal accounts only None 0 (e) Discount allowed (expense) increased Decrease (300) (f) Wages reduced Increase 1,500 (g) Sales returns up ₹600 and purchases returns down ₹600 Decrease (1,200) (h) Purchases increased Decrease (2,000) Net effect Increase 7,500 ₹ Net profit as drafted 42,000 Add: Net effect of rectification 7,500 Corrected net profit 49,500

The increases total 8,000 + 2,500 + 1,500 = 12,000 and the decreases 1,000 + 300 + 1,200 + 2,000 = 4,500; 12,000 − 4,500 = 7,500.

Caution

Do not use the suspense account for a two-sided error. If both the debit and the credit of the original entry were made, the error did not create the difference, and passing its rectification through the suspense account would put the suspense account out of balance. Ask first: did this error, on its own, make the trial balance disagree? Only if the answer is yes does the suspense account appear in its rectifying entry.

docs.title: Balance sheet treatment of a remaining suspense balance
docs.text: If the final accounts must be prepared before all the errors are found, an unexplained suspense balance is shown temporarily in the balance sheet: a debit balance among the assets, a credit balance among the liabilities. It is a sign that the books are not yet correct, and it should be cleared as soon as the errors are traced.

docs.title: 6.6 Rectification in the next accounting period
docs.text:
Example 6.3 Errors found after the books are closed

Errors (b), (c) and (f) of Example 6.2 are discovered only in May 2026, after the 2025-26 accounts have been closed. Rectify them in the books of 2026-27.

Error Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) (b) Furniture A/c ... Dr 8,000 To Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c 8,000 (c) Mohan ... Dr 2,500 To Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c 2,500 (f) Machinery A/c ... Dr 1,500 To Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c 1,500 Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c ... Dr 12,000 To Capital A/c 12,000 (Being the correction of last year's profit transferred to capital)

Purchases, Sales and Wages for 2025-26 were already closed to the profit and loss account, so they are replaced by Profit and Loss Adjustment Account. The three corrections together raise last year's profit by 8,000 + 2,500 + 1,500 = ₹12,000, which belongs to the owner and is credited to capital. (Strictly, depreciation on the furniture and machinery for the part of the year they were held would also need correcting; it is ignored here for simplicity.)

docs.title: 6.7 Errors and the financial statements
docs.text:
Some errors change profit; others change only the balance sheet; some change both. A useful way to think about any error is to trace its effect through the statements:

Error Profit Balance sheet Revenue expenditure treated as capital (repairs debited to Machinery) Overstated Assets overstated Capital expenditure treated as revenue (machinery debited to Repairs) Understated Assets understated Closing inventory overstated Overstated this year; understated next year Assets overstated Credit sale omitted Understated Debtors understated Wrong personal account debited No effect Individual balances wrong; totals right Outstanding expense not recorded Overstated Liabilities understated

Table 6.2. How some common errors affect profit and the balance sheet.

The case of closing inventory shows why errors matter beyond one year: this year's closing inventory is next year's opening inventory, so an overstatement raises this year's profit and lowers next year's by the same amount.

docs.title: 6.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Errors are rectified by entries, never by erasing. Rectifying entry = correct entry − wrong entry.
  • Errors are of omission, commission, principle or compensating. Two-sided errors leave the trial balance in agreement; one-sided errors do not.
  • To locate errors, re-add, halve the difference (wrong side), divide by 9 (transposition or slide), look for the exact amount, and check the books and postings.
  • Before the trial balance, two-sided errors are corrected by journal entries and one-sided errors by a note in the account affected.
  • After the trial balance, a suspense account holds the difference and acts as the second account in the rectification of one-sided errors; when all errors are found it closes.
  • After the final accounts, nominal accounts in rectifying entries are replaced by a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account, whose balance goes to capital.
  • Only errors that touch revenue or expense accounts change profit.

docs.title: 6.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each error and say whether it affects the agreement of the trial balance: (a) ₹2,000 paid for office repairs debited to Building Account; (b) a sale of ₹3,600 to Nisha posted to her account as ₹6,300; (c) a purchase of ₹1,500 from Ali not recorded at all; (d) the wages account undercast by ₹200 and the commission received account undercast by ₹200.

Answer

(a) Error of principle; trial balance agrees. (b) Error of commission (transposition in posting); trial balance does not agree (difference ₹2,700, which is 9 × 300). (c) Complete omission; agrees. (d) Compensating errors; agrees.

Exercise 2

Pass rectifying entries (no suspense account): (a) ₹5,000 received from Dinesh credited to Mahesh; (b) purchase of a typewriter for ₹12,000 debited to Purchases; (c) goods of ₹2,200 bought from Raju entered in the sales book.

Answer Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) (a) Mahesh ... Dr 5,000 To Dinesh 5,000 (b) Office Equipment A/c ... Dr 12,000 To Purchases A/c 12,000 (c) Purchases A/c ... Dr 2,200 Sales A/c ... Dr 2,200 To Raju 4,400

Exercise 3

A trial balance showed the credit side short by ₹2,450, and the difference was put to a suspense account. Errors found: (a) the total of the sales book, ₹28,450, was posted to Sales Account as ₹27,000; (b) a payment of rent ₹1,000 was correctly entered in the cash book but not posted to Rent Account; (c) commission received of ₹1,000 was posted to the debit of Commission Received Account. Pass the entries and prepare the suspense account.

Answer

(a) Sales credited ₹1,450 too little: Suspense A/c Dr 1,450; To Sales A/c 1,450.

(b) Rent debit missing: Rent A/c Dr 1,000; To Suspense A/c 1,000.

(c) Commission debited ₹1,000 instead of credited ₹1,000, so it needs a credit of ₹2,000: Suspense A/c Dr 2,000; To Commission Received A/c 2,000.

Suspense Account

Particulars ₹ Particulars ₹ To Sales A/c 1,450 By Difference in trial balance 2,450 To Commission Received A/c 2,000 By Rent A/c 1,000 Total 3,450 Total 3,450

The credit side was short, so the suspense account opened with a credit balance of ₹2,450. Check: errors (a) and (c) made the credit side short by 1,450 + 2,000 = 3,450, and error (b) made the debit side short by 1,000, so the net shortfall on the credit side was 3,450 − 1,000 = 2,450. The account closes.

Exercise 4

A firm's draft net profit is ₹75,000. Find the corrected profit if: (a) closing inventory was undervalued by ₹4,000; (b) a machine bought for ₹20,000 was debited to Purchases; (c) rent of ₹3,000 received from a tenant was credited to the tenant's personal account instead of Rent Received Account; (d) a sale of ₹6,000 was recorded twice.

Answer

(a) +4,000; (b) +20,000; (c) +3,000 (an income was left out of the profit and loss account); (d) −6,000. Corrected profit = 75,000 + 4,000 + 20,000 + 3,000 − 6,000 = ₹96,000.

Exercise 5

Explain why a suspense account should not be used to rectify an error of principle.

Answer

An error of principle records both a debit and a credit of equal amount, only in the wrong class of account. It does not create any difference in the trial balance, so it is not part of the suspense balance. Rectifying it through suspense would put an amount into the suspense account that was never in it, leaving the account out of balance.

Exercise 6

The difference in a trial balance is ₹810. Suggest two kinds of error to look for first.

Answer

₹810 is divisible by 9 (810 = 9 × 90), so look for a transposition (for example ₹1,900 written as ₹1,090, a difference of 810), and half of 810 is ₹405, so look for an item of ₹405 posted to the wrong side.

docs.title: 6.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 6

Exercise 1

Which error will cause the trial balance to disagree?

  1. Purchase of furniture debited to Purchases
  2. A credit sale omitted completely
  3. The sales book overcast by ₹500
  4. Two equal errors on opposite sides
Answer

The sales book overcast by ₹500

Exercise 2

Repairs to a building, ₹5,000, debited to Building Account. The effect on profit is that it is

  1. overstated by ₹5,000
  2. understated by ₹5,000
  3. unaffected
Answer

overstated by ₹5,000

An expense has been treated as an asset, so expenses are too low and profit too high.

Exercise 3

Errors found after the books are closed are rectified by replacing nominal accounts with

  1. the suspense account
  2. the capital account
  3. the profit and loss adjustment account
  4. the trading account
Answer

the profit and loss adjustment account

Exercise 4

The trial balance difference is ₹360. Half of it suggests looking for an item posted to the wrong side. What amount, in rupees?

Answer

180 / ₹180

Exercise 5

Goods returned by a customer were entered in the purchases returns book. The rectifying entry credits the customer with

  1. the amount of the return
  2. twice the amount of the return
  3. nothing
Answer

docs.title: Chapter 4: Subsidiary Books and the Cash Book
docs.text:
Dividing the journal so that routine transactions are recorded quickly and posted in totals

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain why the journal is divided into subsidiary books and name each book.
  2. Write up the purchases, sales, purchases returns and sales returns books, and post them to the ledger.
  3. Say which transactions are recorded in the journal proper.
  4. Prepare a cash book with discount, cash and bank columns, including contra entries, and post it.
  5. Keep a petty cash book on the imprest system with analysis columns.

docs.title: 4.1 Why the journal is divided
docs.text:
In Chapter 3 every transaction was recorded in a single journal and then posted, one entry at a time, to the ledger. That works for a few transactions. A real business makes hundreds of credit sales and purchases and thousands of cash payments each month, and recording each in the journal with a full narration, then posting each to the ledger twice, would be slow and would invite errors.

Most transactions are of a few repeated kinds: credit purchases of goods, credit sales of goods, returns, and receipts and payments of cash. So the journal is divided into subsidiary books (also called special journals or books of original entry), one for each kind of repeated transaction. The advantages are:

  • Division of work. Different clerks can keep different books at the same time.
  • Saving of time. No narration is needed, because the book itself says what kind of transaction each line is; and the same-sided entries (all credit sales, say) are posted to the ledger as one total at the end of the month instead of one by one.
  • Easy reference. All credit sales are in one place, so questions such as "what were sales in May?" are answered quickly.
  • Better control. Each book can be checked separately, and errors are easier to locate.
Figure 4.1 Subsidiary books and the ledger. Source documents feed seven books of original entry: purchases book, sales book, purchases returns book, sales returns book, cash book, petty cash book and journal proper; all of them are posted to the personal, real and nominal accounts of the ledger. Book Records Source document Purchases book Credit purchases of goods for resale Supplier's invoice (inward invoice) Sales book Credit sales of goods Copy of the sales invoice (outward invoice) Purchases returns book Goods returned to suppliers Debit note Sales returns book Goods returned by customers Credit note Cash book All receipts and payments of cash and through the bank Receipts, cash memos, cheque counterfoils, pay-in slips Petty cash book Small cash payments Petty cash vouchers Journal proper Every transaction that does not belong in another book Vouchers, memos

Table 4.1. The subsidiary books.

docs.title: 4.2 The purchases book
docs.text:
The purchases book (purchases journal, purchases day book) records credit purchases of goods only. Cash purchases of goods go in the cash book; purchases of assets on credit, such as furniture or machinery, go in the journal proper, because they are not goods for resale.

The usual columns are: date, name of the supplier with brief details of the goods, invoice number, ledger folio, a details column for the working, and the amount (net of trade discount).

  • May 20: from Jain Bros, 40 ties at ₹200 each.
  • May 24: from Office Mart, a computer for office use, ₹45,000 on credit.

The sales book (sales journal, sales day book) records credit sales of goods only. Cash sales go in the cash book; sales of old assets on credit go in the journal proper. Its form is the same as that of the purchases book.

docs.title: 4.4 The returns books
docs.text:
Goods are returned when they are damaged, defective or not as ordered.

When the business returns goods to a supplier, it sends a debit note, so called because it tells the supplier that his account is being debited in the buyer's books. These returns are recorded in the purchases returns book (returns outward book). Each supplier's account is debited, and Purchases Returns Account is credited with the monthly total.

When a customer returns goods, the business issues a credit note, telling the customer that his account has been credited. These returns are recorded in the sales returns book (returns inward book). Each customer's account is credited, and Sales Returns Account is debited with the monthly total.

docs.title: 4.5 The journal proper
docs.text:
Whatever does not belong to any of the special books is recorded in the journal proper. The main items are:

  • opening entries at the start of the year;
  • credit purchases and sales of assets other than goods (a machine bought on credit, old furniture sold on credit);
  • adjustment entries at the end of the year: outstanding and prepaid expenses, accrued income, depreciation, provisions (Chapters 7 and 8);
  • transfer entries, such as moving the balance of drawings to capital;
  • closing entries, which transfer revenue and expense balances to the trading and profit and loss account;
  • rectification entries that correct errors (Chapter 6);
  • other non-cash items: goods taken by the owner, goods lost by fire, bad debts written off, bills of exchange accepted or dishonoured (Chapter 5) and interest on capital.

docs.title: 4.6 The cash book
docs.text:
The cash book records every receipt and payment of cash, and every deposit into and withdrawal from the bank. It is unusual among the subsidiary books: it is both a book of original entry, because transactions are first recorded in it, and a ledger account, because it takes the place of Cash Account and Bank Account in the ledger. A separate Cash Account is therefore not kept in the ledger; the balance of the cash book is the cash balance.

Like Cash Account, it has a debit (receipts) side and a credit (payments) side. Its common forms are:

  • the simple cash book, with one amount column on each side, for cash only;
  • the cash book with cash and bank columns, which records both cash and bank transactions;
  • the cash book with discount, cash and bank columns (often called the three-column cash book), which also records cash discounts allowed and received;
  • the petty cash book, for small payments.

docs.title: Contra entries
docs.text: A transaction that involves both cash and bank, such as depositing cash in the bank or withdrawing cash from the bank for office use, affects two columns of the same cash book. Both sides of the entry are made in the cash book itself: depositing cash is entered in the bank column on the debit side and in the cash column on the credit side. Such an entry is called a contra entry and is marked "C" in the folio column, meaning that no posting to the ledger is needed: the double entry is complete within the book.

docs.title: The discount columns
docs.text:
Cash discount is recorded alongside the payment or receipt that earned it, in a discount column on each side. On the debit side, the discount column records discount allowed to customers; on the credit side, discount received from suppliers. The discount columns are memorandum columns: they are not balanced, because they are not part of the cash or bank balance. Their totals are posted at the end of the period: the debit-side total to the debit of Discount Allowed Account, and the credit-side total to the credit of Discount Received Account. The individual discounts are posted to the customers' and suppliers' accounts along with the cash.

Example 4.4 Cash book of Rao Traders with discount, cash and bank columns

Transactions for June 2025:

The cash column can never show a credit balance: payments of cash cannot exceed the cash available. The bank column can, when the bank allows an overdraft; a credit balance in the bank column means the business owes the bank. Also remember that a cheque received and deposited on the same day is entered directly in the bank column; a cheque received and kept for a few days is first entered in the cash column (treated as cash in hand) and then shown as a contra entry when it is deposited.

docs.title: 4.7 The petty cash book
docs.text:
A business makes many small payments: postage, courier charges, bus and taxi fares, tea for visitors, small stationery. Recording each in the main cash book would clutter it. Instead, a petty cashier is given a fixed sum to make such payments and records them in a petty cash book.

Under the imprest system, the petty cashier starts each period (a week or a month) with a fixed amount, called the imprest. At the end of the period the chief cashier reimburses exactly the amount spent, so that the petty cashier begins the next period with the full imprest again. The system has two advantages: the petty cash in hand can be checked at any time (cash in hand plus vouchers for payments made should equal the imprest), and the main cash book records only one reimbursement per period.

The analytical petty cash book has a column for the total of each payment and a column for each common type of expense, so that at the end of the period the total of each expense column can be posted to the corresponding ledger account.

Example 4.5 Petty cash book on the imprest system

The petty cashier of Rao Traders receives an imprest of ₹5,000 on 1 June 2025. Payments in June: Jun 2 postage ₹120; Jun 4 bus fare ₹80; Jun 6 stationery ₹450; Jun 9 tea and snacks ₹260; Jun 12 courier ₹340; Jun 15 taxi fare ₹520; Jun 19 printer paper ₹600; Jun 22 refreshments for visitors ₹380; Jun 25 cleaning charges ₹300; Jun 28 auto fare ₹150.

docs.text:
Book Individual items posted to Total posted to Purchases book Credit of each supplier's account Debit of Purchases Account Sales book Debit of each customer's account Credit of Sales Account Purchases returns book Debit of each supplier's account Credit of Purchases Returns Account Sales returns book Credit of each customer's account Debit of Sales Returns Account Cash book (cash and bank columns) The opposite side of each account named (contra entries not posted) No total: the cash book is itself the cash and bank account Cash book (discount columns) Each customer's or supplier's account, with the cash Debit of Discount Allowed; credit of Discount Received Petty cash book None individually Each expense column total to the debit of its expense account

Key idea

Subsidiary books do not abandon double entry. They only change the order: personal accounts are posted item by item, and the matching nominal account (purchases, sales, returns, discounts, expenses) is posted once, with the period's total. The debits still equal the credits.

docs.title: 4.9 A note on indirect taxes
docs.text: In practice, invoices for sales and purchases carry indirect tax (in India, goods and services tax). When the business is registered for such a tax, tax collected on sales is not revenue of the business but a liability to the government, and tax paid on purchases can usually be set off against it. The subsidiary books therefore have extra columns for the tax, and the tax totals are posted to separate tax accounts, not to Sales and Purchases. The rates and the details of set-off depend on the law in force; the examples in this book leave tax out so that the accounting principles stand out clearly.

docs.title: 4.10 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The journal is divided into subsidiary books so that routine transactions are recorded quickly, posted in totals and checked separately.
  • The purchases book records credit purchases of goods; the sales book records credit sales of goods; both record amounts net of trade discount.
  • The purchases returns book (debit notes) and the sales returns book (credit notes) record returns.
  • The journal proper records everything else: opening, adjustment, transfer, closing and rectification entries, and credit dealings in assets.
  • The cash book is both a book of original entry and a ledger account. Contra entries between cash and bank are marked C and not posted. Discount columns are memorandum columns whose totals are posted.
  • The petty cash book, kept on the imprest system, records small payments; the amount spent is reimbursed each period and the expense column totals are posted.

A petty cashier works on an imprest of ₹3,000 a week. During one week she spends ₹420 on postage, ₹960 on conveyance and ₹735 on stationery. How much is in hand at the end of the week, and how much will the chief cashier pay her?

Spent: 420 + 960 + 735 = ₹2,115. In hand: 3,000 − 2,115 = ₹885. Reimbursement: ₹2,115, which restores the imprest to ₹3,000.

Exercise 5

Why are the discount columns of a cash book not balanced, while the cash and bank columns are?

The cash and bank columns are accounts: they record money held, so their balances are real amounts carried forward. docs.title: Chapter 2: The Accounting Equation
docs.text:
Every transaction keeps the two sides in balance

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. State the accounting equation and rearrange it to find any one of its terms.
  2. Explain why every transaction leaves the equation in balance.
  3. Show the effect of a series of transactions on assets, liabilities and capital in a table.
  4. Explain how revenue, expenses and drawings change capital, using the expanded equation.
  5. Prepare a simple balance sheet from the final balances.
  6. Find the profit of a period from the opening and closing capital.

docs.title: 2.1 Resources and claims
docs.text:
Look at any business at a moment in time and you can ask two questions about it. What does it have? Cash, goods, furniture, money owed to it by customers: these are its resources, its assets. Where did those resources come from? Some came from the owner, who put money in; the rest came from outsiders, who lent money or supplied goods on credit. Every rupee of resources has a source, and every source has a claim on the resources.

The claims of outsiders are liabilities. The claim of the owner is capital (also called owner's equity or net worth). Because every resource came from somewhere, the total of the resources must equal the total of the claims on them:

\[ \text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital} \]

This is the accounting equation. It is not a fact that has to be checked; it is true by construction, because capital is defined as whatever is left of the assets after the liabilities have been met. It is the direct consequence of the dual aspect concept of Chapter 1: every transaction has two sides, and recording both keeps the equation true.

docs.title: Three forms of the equation
docs.text:
The equation can be rearranged to find any one of its terms when the other two are known.

\[ \text{Capital} = \text{Assets} - \text{Liabilities} \] \[ \text{Liabilities} = \text{Assets} - \text{Capital} \]

The first rearrangement is especially useful: the owner's capital is what would be left for the owner if all the assets were turned into cash at their book values and all the liabilities were paid.

Example 2.1 Finding the missing term

Case Assets (₹) Liabilities (₹) Capital (₹) Working (a) 5,00,000 1,20,000 3,80,000 5,00,000 − 1,20,000 (b) 4,65,000 85,000 3,80,000 85,000 + 3,80,000 (c) 2,40,000 90,000 1,50,000 2,40,000 − 1,50,000

docs.title: 2.2 How transactions affect the equation
docs.text:
Every transaction changes at least two items, and it always changes them in a way that keeps the two sides equal. There are only a few patterns:

Pattern Effect on the equation Example One asset up, another asset down Total assets unchanged Buying furniture for cash Asset up, liability up Both sides rise by the same amount Buying goods on credit; taking a loan Asset down, liability down Both sides fall by the same amount Paying a creditor Asset up, capital up Both sides rise Owner brings in cash; earning revenue Asset down, capital down Both sides fall Paying an expense; owner withdraws cash One liability up, another down Right side unchanged A creditor's debt is converted into a loan Liability up, capital down Right side unchanged An expense is incurred but not yet paid

Table 2.1. The patterns by which a transaction can change the accounting equation.

Key idea

No transaction can change only one side of the equation by itself. Either both sides change by the same amount, or one side has an increase and a decrease of the same amount. That is why the equation always balances.

docs.title: 2.3 Revenue, expenses and drawings
docs.text:
Capital does not stay fixed after the owner's first investment. It changes for four reasons:

  • it increases when the owner brings in more money or goods (additional capital);
  • it increases when the business earns revenue;
  • it decreases when the business incurs expenses;
  • it decreases when the owner withdraws money or goods (drawings).

Revenue and expenses together make the profit or loss. So the capital at the end of a period is:

\[ \text{Closing capital} = \text{Opening capital} + \text{Additional capital} + \text{Profit} - \text{Drawings} \]

(with a loss subtracted instead of a profit added). Writing capital in full gives the expanded accounting equation:

\[ \text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Opening capital} + \text{Revenue} - \text{Expenses} - \text{Drawings} \]

Why do revenue and expenses belong to capital? Because the owner is entitled to whatever profit the business makes and bears whatever loss it suffers. When goods costing ₹30,000 are sold for ₹42,000 in cash, cash rises by ₹42,000, inventory falls by ₹30,000, and the net increase in assets of ₹12,000 belongs to the owner: capital rises by ₹12,000, the profit on the sale.

Caution

Drawings are not an expense. They reduce capital directly, but they are not costs of earning revenue, so they do not reduce profit. Paying the shop's rent is an expense; paying the owner's house rent from the shop's cash is drawings. Both reduce capital, but only the first reduces profit.

docs.title: 2.4 A worked example: Asha Stationers
docs.text:
The best way to see the equation at work is to follow a business through its first transactions. Asha opens a stationery shop, Asha Stationers, in April 2025.

Example 2.2 The transactions of Asha Stationers

  1. Asha starts the business with cash ₹1,50,000.
  2. She deposits ₹80,000 of the cash in a bank account in the name of the business.
  3. She buys furniture for ₹25,000, paying by cheque.
  4. She buys goods (stationery) for ₹60,000 on credit from Ravi Traders.
  5. She sells goods that cost ₹30,000 for ₹42,000 in cash.
  6. She sells goods that cost ₹20,000 to Kiran on credit for ₹27,000.
  7. She pays Ravi Traders ₹40,000 by cheque.
  8. Kiran pays ₹15,000 in cash.
  9. She pays the shop's rent of ₹6,000 in cash.
  10. She withdraws ₹5,000 in cash for personal use.
  11. She pays a salary of ₹8,000 to an assistant by cheque.

Analysis of each transaction.

No. Items affected Reasoning 1 Cash +1,50,000; Capital +1,50,000 The business receives cash and owes it to Asha as capital 2 Cash −80,000; Bank +80,000 One asset exchanged for another 3 Bank −25,000; Furniture +25,000 One asset exchanged for another 4 Inventory +60,000; Creditors +60,000 An asset is acquired and a liability is created 5 Cash +42,000; Inventory −30,000; Capital +12,000 Assets rise by 12,000 net; the profit belongs to the owner 6 Debtors +27,000; Inventory −20,000; Capital +7,000 Kiran now owes 27,000; profit 7,000 7 Bank −40,000; Creditors −40,000 An asset is used to pay a liability 8 Cash +15,000; Debtors −15,000 One asset exchanged for another 9 Cash −6,000; Capital −6,000 An expense reduces capital 10 Cash −5,000; Capital −5,000 Drawings reduce capital 11 Bank −8,000; Capital −8,000 An expense reduces capital

The equation after each transaction (amounts in ₹; the balance line shows the position after the transaction above it).

No. Cash Bank Inventory Debtors Furniture = Creditors Capital 1 +1,50,000 +1,50,000 Balance 1,50,000 0 0 0 0 = 0 1,50,000 2 −80,000 +80,000 Balance 70,000 80,000 0 0 0 = 0 1,50,000 3 −25,000 +25,000 Balance 70,000 55,000 0 0 25,000 = 0 1,50,000 4 +60,000 +60,000 Balance 70,000 55,000 60,000 0 25,000 = 60,000 1,50,000 5 +42,000 −30,000 +12,000 Balance 1,12,000 55,000 30,000 0 25,000 = 60,000 1,62,000 6 −20,000 +27,000 +7,000 Balance 1,12,000 55,000 10,000 27,000 25,000 = 60,000 1,69,000 7 −40,000 −40,000 Balance 1,12,000 15,000 10,000 27,000 25,000 = 20,000 1,69,000 8 +15,000 −15,000 Balance 1,27,000 15,000 10,000 12,000 25,000 = 20,000 1,69,000 9 −6,000 −6,000 Balance 1,21,000 15,000 10,000 12,000 25,000 = 20,000 1,63,000 10 −5,000 −5,000 Balance 1,16,000 15,000 10,000 12,000 25,000 = 20,000 1,58,000 11 −8,000 −8,000 Balance 1,16,000 7,000 10,000 12,000 25,000 = 20,000 1,50,000

Check of the final position.

Assets: 1,16,000 + 7,000 + 10,000 + 12,000 + 25,000 = ₹1,70,000.

Liabilities + Capital: 20,000 + 1,50,000 = ₹1,70,000.

The equation balances after every single transaction, as it must.

Notice that Asha's capital ends where it began, at ₹1,50,000. That is not because nothing happened: the business made a profit, and Asha withdrew exactly that much. The profit can be read from the capital column:

Item ₹ Profit on cash sale (transaction 5) 12,000 Profit on credit sale (transaction 6) 7,000 Gross profit on sales 19,000 Less: Rent (transaction 9) 6,000 Less: Salary (transaction 11) 8,000 Net profit 5,000

Table 2.2. The profit of Asha Stationers, taken from the capital column.

Capital therefore moved as follows: opening capital 1,50,000 + profit 5,000 − drawings 5,000 = closing capital 1,50,000.

Figure 2.1 The final position of Asha Stationers. A bar for the assets of Asha Stationers (cash 1,16,000, bank 7,000, inventory 10,000, debtors 12,000, furniture 25,000, total ₹1,70,000) stands level with a bar for the claims on them (creditors 20,000 and capital 1,50,000, total ₹1,70,000).

docs.title: 2.5 The balance sheet
docs.text:
The final balances of the table can be set out as a balance sheet: a statement of the assets, liabilities and capital of the business at a date. The traditional form used in India places capital and liabilities on the left and assets on the right; the two totals must agree. (Chapter 8 develops the balance sheet fully, and Chapter 11 shows the vertical form used by companies.)

Example 2.3 Balance sheet of Asha Stationers

Balance Sheet of Asha Stationers as at 30 April 2025

Liabilities and capital ₹ Assets ₹ Capital (1,50,000 + profit 5,000 − drawings 5,000) 1,50,000 Furniture 25,000 Creditors 20,000 Inventory 10,000 Debtors 12,000 Cash at bank 7,000 Cash in hand 1,16,000 Total 1,70,000 Total 1,70,000

The working shown against capital tells the reader how the closing capital was reached: opening capital, plus the profit of the period, less the owner's drawings.

The balance sheet is a snapshot: it describes the position at one moment. The profit of ₹5,000 describes what happened over a period. Chapter 8 presents the profit in a separate statement, the trading and profit and loss account, and links the two.

docs.title: 2.6 Finding profit from capital
docs.text:
The expanded equation gives a way to find the profit of a period even when detailed records have not been kept. If the capital at the beginning and at the end of a period is known (each found as assets minus liabilities), then rearranging the capital formula gives:

\[ \text{Profit} = \text{Closing capital} - \text{Opening capital} + \text{Drawings} - \text{Additional capital} \]

Drawings are added back because they reduced the closing capital without being a loss. Additional capital is deducted because it increased the closing capital without being a profit.

Example 2.4 Profit from opening and closing capital

A trader keeps incomplete records. On 1 April 2025 her capital was ₹3,20,000. On 31 March 2026 her business assets were ₹5,10,000 and her business liabilities ₹1,30,000. During the year she withdrew ₹4,000 a month for household expenses and brought in ₹20,000 from a personal fixed deposit.

Item ₹ Closing capital (5,10,000 − 1,30,000) 3,80,000 Add: Drawings (4,000 × 12) 48,000 4,28,000 Less: Additional capital 20,000 Adjusted closing capital 4,08,000 Less: Opening capital 3,20,000 Profit for the year 88,000

Check: 3,20,000 + 20,000 + 88,000 − 48,000 = 3,80,000, which is the closing capital.

This method, sometimes called the net worth method or the statement of affairs method, finds the total profit but not how it was earned: it gives no figure for sales, gross profit or any expense. That is its weakness, and the reason double-entry records (Chapter 3) are kept.

docs.title: 2.7 From the equation to debit and credit
docs.text:
Recording every transaction in a table with one column per item works for eleven transactions but not for eleven thousand. Real businesses have hundreds of items, each needing its own record. The solution, developed over centuries, is to give each item its own account, with two sides: one for increases and one for decreases. The left side of an account is called the debit side and the right side the credit side.

The equation decides which side is which. Assets are on the left of the equation, so increases in assets are recorded on the left (debit) side of their accounts. Liabilities and capital are on the right of the equation, so increases in them are recorded on the right (credit) side. Since revenue increases capital, revenue is credited; since expenses and drawings decrease capital, they are debited.

Type of account Increase recorded as Decrease recorded as Asset Debit Credit Liability Credit Debit Capital Credit Debit Revenue (income) Credit Debit Expense Debit Credit Drawings Debit Credit

Table 2.3. The direction of increase for each type of account, read off the accounting equation.

Because every transaction keeps the equation in balance, every transaction must produce debits and credits of equal total. That is the principle of double entry, the subject of the next chapter.

Example 2.5 Reading three transactions as debits and credits

Transaction Debit Credit Why Asha starts with cash ₹1,50,000 Cash ₹1,50,000 Capital ₹1,50,000 Asset up (debit); capital up (credit) Buys goods on credit ₹60,000 Purchases (goods) ₹60,000 Ravi Traders ₹60,000 Goods up (debit); liability up (credit) Pays rent ₹6,000 in cash Rent ₹6,000 Cash ₹6,000 Expense up (debit); asset down (credit)

docs.title: 2.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Assets are the resources of a business; liabilities are outsiders' claims on them and capital is the owner's claim. Assets = Liabilities + Capital, always.
  • Capital = Assets − Liabilities; Liabilities = Assets − Capital.
  • Every transaction either changes both sides by the same amount or changes one side by equal and opposite amounts, so the equation always balances.
  • Revenue increases capital; expenses and drawings decrease it. Closing capital = Opening capital + Additional capital + Profit − Drawings.
  • The balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and capital at a date; its two sides agree.
  • Profit = Closing capital − Opening capital + Drawings − Additional capital.
  • Increases in assets, expenses and drawings are debits; increases in liabilities, capital and revenue are credits.

docs.title: 2.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Find the missing figure in each case: (a) assets ₹7,50,000, liabilities ₹2,10,000; capital? (b) capital ₹4,20,000, liabilities ₹1,35,000; assets? (c) assets ₹3,60,000, capital ₹2,95,000; liabilities?

Answer

(a) Capital = 7,50,000 − 2,10,000 = ₹5,40,000. (b) Assets = 1,35,000 + 4,20,000 = ₹5,55,000. (c) Liabilities = 3,60,000 − 2,95,000 = ₹65,000.

Exercise 2

Show the effect on the accounting equation of each transaction of Raj's new business, and the final position: (1) started with cash ₹2,00,000; (2) bought machinery for cash ₹70,000; (3) bought goods on credit from Mohan ₹50,000; (4) sold goods costing ₹30,000 for ₹45,000 on credit to Neha; (5) paid Mohan ₹35,000 in cash; (6) received ₹25,000 from Neha; (7) paid wages ₹4,000; (8) withdrew ₹3,000 for personal use.

Answer No. Cash Inventory Debtors Machinery = Creditors Capital 1 +2,00,000 +2,00,000 2 −70,000 +70,000 3 +50,000 +50,000 4 −30,000 +45,000 +15,000 5 −35,000 −35,000 6 +25,000 −25,000 7 −4,000 −4,000 8 −3,000 −3,000 Final 1,13,000 20,000 20,000 70,000 = 15,000 2,08,000

Assets: 1,13,000 + 20,000 + 20,000 + 70,000 = ₹2,23,000. Liabilities + Capital: 15,000 + 2,08,000 = ₹2,23,000. Profit = 15,000 − 4,000 = ₹11,000; capital = 2,00,000 + 11,000 − 3,000 = ₹2,08,000.

Exercise 3

For each transaction, say whether total assets increase, decrease or stay the same: (a) bought furniture for cash; (b) took a bank loan; (c) paid a creditor; (d) owner withdrew cash; (e) received cash from a debtor; (f) bought goods on credit.

Answer

(a) same (one asset for another); (b) increase (cash up, liability up); (c) decrease (cash down, liability down); (d) decrease (cash down, capital down); (e) same (one asset for another); (f) increase (inventory up, liability up).

Exercise 4

A shopkeeper's capital was ₹2,50,000 on 1 April 2025. On 31 March 2026 his assets were ₹4,30,000 and his liabilities ₹1,10,000. During the year he introduced further capital of ₹30,000 and withdrew ₹60,000. Find his profit or loss.

Answer

Closing capital = 4,30,000 − 1,10,000 = ₹3,20,000. Profit = 3,20,000 − 2,50,000 + 60,000 − 30,000 = ₹1,00,000. Check: 2,50,000 + 30,000 + 1,00,000 − 60,000 = 3,20,000.

Exercise 5

A business has assets of ₹6,00,000 and liabilities of ₹2,00,000. An expense of ₹10,000 is incurred but not yet paid. Show the effect on the equation and give the new totals.

Answer

Liabilities (outstanding expense) rise by ₹10,000 and capital falls by ₹10,000; assets are unchanged. Before: 6,00,000 = 2,00,000 + 4,00,000. After: 6,00,000 = 2,10,000 + 3,90,000. The right side has an equal increase and decrease.

Exercise 6

Is it possible for capital to be negative? What would it mean?

Answer

Yes. If liabilities exceed assets, Capital = Assets − Liabilities is negative. It means that the business owes outsiders more than it owns, usually because of accumulated losses or heavy drawings; the owner would have to pay in money from outside to settle all the debts.

docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 2

Exercise 1

Assets are ₹8,00,000 and liabilities ₹2,50,000. What is the capital, in rupees?

Answer

550000 / 5,50,000 / ₹5,50,000 / 550,000

Exercise 2

Which transaction increases both assets and liabilities?

  1. Paying a creditor
  2. Buying goods on credit
  3. Buying furniture for cash
  4. The owner withdrawing cash
Answer

Buying goods on credit

Exercise 3

Goods costing ₹10,000 are sold for ₹13,000 in cash. By how much does capital change?

  1. Increases by ₹13,000
  2. Increases by ₹3,000
  3. Decreases by ₹10,000
  4. Does not change
Answer

Increases by ₹3,000

Cash rises by 13,000 and inventory falls by 10,000; the net gain of 3,000 is profit, which belongs to the owner.

Exercise 4

Drawings of the owner

  1. reduce profit and capital
  2. reduce capital but not profit
  3. reduce profit but not capital
  4. increase liabilities
Answer

reduce capital but not profit

Exercise 5

Opening capital ₹1,00,000; closing capital ₹1,30,000; drawings ₹20,000; no additional capital. What is the profit, in rupees?

Answer

50000 / 50,000 / ₹50,000

1,30,000 − 1,00,000 + 20,000 = 50,000.

Exercise 6

An increase in an expense account is recorded as a

  1. debit
  2. credit
Answer

debit

Expenses reduce capital, and decreases in capital are debits.
